t.omori katsuyama stone circle@40.7,140.4:
Over three thousand years ago, Jomon people in northern Japan arranged stones into circles on a terrace at the foot of Mount Iwaki, the conical volcano that dominates the Tsugaru plain in Aomori prefecture. The Omori Katsuyama stone circle is one of these monuments, with a ring of standing and placed stones that may have been used for rituals, burials or marking the seasons. It is part of the Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2021, which celebrates a culture of hunter-gatherers who settled in permanent villages and made pottery for over ten thousand years.

The site is quiet and open, with views toward Iwaki and the surrounding countryside. The Jomon people lived from fishing, hunting and gathering nuts, and their pottery, decorated with rope patterns, gave the period its name. Nearby, Sannai-Maruyama in Aomori city is the largest Jomon site and has a museum and reconstructed buildings.

The Tsugaru plain is apple country. Hirosaki, a castle town of over one hundred and seventy thousand people, is the centre of Japan's apple production, and in autumn the orchards are full of red fruit. Hirosaki castle is famous for its cherry blossoms in late April and early May. The town has fuel, restaurants and accommodation.

For riders, the Iwaki Skyline is a toll road that climbs the volcano in dozens of hairpins to a car park, from where a chairlift and path lead to the summit. The roads around the plain are flat and quiet, and the coast to the west, along the Sea of Japan, offers dramatic cliffs and the Shirakami mountains, a UNESCO-listed beech forest. Winters here are snowy and long, so the riding season runs from late spring to autumn. Try the local apple juice, cider and pie, and the hearty soups of Tsugaru.
t.sanctuary of asklepios at epidaurus@37.6:
Drop a coin in the centre of the orchestra at Epidaurus and people sitting in the top row, fifty-odd rows above, will hear it. The theatre of the sanctuary of Asklepios, built in the fourth century BC, is famous for its acoustics and its almost perfect state of preservation, and it still hosts performances of ancient drama during the summer festival. But the theatre was only part of the sanctuary. Epidaurus was the most famous healing centre of the ancient Greek world, where the sick came to sleep in the sacred buildings and hope that the god Asklepios would visit them in a dream with a cure.

The site lies in a green valley of the Argolid, surrounded by pine-covered hills, near the village of Ligourio. The ruins of the sanctuary include temples, a stadium, a gymnasium and the mysterious Tholos, a circular building whose underground labyrinth may have housed sacred snakes. A museum displays inscriptions recording the miraculous cures. On the coast nearby, Palaia Epidavros has a smaller theatre by the sea, a harbour and a sunken town visible under the water.

The riding in the Argolid is a delight. The roads from Nafplio pass through orange groves and olive trees, and then climb into the hills with long sweeping bends and views across the Saronic Gulf. The coast road toward Palaia Epidavros and on to the Methana peninsula is twisty and beautiful, with small coves and blue water at every turn. Summer heat is intense, so ride early and late. Traffic is light, except on festival nights, when everyone heads for the theatre. Watch for gravel in the corners and goats in the road.

Ligourio has fuel, cafés and tavernas; Nafplio, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the main town of the area, a beautiful Venetian port with a fortress above. Greek food here means grilled meats, fresh fish, salads and the excellent local oranges. Visit the sanctuary early in the morning before the coaches arrive, and climb to the top row of the theatre. Sit quietly, and listen: the sound of someone talking in the orchestra comes up clear and close, as it did for audiences two and a half thousand years ago.
t.oyu stone circles@40.3,140.8:
Two great rings of river stones lie in a quiet field on a plateau near Kazuno, in the north of Akita prefecture, and at the heart of each stands a small arrangement of upright stones that has been called a sundial. The Ōyu Stone Circles, known as Manza and Nonakadō, were built by the Jōmon people around four thousand years ago, and they are the largest stone circles in Japan. Beneath and around them archaeologists have found graves, suggesting they were places of burial and ceremony. Some researchers believe the circles were aligned with the setting sun at the summer solstice. Since 2021 they have formed part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Jōmon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan.

The Jōmon were hunter-gatherers who lived in Japan for over ten thousand years, famous for their elaborate cord-marked pottery, and they built settlements, shell mounds and ritual sites across the north of the country. A museum on site displays finds and explains their way of life, and reconstructed buildings give a sense of what a village might have looked like.

The area around Kazuno is mountainous and green, with rice fields in the valleys and thick forests on the slopes. Winters are long and snowy; summers are short and warm. The region is known for its hot springs and for the cuisine of Akita: kiritanpo, rice pounded and grilled on cedar sticks, then simmered in a hot pot with chicken, and the local Hinai chicken from Ōdate.

For riders, the area is a gateway to some of the best roads in northern Japan. To the north lies Lake Towada, a large caldera lake surrounded by forest, with roads that wind along its shores and down the beautiful Oirase stream. To the south, the Hachimantai Aspite Line climbs over the volcanic plateau of Hachimantai, with steaming vents, alpine meadows and views; it is closed in winter and opens in spring between walls of snow. Surfaces are generally excellent, and traffic is light outside holidays.

Kazuno has fuel, shops and restaurants, and there are hot spring hotels in the area. Fuel stations in the mountains are scarce, so fill up in town. Autumn foliage here is superb, usually in October; in spring, cherry blossoms arrive later than in the south, in late April or early May.
t.minoan palatial centres@35.2,24.9:
High on the northern flank of Psiloritis, the mountain the ancients called Ida, the road from Anogeia climbs onto a stony plateau, and at around 1,200 metres you come upon a Minoan building standing alone among the scrub and grazing goats. This is Zominthos, a large Bronze Age complex that excavations have shown to be more than a mountain shelter: it had dozens of rooms, workshops and storage spaces, and it sat on the ancient route toward the sacred Idaean Cave, where myth says Zeus was raised. In 2025 it was included with Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and others among the Minoan Palatial Centres listed by UNESCO, which gives you an idea of its importance.

Anogeia, a few kilometres below, is a village with a fierce reputation. During the Second World War it supported the resistance and was implicated in the 1944 abduction of the German commander General Kreipe, and in reprisal the occupying forces destroyed the village and killed many of its men. It was rebuilt and remains proudly Cretan, known for its music, especially the lyra, its woven textiles and its shepherding tradition. The local food is mountain food: lamb, goat, graviera cheese and thick yoghurt, with raki to finish.

The ride up is the reason most bikers come. From Anogeia the road winds steadily upward through rocky hillsides with long, flowing bends and wide views back toward the north coast, then crosses the plateau toward the Nida basin beneath the summit of Psiloritis. The surface is generally decent but can be broken in places, with gravel, fallen stones and the occasional goat or sheep standing exactly where you want to be. Wind on the plateau can be strong and cold even in summer, and snow closes the upper road in winter. Late afternoon light here is extraordinary, turning the limestone gold.

For fuel, rely on Anogeia or the larger villages and towns below; nothing is available on the plateau, and Gazi near Heraklion is the nearest sizeable town. Anogeia has tavernas and cafés where the old men play tavli and the coffee is strong. Bring water up the mountain, park near the site, and walk around the excavated rooms, imagining Minoan pilgrims pausing here on their way to the cave. Then continue to the Nida plateau if the weather allows, because the view of the summit from there is worth every curve.
t.goshono site@40.2,141.3:
In the hills of northern Iwate, a short ride from the town of Ichinohe, a group of round houses with grass-covered roofs sits in a quiet clearing among cedar and broadleaf woods. They look like something out of a fairy tale, low mounds with doorways and smoke holes, and they are reconstructions of pit dwellings from the Jomon period, the long prehistoric era of hunter-gatherers who lived in Japan from around fifteen thousand years ago until the arrival of rice farming. The Goshono site was a large settlement in the middle Jomon period, and excavations found that some houses here were roofed with earth rather than thatch, which is why the reconstructions look the way they do. Since 2021 it has been one of the components of the World Heritage site of the Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan.

The Jomon people are famous for their pottery, decorated with cord-marked patterns from which the period takes its name, and for their strange, goggle-eyed clay figurines. They lived in a rich forest and coastal environment, gathering chestnuts and walnuts, fishing and hunting, and they built permanent villages, stone circles and burial grounds without agriculture as we know it. The museum at Goshono explains this well, and the site itself, with its woods and open meadow, gives a sense of the landscape they knew.

The riding in this part of northern Tohoku is gentle and green. The Mabechi river valley runs north through Ichinohe toward Hachinohe and the Pacific, and the roads follow it through rice paddies, small villages and wooded hills, with easy bends and light traffic. Head west into the mountains toward Lake Towada and Hachimantai and the roads become more serious, climbing through beech forests with tight hairpins and splendid views. Autumn colours here are spectacular in October, but winter brings deep snow, and mountain roads close.

Ichinohe is a small town with fuel, convenience stores and a few restaurants, so you are well covered. Northern Iwate is known for its buckwheat noodles and for hearty local dishes; try a bowl of soba or a plate of local beef if you see it on a menu. Leave the bike in the site car park, walk among the reconstructed houses, and step inside one if you can. It is dark, cool and smells of earth and smoke, and it is easy to imagine a family sitting around the fire five thousand years ago.
t.shirakami sanchi@40.5,140.1:
Shirakami-Sanchi is one of the largest remaining virgin beech forests in East Asia, a vast tract of mountains straddling the border between Aomori and Akita prefectures in northern Honshu. It joined the World Heritage list in 1993, one of Japan's first natural sites, and the core area is left almost untouched, with no roads or facilities. Siebold's beech, a species found only in Japan, dominates the forest, and it shelters black bears, Japanese serows, golden eagles and the black woodpecker. The trees are at their most beautiful in autumn, when they turn gold and copper, and in spring when the new leaves are a startling pale green.

People have lived around these mountains for thousands of years, and the region is dotted with Jomon sites, including stone circles in the Akita and Aomori countryside. The mountain villages have a tradition of matagi hunters, who hunted bears and other game in the forest under strict rules and rituals. Today the forest is a place for hiking, with trails on the periphery leading to waterfalls, lakes and viewpoints, the best known being the Juniko lakes on the western side and the Anmon falls on the northern side.

The southern approach, from Noshiro or Takanosu in Akita, follows river valleys into the hills on roads that become narrower and twistier as they climb. The western coast road along the Sea of Japan, on the Gono line side, is a superb ride, with rugged cliffs, fishing villages and views of the mountains rising inland. Roads inside the forest area are few and some are unpaved or closed in winter, which here lasts a long time, with heavy snow from December to April. Summer can be humid, and sudden heavy rain is common. Watch for wildlife on the road, especially at dusk.

Noshiro, with around fifty thousand people, is the nearest larger town on the Akita side and has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Hirosaki is the main town on the Aomori side. Smaller villages around the edges have convenience stores and occasional petrol stations, but plan ahead. Pack water and snacks, choose a short trail to a waterfall or viewpoint, and spend an hour among the beeches. The silence and the green light under the canopy are quite something.
t.butrint@39.7,20.0:
At the southern tip of Albania, on a wooded headland between a lagoon and the narrow Vivari channel, the ruins of Butrint have been layering up for close to three thousand years. Greek colonists from Corfu, just across the strait, built a sanctuary and a theatre here; the Romans made it a colony and added baths, an aqueduct and villas; the Byzantines raised a great baptistery with a mosaic floor of birds and animals; and the Venetians left a fortified tower and a triangular castle by the water. Wandering the shaded paths among laurel and eucalyptus, you move from one century to the next in a few steps, with frogs croaking in the flooded parts of the agora and the lagoon glinting through the trees. The site has been on the UNESCO list since 1992 and is the heart of a national park.

The wetlands around the lagoon are rich in birds, from herons and egrets to cormorants, and in spring the marshes are noisy with frogs and loud with nightingales. Mussel farms dot Lake Butrint, and the local seafood, especially mussels, is excellent. A small cable ferry crosses the Vivari channel just beside the ruins, carrying vehicles across toward the Greek border region, which turns the area into a handy shortcut as well as a destination.

The ride down from Sarandë is short and pleasant, running past the beach resort of Ksamil with its small islands and turquoise water, then through olive groves and along the edge of the lagoon. The road is generally in good condition, but summer traffic can be heavy, and Albanian driving habits take some getting used to: overtaking on blind bends, sudden stops and pedestrians walking along the road. Head inland from Sarandë and the roads climb over the hills toward the Blue Eye spring and the Drino valley, with curves and views in every direction. Spring and early autumn are ideal; high summer is hot and crowded.

Sarandë, about fourteen kilometres away, has fuel, cafés, restaurants and accommodation, and Ksamil has plenty of seasonal places to eat. Try grilled fish, mussels from the lake, or byrek, a flaky pie with cheese or spinach. There is an entry fee, and an early arrival beats both the heat and the tour groups coming over from Corfu by boat. Bring water and comfortable shoes, walk the full loop to the Venetian castle, and look across the channel at the hills of Greece.
t.jomon prehistoric sites in northern japa:
At the foot of Mount Iwaki, the solitary volcano that rises above the Tsugaru plain in Aomori prefecture, there is a flat terrace where people of the Jomon period laid out a large oval ring of stones a few thousand years ago. The Omori Katsuyama stone circle is one of the sites that make up the Jomon Prehistoric Sites of Northern Japan, listed by UNESCO in 2021, and it is a quiet, grassy place where you can stand in the middle and look straight up at the mountain the builders must have looked at every day.

The Jomon were hunter-gatherers who lived in settled villages for more than ten thousand years, fishing, collecting nuts and making some of the oldest pottery in the world, decorated with cord-marked patterns that gave the culture its name. Stone circles such as this one belong to the later part of the period and seem to have been places of ritual and burial. Their exact meaning is still debated, which suits the atmosphere: there are no reconstructed buildings, just the stones, the grass and the view.

The site lies within Hirosaki city, the historic castle town of the Tsugaru domain, known for its cherry blossoms in late April and for apples, which are grown in orchards all around the base of the mountain. In autumn the trees are heavy with fruit and the roadside stands sell them by the bag.

For riders, the great attraction nearby is the Tsugaru Iwaki Skyline, a toll road that climbs the flank of Mount Iwaki through a famous sequence of sixty-nine numbered hairpins to a car park at around the eighth station, from where a lift and a path go on toward the summit. It is a tight, steep, technical climb with superb views across the plain to the Sea of Japan, and it is closed in winter, usually from autumn to spring because of the heavy snow; check the opening dates before you go. The roads around the mountain through the orchards are gentle and pretty, and the coast road on the west side is wild and empty.

Fuel is easy in Hirosaki, and the larger towns of Goshogawara and Aomori are both within half an hour. Hirosaki's cafés and noodle shops make a good base, and the castle park is a lovely place to sit after a day in the saddle.
t.archaeological site of mystras@37.1,22.4:
Mystras is a whole Byzantine city draped down a steep hillside, a few kilometres west of modern Sparta, at the foot of the Taygetos mountains. It began in 1249, when William II of Villehardouin, a Frankish prince ruling the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade, built a castle on the summit. Within a few years the Byzantines had taken it back, and Mystras grew into the capital of the Despotate of the Morea, a centre of learning and art in the last centuries of the empire. The philosopher Gemistos Plethon taught here, and in 1449 Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last Byzantine emperor, was crowned here before leaving for Constantinople, where he died when the city fell in 1453.

Today the site is a maze of ruined houses, palaces, churches and monasteries, connected by steep paths and stairways. The churches hold some of the finest late Byzantine frescoes in Greece, delicate and full of movement. The Pantanassa convent is still inhabited by a few nuns, and its courtyard, with flowers and a view across the plain, is a place of calm. The climb from the lower gate to the castle on the summit is long and steep; there is an upper entrance, so plan accordingly, and carry water in summer.

The plain below is a sea of orange and olive groves, and in spring the scent of blossom fills the air. Sparta is a modern town, rebuilt in the nineteenth century on a grid plan, with little left of the ancient city, but it has fuel, garages, cafés and restaurants, and an olive oil museum.

The ride from Sparta to Kalamata over the Taygetos through the Langada gorge is one of the great roads of Greece. It climbs from the plain into the mountains in a long series of bends, then threads through the gorge, with cliffs rising on both sides and pine and fir trees clinging to the rock, before descending in a cascade of hairpins towards the Messinian Gulf. The surface is generally decent but can be broken in places, and rockfalls are possible after rain. Take your time.

Go in spring or autumn. Summer heat in the Laconian plain is intense, and Mystras offers little shade. On a clear day in April, with snow still on the Taygetos summits and the orange trees in flower, it is unforgettable.
t.kamegaoka burial site@40.9,140.3:
In 1887, a farmer digging in the fields near Kamegaoka, in the Tsugaru region of northern Honshu, found a strange clay figure: a stocky body covered with patterns and a face dominated by huge eyes like snow goggles. The shakōki-dogū, the goggle-eyed figurine, became one of the most famous objects of the Jōmon culture, the hunter-gatherers who lived in Japan for more than ten thousand years and made some of the oldest pottery in the world. Kamegaoka was a burial and settlement site of the final Jōmon period, about three thousand years ago, and it has yielded lacquerware, pottery and figurines of remarkable sophistication. It is part of the Jōmon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The site itself is a quiet field on a low terrace, with a small monument and a statue of the figurine. More striking is the railway station of Kizukuri, in the nearby town of Tsugaru, whose façade is a giant replica of the goggle-eyed figure, with eyes that light up when trains arrive. It is one of the oddest buildings in Japan, and locals are rather fond of it.

The Tsugaru plain is a broad, fertile landscape of rice fields and apple orchards, framed by the perfect volcanic cone of Mount Iwaki, the local Fuji. Aomori prefecture produces more apples than any other in Japan, and in autumn the orchards are heavy with red fruit. To the west, the Shichiri-Nagahama coast runs along the Sea of Japan, with dunes and pine forests, and Lake Jūsan, a brackish lagoon nearby, is famous for its clams.

The riding is relaxed. The roads across the plain are straight and flat, with little traffic, and the coast road along the Sea of Japan is pleasant, with sea views and fresh wind. For more challenge, the Iwaki Skyline, a toll road climbing the flank of Mount Iwaki in dozens of hairpins, is a classic, open in the warmer months, with spectacular views from the top. Further south, the Shirakami mountains, with their ancient beech forests, offer wild, winding roads.

Goshogawara and the town of Tsugaru have fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. Winters here are long and very snowy; the riding season runs from spring to autumn. Try the local soba, or a bowl of scallops from Mutsu Bay.
t.komakino stone circle@40.7,140.7:
Four thousand years ago, someone on this hillside in northern Honshu lined up stones in a ring and built another ring around it, and they did it carefully enough that the circles are still there. Komakino is a Jōmon stone circle, from the hunter-gatherer people who lived in Japan long before rice farming, and it is one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of Jōmon prehistoric sites in northern Japan, added in 2021. The arrangement is quite small and elegant, a double ring of river stones in a grassy field, and nobody knows for sure what it was for. Graves, ceremonies and a calendar of the seasons are all guesses, and it is better to stand there and hold the question than to pretend to an answer.

It is close to Sannai-Maruyama, the great settlement site on the edge of Aomori city, where you can walk through reconstructed longhouses and a huge six-pillar tower and see how these people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering chestnuts. Together the two places show that northern Japan had a long and settled culture, rich enough to build monuments, many thousands of years before the first emperors.

Aomori is a city of nearly three hundred thousand with every service, and Namioka, a smaller town to the south-west, is quiet and rural, with apple orchards all around. Aomori is Japan's great apple region, and in late summer and autumn the roadside stalls sell fruit, juice and apple pies. Fuel is easy in the city and in the larger towns along the main roads, but remote areas have fewer pumps.

The riding is worth the journey. Just south of the city the Hakkōda mountains rise out of beech forest, and the road over them, with its views, volcanic scenery and long gentle bends, is one of the best in the north. It is closed by deep snow in winter, and opens in spring, when walls of snow still line the road in April. Beyond are Lake Towada and the Oirase stream, one of the loveliest forest roads in Japan, especially in October, when the maples turn red. Summers are cool, mist is common, and the weather can change quickly on the high ground, so bring a layer.
t.kitakogane site@42.4,140.9:
Hokkaido does not usually come to mind when people talk about ancient Japan, yet the shell heaps around Uchiura Bay are some of the oldest signs of settled life in the archipelago. Kitakogane sits on the edge of the bay near Date, roughly halfway between Muroran and the volcanic country around Lake Toya. The Jomon people who lived here gathered shellfish, hunted deer and fished, and they threw the shells onto the same pile for centuries, which is why a modern visitor can read a kitchen midden like a diary. It belongs to the group of northern Jomon sites that UNESCO listed in 2021.

What survives is subtle. The shell mound is a gentle mound, not a monument, and there is a small museum nearby that explains what the shells, stone tools and burial remains tell us. Early Jomon people were not nomads in the way the textbooks used to say; they lived in villages and kept their dead in ordered places, and some of the oldest evidence in Hokkaido comes from sites like this one. Visit with the right expectations and it becomes moving rather than disappointing: this is a place where the Pacific has been feeding people for several thousand years.

The coast road along Route 37 is easy and pleasant riding, with long, gentle bends along the water and views across Funka Bay toward the Shiribeshi mountains when the weather behaves. Fog rolls in from the sea in early summer and can turn a bright morning into a grey one in minutes, so wear something warm. The bay is also a working fishery, and the scallops here are famous, so a seafood lunch in Date or Muroran is a reasonable priority. Muroran, to the east, is a steel and port city with a surprisingly dramatic coastline, including the Chikyu-misaki headland, which is worth a detour.

The volcanic backdrop is hard to miss. Mount Usu erupted in 2000 and again in the 1970s, and the lava domes and steaming scars are still visible around Lake Toya. Date has fuel and shops in plenty. Winters are long and snowy, so this is a ride for June through October.
t.lorne@-38.5,144.0:
Lorne is where the Great Ocean Road stops being a seaside drive and starts behaving like a mountain road. The town sits on Louttit Bay with the Otway Ranges standing right behind it, steep and thick with eucalypt, tree ferns and the odd waterfall. About twelve hundred people live here, a number that swells enormously in the Australian summer holidays, when Melbourne decamps to the beach and the main street fills with surfboards and ice cream.

For a rider, Lorne is the natural place to eat. The strip along Mountjoy Parade has bakeries, cafes and fish and chips, and the pier is a good place for a coffee with a view of the bay. There is a fuel station in town, which matters because the road beyond is long, and the nearest other sizeable town back along the coast is Anglesea. Weekends and school holidays are busy, and parking a bike is easier than parking a car, though a sand-covered bay can be tricky underfoot.

The Great Ocean Road itself was built between 1919 and 1932 by returned soldiers from the First World War, as a memorial to those who did not come home. They worked with picks, shovels and wheelbarrows on a cliff face that drops straight into Bass Strait, and you can feel the difficulty in how the road clings to the rock. West of Lorne the bends tighten around Cape Patton, and the sea shows up and vanishes with every corner. Speed limits here are enforced seriously, and tour coaches are slow, so patience is part of the deal.

Inland from the town the Otway rainforest has real depth. Erskine Falls is a short drive away, and the forest holds mountain ash, myrtle beech and ferns that look like they belong in the Jurassic. Koalas sleep in the trees, kookaburras laugh at dawn, and the air smells of wet bark and salt. Early morning is the best time to see the coast before the traffic builds, and autumn is a lovely season when the summer crowds have gone but the weather often stays mild.
t.twelve apostles@-38.7,143.1:
Everyone calls them the Twelve Apostles, which is generous. There were never twelve, and the original name was the Sow and Piglets, a rather less holy image that tourism officials decided to retire. Today about eight limestone stacks stand in the surf off Port Campbell National Park, and one collapsed in 2005 in front of a crowd of onlookers. The cliffs are made of soft limestone, and the Southern Ocean is working on them constantly, so the view is never the same twice.

The stacks form because waves cut caves into headlands, the caves become arches, and the arches fall to leave isolated pillars. Eventually the pillars fall too. It is a process that is visible in a lifetime, and this stretch is called the Shipwreck Coast for a reason. A short drive west, Loch Ard Gorge marks the site where the clipper Loch Ard struck the cliffs in 1878, and only two young people survived, Tom Pearce and Eva Carmichael.

For riders, the Apostles are the highlight of the Great Ocean Road, and also its most crowded point. The viewing platforms are reached by a walkway from a big car park, and the midday crowds can be thick with tour buses and selfie sticks. Go at sunrise or an hour before sunset, when the stone glows and the visitors are fewer. The road here is mostly straight and open, running across wind-bent coastal heath, and gusts from the southwest can hit hard on the exposed stretches. A windproof layer is essential even in summer, since the temperature can drop abruptly.

The nearest big services are at Port Campbell, a small seaside village a few kilometres along the coast, while Timboon and Cobden inland are quieter dairy towns that also have fuel. Cobden is known for cheese and Timboon for whisky made at a local distillery. Watch for little penguins, which nest along parts of this coast, and for wildlife on the road at dusk, when wallabies and kangaroos are most active. Let the ocean do the talking.
t.torquay@-38.3,144.3:
Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road begins, or ends, depending on which way you ride. It is a town of about thirteen thousand people on the edge of Bass Strait, and it has a reputation that has little to do with motorcycles: this is the capital of Australian surfing. Bells Beach, a few minutes down the coast, hosts one of the world's oldest surf competitions, held every Easter, and the town gave birth to brands such as Rip Curl and Quiksilver that have since gone global. Surf World, the museum in town, tells the story with boards, photographs and a lot of sun-bleached nostalgia.

Coming back to Torquay at the end of a day on the coast is a pleasant thing. The town has everything a rider needs: fuel at several stations, supermarkets, cafes, and motels and holiday flats in all sizes. Its main street has surf shops and bakeries, and the esplanade lets you wander along the beach with a coffee and watch the surfers in their wetsuits. Jan Juc, a few kilometres away, is another surfing village that is quieter and more residential.

The riding into Torquay depends on the direction you travel. From Anglesea the road runs through low coastal scrub and heath, with the sea on one side and a few breaks in the vegetation where beaches appear. It is a fine road on a good day, but the traffic is thick at weekends, and the surface can be sandy where drifts cross it. Coming from Melbourne, the main road passes Geelong and the long suburban fringe, which is not exciting but is fast. The key is to avoid peak traffic on Friday evenings and Sunday afternoons.

Weather is changeable, as in all of Victoria, and the wind is a factor. The water is cold, even in summer, and the surf breaks come from big Southern Ocean swells. Sunset over the bay, with the light turning pink on the cliffs, makes a decent end to a ride. Have a meal, take the gear off and leave the road until tomorrow.
t.cape otway@-38.9,143.5:
The lighthouse at Cape Otway has been guiding ships through Bass Strait since 1848, and it is the oldest surviving lighthouse on the Australian mainland. The cape is the point where the Otway Ranges meet the sea, and it is where the Southern Ocean and Bass Strait collide, which makes the water among the roughest in the world. Hundreds of ships were wrecked along this stretch, and the lighthouse was built because too many had gone down with their cargo and crew.

To reach it you leave the Great Ocean Road and take a side road of about twelve kilometres through the forest, a pretty ride through tall eucalypts and manna gums. This is koala country, and you will often see them in the trees beside the road, sitting in forks like furry bags. The surface is paved, narrow and often busy with tour buses and rental cars, so keep your speed down, and watch for wildlife on the road, especially at dawn and dusk.

The wider region is a mix of rainforest and heath. Mountain ash, among the tallest flowering trees on earth, grows in the gullies, with tree ferns and mosses beneath, and the soil is rich enough to hold glow-worm colonies in places like Melba Gully. Closer to the coast, the vegetation is wind-bent and low, and the cliffs are limestone and sandstone. Whales visit offshore from roughly June to September, and from the cape you may see southern right whales with calves.

Apollo Bay, about eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town and the place for fuel, food and rooms, since the cape has only a small cafe and a few cottages. The weather can change fast, and cold southwesterlies are common, so layers matter. The best light for the coast comes in the late afternoon, when the sun drops over the sea. There is an entry fee for the lighthouse precinct, which funds its upkeep. Pay it, climb the tower if the weather is clear, and take in the long view over the strait.
t.old town of kuldiga@57.0,22.0:
Kuldīga, in western Latvia, is a small brick town with a waterfall, and it is nicer than that sounds. The Venta river drops over a low, wide ledge right beside the old centre, and the Venta Rapid, about two hundred and fifty metres across, is billed as the widest waterfall in Europe. It is only a couple of metres high, so do not expect a roar, but the sheer breadth of it, with the old town behind, makes a gentle and slightly surprising picture. In spring, around April and May, fish leap up the rapid to spawn, and locals gather on the bridge to watch.

The bridge is a story of its own. The brick arches that cross the Venta were built in the nineteenth century and are among the longest of their kind in Europe, and they are just as attractive from below as from above. The old town clusters around it, with wooden houses, narrow streets and cobbles, and in 2023 it was inscribed by UNESCO. Kuldīga was once the seat of the Duchy of Courland, and Duke Jacob, who ruled in the seventeenth century, founded colonies as far as Tobago and Gambia, which is a lot of ambition for a province of this size.

On a motorbike, this is a restful place to break a long day between Klaipėda and the Estonian islands. Latvian roads in Kurzeme are flat, straight and generally good, with forests of pine and spruce, and a few stretches of gravel if you leave the main road. Traffic is light, but timber lorries and sleepy farm vehicles can surprise you. Watch for speed limits through villages, which are tightly enforced.

Kuldīga has about thirteen thousand people, so fuel, food and cafes are all easy. Look for cafes near the Venta, where terrace seating gives you the waterfall view with a coffee and a slice of something sweet. Alsunga and Skrunda, farther off, are much smaller. It is a good town to walk after a day in the saddle.
t.archaeological site of olympia@37.6,21.6:
Every four years, for more than a thousand years, a truce was declared across the Greek world so that athletes could travel to Olympia. The sanctuary lies in a green valley in the western Peloponnese, where the Alfeios river meets a smaller stream, below the pine-covered Hill of Kronos. The traditional date of the first Games is 776 BC, and they carried on until the Roman emperor Theodosius put an end to pagan festivals at the end of the fourth century AD. The statue of Zeus made by Phidias for the temple here, a giant seated figure of gold and ivory, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, though it has long since vanished.

What survives is the field of ruins: the temple of Hera, the stadium with its stone starting line, the palaestra and the workshop of Phidias. Each time a modern Games is held, the Olympic flame is lit here in front of the temple of Hera, using a parabolic mirror and the rays of the sun. The museum is excellent, with the sculptures from the temple of Zeus and the bronze helmets and votive offerings left by athletes and cities.

The ride that brings you here from Mystras, the Byzantine hill-town near Sparta, crosses the high interior of the Peloponnese, a landscape of mountains, gorges and small villages. The roads climb through fir and chestnut, with plenty of bends and long views, then drop into the olive groves of the western plain. Surfaces are generally good on the main roads and patchy on the minor ones, and goats and sheep are frequent. Heat in July and August is intense, so start early and carry water. Autumn is lovely, with soft light and cool air.

Archaia Olympia, the village by the site, has a little over a thousand people and a lot of tavernas. For fuel, Pyrgos, about seventeen kilometres away, with twenty-two thousand people, is the town to count on, though pumps can be found nearer. The site closes in the late afternoon, and the light then is superb.

Try the local honey and the sheep's cheese, and a glass of cold white wine in a taverna under the plane trees is a fitting end to the day.
t.monastery of daphni@38.0,23.6:
Daphni sits beside the Sacred Way that ran from Athens to Eleusis, on the western edge of the city, and it is one of the finest Byzantine monuments in Greece. The monastery was founded in the early Christian centuries on the site of a temple of Apollo, and the present church dates from about the eleventh century, with a dome set on a square plan and eight sides inside. The mosaics are the reason to come. In the dome the Christ Pantocrator looks down with a stern, brooding face, and around the walls are scenes from the life of Christ in gold and deep colours. The best are the Baptism, the Crucifixion and the Anastasis, with figures drawn with grave dignity.

The monastery has seen a lot. After the Fourth Crusade the Frankish Duke of Athens gave it to the Cistercians in 1207, and its walls and cloister bear traces of Gothic work, and later the Orthodox monks returned. The Ottomans used it, the Greeks used it as a military barracks, and in 1999 an earthquake damaged the church and closed it for years, with repairs and restoration carried out slowly. It is now back on the cultural itinerary, but opening hours change, so check before you go. Its monastery walls are fortress-like, and the grounds have pines and a small museum.

Riding to Daphni is an exercise in Athenian traffic. The old road from the centre follows Iera Odos, the Sacred Way, through Chaidari, a dense suburb of about forty-five thousand people, with traffic lights, buses and impatient drivers. Scooters are everywhere and the locals ride aggressively, so keep your wits and your distance. Heat in summer is fierce, and midday makes a car park an oven, so come early in the morning. In spring, the pines around the monastery smell of resin, and the light is gentle.

Fuel is no problem in Chaidari, and cafes and bakeries abound. Try a spinach and cheese pie, or a glass of freddo espresso, the cold iced coffee that Athenians drink all year. Parking near the site is limited, but a motorcycle can usually squeeze in. Combine the visit with the nearby coast at Elefsina, the ancient Eleusis, where the Mysteries took place for nearly two thousand years, and where the pilgrimage from Athens ended. Wear sunscreen and take water, because the grounds offer little shade.
t.zominthos@35.2,24.9:
Zominthos is a mountain meadow on the north-eastern shoulder of Mount Psiloritis, or Ida, the highest peak in Crete at 2,456 metres, and at about twelve hundred metres altitude it is cool, green and silent even in August. It was the site of a Minoan settlement, a large two-storey building of the middle Bronze Age, excavated from 1982 by the archaeologist Yiannis Sakellarakis, and the stone walls and rooms still stand among the grass. It was probably a way station on the path to the sacred Idaean Cave, where legend says the infant Zeus was hidden from his father Kronos and raised by nymphs and goats. A pilgrim route ran through here for thousands of years.

The ride up from Anógeia, a mountain village about five kilometres below, is half the pleasure. The village is famous for weaving, for its musicians, including the Xylouris family, and for its stubborn role in the Resistance, for which it was burned by the Germans in 1944. From the village the road climbs through bare rock and scrub, with long views down to the sea. It is narrow, with blind bends, and parts of the surface are broken, patched or gravelly, so a gentle pace and good tyres matter. Sheep and goats wander over it, bells clanking, and shepherds may step out to say hello. Check the current state of the road in Anógeia, because it is subject to repairs and winter damage.

The weather changes fast at this height. Mist can fill the plateau within minutes, and in winter snow can close the road. Summer is the sensible season, from May to October, with clear skies and a lovely scent of thyme and sage. In spring there are wild tulips and cyclamen in the rocks. The mountain air is thin and clean, and the quiet is surprising on an island that gets millions of tourists.

A small taverna operates near the site in the season, serving local cheese, boiled goat and herbal tea, and it is worth lingering over. Take warm clothes, even in July, and a hat. Walk the ruin slowly, and look up at the great bulk of Ida, with its summit often wrapped in cloud.
t.meteora@39.7,21.6:
Meteora is the kind of place you assume is a trick of photography until you round the bend. Enormous grey pillars of rock rise out of the Thessaly plain, some more than 300 metres high, and on top of several of them sit monasteries, walls and windows flush with the cliff edge. The name means suspended in the air, and the sandstone and conglomerate towers were shaped over millions of years by water, wind and earthquakes, long before anyone thought to build on them.

Hermits settled in caves here around the eleventh century, and by the fourteenth, with the Byzantine Empire under threat from the Ottomans, monks built monasteries on the summits for safety. Materials and people were hauled up by ropes and nets, or by long ladders that could be pulled up after use, and there are stories of monks who dangled in baskets for hours. At its height there were over twenty monasteries, and six are still active today, including Great Meteoron, Varlaam and Roussanou. Visitors need to dress modestly, with covered knees and shoulders, and the monasteries keep different closing days, so check locally.

From Kalambaka, the town at the foot of the rocks, a short loop road winds up among the pillars, with sharp bends and lookout points. Light is best at sunrise and sunset, when the rock glows copper and gold. Summer is hot and crowded, so spring and autumn make better visits. Beyond Meteora, the ride heads into the Pindus mountains, a range of forested ridges and deep gorges, with the high villages of Metsovo and the stone bridges of Epirus, where roads are twisty and traffic is thin.

Kalambaka, with eight thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and many guesthouses, and Kastraki, a village right under the rocks, is quieter, with simple tavernas serving grilled meat and fresh bread. The roads in the Pindus can be closed by snow in winter, and fuel stations in the mountains are sparse, so fill up before leaving town. Sit down for a coffee at a table with a view and watch the evening light change.
t.salonga national park@-2.0,21.0:
Salonga is a place you read about rather than ride to, so let us be honest from the start. It is the largest tropical rainforest national park in Africa, a block of lowland forest in the central basin of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, bigger than Belgium, split into a northern and a southern sector with a corridor of villages between them. UNESCO listed it in 1984, and since 1999 it has also been on the list of sites in danger, because of poaching, conflict and the sheer difficulty of guarding something so large.

There is no road through it. Rivers, mainly the Lokoro, Luilaka and their tributaries, are the real highways, and travel is by pirogue and small boat, with some tracks and old logging roads on the margins. For a motorcycle rider the practical conclusion is that the nearest places that matter, such as Boende, Monkoto and Oshwe, are reached by long, rough, sometimes impassable earth tracks, with fuel carried in drums and mud that can swallow a bike in the wet season. Anyone who attempts this needs local guides, up-to-date security information and a good deal of time.

What the forest holds justifies the effort for specialists. Salonga shelters the bonobo, our closest relative besides the chimpanzee, found only south of the Congo river and known for resolving conflict with affection rather than violence. It also holds forest elephants, the Congo peafowl, which was unknown to Western science until 1936, and a vast number of small and secretive species. The canopy is thick enough that most of the park feels like a green twilight, the air heavy with the smell of wet leaf and fruit, with the loud calls of hornbills and monkeys overhead.

The human history matters as well. People live all around the park and, in the past, within its limits. Conservation here works best where local communities have a stake in it, and some projects have tried to link protection with jobs, schools and clinics. Look at this stop as a window onto a very large place that deserves our attention, not a destination for casual travel.
t.ioannina@39.7,20.9:
Ioannina wraps itself around a lake, and the lake is the first thing to understand about it. Lake Pamvotida lies flat and grey-green beside the city, with a small wooded island in the middle that holds a cluster of monasteries and a village, reached by a short boat from the waterfront. Behind the city rise the limestone ranges of Epirus, the Pindus mountains, which isolated this part of north-west Greece for centuries and gave it a character quite unlike the islands and the south.

The history is thick here. In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries Ioannina was the capital of Ali Pasha, an Ottoman governor who ran his own near-independent state from the fortress of Its Kale, a walled citadel on a peninsula above the water. The mosque of Aslan Pasha and the Fethiye mosque still stand inside the walls, and silversmiths still work in the narrow lanes. Byron visited Ali Pasha in 1809 and wrote admiringly of him. The old town also had a long-established Jewish community, the Romaniotes, whose synagogue survives, a reminder of the many lives that crossed the place.

For a rider, Ioannina is a good base. To the north the Zagori villages, with their stone bridges and slate roofs, sit below the Vikos Gorge, one of the deepest in the world for its width, and the lanes that climb to them are narrow, steep and magnificent. To the east the road climbs over the Pindus toward Metsovo, high on the Katara pass, then down to the plains of Thessaly and the strange rock pillars of Meteora. The modern Egnatia motorway has made the journey faster, but the old road still has more character, with long bends, forests of oak and beech and small villages. Surfaces are generally good, though rockfall and frost damage appear in the mountains, and in winter snow can close the heights.

Ioannina has plenty of fuel stations, shops and places to eat, from tavernas serving grilled meat to pastry shops that sell the local milk pies and syrupy sweets. Summers are hot, so start early, and spring and autumn are best for the mountain loops. A walk around the citadel at sunset, with the lake turning gold below, is a fine way to end a day.
t.klaipeda@55.7,21.1:
Klaipėda is the sea gate of Lithuania, and for most of its history it belonged to somebody else. The Teutonic Knights built a castle at the mouth of the Danė river in 1252, and for seven centuries the town was known as Memel, part of Prussia and then Germany, until it was returned to Lithuania in 1923. Traces of the old name and culture remain in the half-timbered warehouses of the old town, a few of which have been carefully restored, and in a bronze statue of Ännchen von Tharau, the heroine of a seventeenth century German song, standing in the market square.

The city is bright and busy, with a big port, container cranes and a long seafront. Across the narrow strait of the Curonian Lagoon lies the Curonian Spit, a thin ribbon of sand dunes and pine forest about a hundred kilometres long, shared with Russia, that is a UNESCO World Heritage site. A short ferry ride from the old town takes you to Smiltynė, where a small sea museum and dolphinarium stand, and from there a road runs south along the spit through fishing villages and past some of the highest drifting dunes in Europe, ending at Nida. Amber, washed up by storms on the Baltic shore, is sold in shops all over town and is part of the local culture.

For riders, Klaipėda is an excellent base for exploring west Lithuania and the Latvian border. Roads in the region are mostly flat and straight, passing through forests of pine and birch and fields of rye, and the surface is generally good, though some secondary roads have potholes or patches. The route south of the town runs close to the sea, and the one north leads toward Latvia and the town of Kuldīga, whose old brick centre and the Venta Rapid, a waterfall about two hundred and fifty metres wide, said to be the widest in Europe, make a good destination. Summer evenings stay light until very late, and winter brings ice and snow, so the best months are from May to September.

Fuel is abundant in town and on the highway, as are cafés and restaurants serving smoked fish, potato pancakes and cold beet soup. In July the city holds a sea festival, with ships and music along the river. A walk along the Danė at dusk, past the old warehouses, is a good end to the day.
t.sigulda@57.2,24.9:
Sigulda lies in the valley of the Gauja river, about fifty kilometres from Riga, and it behaves like a small Switzerland dropped into the Baltic plain. The land here is deeply cut by the river and its sandstone cliffs, covered in pine and birch forest, and the whole area forms the Gauja National Park, the largest in Latvia. Three castles face one another across the valley, and a cable car crosses it, giving the visitor views of the forest, the river and the autumn colours, which in October are among the best in the Baltic region.

The history is that of the Livonian crusaders. In the early thirteenth century, the Sword Brethren, a German military order, built a stone castle at Sigulda, whose ruins stand in a park near the town, and Bishop Albert of Riga founded Turaida Castle across the valley in 1214, its red brick towers still rising above the trees. A local legend tells of the Rose of Turaida, a girl named Maija who, according to the story, died in 1620 rather than betray her love, and her grave beneath a linden tree is a place of pilgrimage for newlyweds. Gutmanis Cave, the largest cave in the Baltic states, has walls covered with graffiti dating back centuries.

For riders, the loop around Gauja National Park is relaxing, with winding roads through woods and farmland, small villages with wooden houses, and views over the river valley. Surfaces are mostly good, with some sections of gravel on side roads. Latvia's drivers can be fast, but traffic outside Riga is light. In winter, Sigulda is a centre for bobsleigh, with an Olympic-standard track that attracts competitors, and the area is cold and snowy, so most riders visit between May and October.

Fuel and supplies are easy to find in Sigulda, which has about ten thousand people, plus small cafés that serve rye bread, smoked fish and local beer. The paths along the river are good for stretching after a ride. The mosquitoes in summer can be fierce near the water, so carry repellent. Take the cable car if the weather is clear, and watch the forest roll out beneath you in every direction.
t.historic centre@59.4,24.7:
Tallinn's old town is the best-preserved medieval city centre in northern Europe, and it has been protected by a ring of walls and towers that still stand for most of their length. UNESCO listed it in 1997. The city grew rich as a Hanseatic port, and its merchants built tall stone houses with steep roofs, guild halls and churches that are still in use. The town is divided into two parts, the Upper Town on the limestone hill of Toompea, where the rulers lived, and the Lower Town below, where the merchants and craftsmen did business, and for centuries the two had separate governments and sometimes separate laws.

The main square, Raekoja plats, has a Gothic town hall and one of the oldest pharmacies in Europe, which has been in business since the fifteenth century. In the Upper Town, the onion domes of the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, built by the Russian Empire in the early twentieth century, face the medieval Dome Church, a nice reminder of the layers of power. Narrow lanes run between the houses, with courtyards and workshops, and the best views over the red roofs and the sea come from the platforms on Toompea. In summer, the light lasts until very late, and in June it barely gets dark.

The ride starts and ends here, heading west to Haapsalu, a seaside town with a ruined bishop's castle and a ghost story about a white lady, and passing through flat coastal landscape, with pine forests, farmland and long views of the Baltic. Roads in Estonia are smooth and often empty, and speed limits are low and enforced by cameras, with fines that are not trivial. Elk and deer cross the roads, particularly at dusk, and a collision is serious.

Ferries to Helsinki run several times a day and take about two hours, so many travellers combine the two cities. Fuel stations are plentiful and everything works, including card payment almost everywhere. Eat black bread, smoked fish and the local dark beer, and try the traditional dish of blood sausage with lingonberry. The best seasons are June to September, when daylight is long and the sea is warm enough to swim, though the cold water takes some courage. Winters are dark and snowy, and the old town looks magical under snow.
t.tallinn@59.4,24.8:
Tallinn is a medieval city that kept its walls, and the thick stone towers and steep red roofs of its old town make it among the best-preserved in northern Europe. It grew rich as a Hanseatic port, trading with Novgorod and Lübeck, and the merchants' houses and guildhalls built in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries still line the cobbled lanes. Above it all stands Toompea, the hill of the castle and the parliament, with the onion domes of the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, built in the 1890s when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire, still dominating the view.

The city has an ironic, sophisticated modern face as well. Estonia regained its independence in 1991 after a Singing Revolution, in which hundreds of thousands gathered to sing banned national songs, and the Baltic Way of 1989, when two million people joined hands in a human chain from Tallinn to Vilnius. Today Estonians are famous for their digital services, and almost everything can be done online. In Kadriorg, a park east of the old town, Peter the Great's baroque palace stands among gardens and fountains, and the seaside promenade of Pirita, with its yacht harbour, reaches toward the forest.

For riders, the city is the start of an easy run east along the Gulf of Finland to Lahemaa National Park, about seventy kilometres away. The road passes through pine forest, then leads to a coast of small bays and fishing villages, with enormous granite boulders left by the ice sheets lying in fields and on the beach. In the park, grand manors such as Palmse and Sagadi, built by Baltic German landowners, stand among old parks, and bogs have boardwalk trails. The roads are mostly smooth, with long gentle bends and little traffic, and in summer it hardly gets dark until nearly midnight, so evening rides are a delight. Winter, however, is cold and icy, and riders mostly stay home.

Fuel stations are plentiful in Tallinn and its suburbs, and along the main road east, with smaller ones in towns such as Kose. Estonian police are strict about speed, with cameras and patrols, and headlights must be on all day. Food is a pleasure, with black rye bread, smoked fish, sour cream soups and, in the old town, medieval-themed taverns serving roast boar and honey beer. A walk on the town wall at dusk, when the lamps come on and the towers glow, is a lovely way to end a day.
t.jurmala@57.0,23.8:
A dune forest and a long white beach is not the first thing most people expect near Riga, but that is what Jūrmala is. The town is a string of seaside villages strung along a narrow strip of land between the Gulf of Riga and the Lielupe river, about twenty-five kilometres west of the capital. Over fifty thousand people live here, and in the Soviet era it was the main resort of the Baltic region, a place where party officials and ordinary workers took their holidays. Today it keeps that holiday atmosphere, with spa hotels, sanatoriums and a very long beach of soft pale sand that stretches for some thirty kilometres.

Much of Jūrmala's character comes from its wooden architecture. Pine-lined streets are full of nineteenth and early twentieth century villas, with carved verandas, turrets and painted shutters, many restored in recent years. Jomas iela, the main pedestrian street in Majori, is lined with cafes, shops and small restaurants, and in summer it fills up with strollers. In the dunes behind the beach, the smell of pine resin and salt air makes for a pleasant walk, and the sea is shallow and cold even in July.

The ride starts easily here. Roads in the area are flat and straight, with speed limits that are lower than you might expect and police who enforce them, so keep an eye out. The A10 and the old road towards Kurzeme lead west along the coast and through forest, and you will soon be out among farms and small wooden villages. The scenery is gentle, and the coastline is more about space and quiet than about drama. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, when Riga empties toward the beach, so go early or midweek if you can.

Jūrmala is large enough for fuel, food and any repairs, and the stations along the main road are frequent. Piņķi, a smaller place to the east, also has services. Past here, as the road leaves the built-up area, stations are fewer, so it is sensible to arrive in Kurzeme with a full tank.

Try the smoked fish sold in small stalls, and a cup of strong coffee on a veranda. Late June, around the midsummer festival of Jāņi, is a special time to be in Latvia, with wreaths, bonfires and a very long twilight.
t.melbourne victoria@-37.2,144.9:
Kilmore has a fair claim to be the oldest inland town in Victoria, and the stone buildings along its main street back it up. It sits in a gap in the Great Dividing Range, a natural passage that the early overlanders used on the road between Melbourne and the Murray, and the Hume Highway still slips through here today. This stop lies a little south of the town, in sheep and cattle country between Kilmore, Broadford and Lancefield, where the land rolls in broad folds of yellow-brown grass and dark clumps of gum trees.

The area has known hard times. In February 2009 the bushfires of Black Saturday started near Kilmore East and swept through the hills to the north and east, and the scars on the landscape and in the community are still part of the local story. The regrowth is lush now, but locals remember, and you will see memorials and signs of the recovery as you ride. In summer, the fire risk remains real, and on days of extreme fire danger, riding in the forest is a poor idea.

Lancefield, to the west, has a different claim to fame. A swamp near the town produced one of the richest deposits of ice age animal bones in Victoria, including those of giant kangaroos and wombat-like creatures, and the find gave scientists a window into the megafauna that once roamed here. Today the town is a quiet place with a handsome bluestone hotel and a few cafes, a pleasant stop on a Sunday ride.

For fuel and supplies, Kilmore, with nearly eight thousand people, has petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a good selection of pubs. Broadford is smaller but has the basics, and Lancefield has a general store. The riding here is mostly easy, with long bends and gentle hills, and a good surface on the main roads. Early morning, when mist lies in the hollows and the paddocks glisten with dew, is the best time to be on the road. Expect kangaroos in the evening and be generous with your braking distance.
t.athens@38.0,23.7:
Athens has more motorbikes per street than almost any city in Europe, and the drivers are used to them. Scooters thread through every gap, couriers weave between buses, and the whole basin between Mount Hymettus and the sea hums at a pitch that a visitor from the north needs a day to tune into. At the centre of the din the Acropolis stands on its limestone rock, the Parthenon's marble glowing gold at sunset, and it makes the whole mess of concrete around it seem like a footnote.

The monuments are old beyond easy comprehension. The Parthenon was built in the fifth century BC under Pericles, and the theatre of Dionysus beneath it saw the first performances of Sophocles and Euripides. Below the rock lies Plaka, a maze of lanes and stairways where tavernas spill onto the pavement, and the ancient Agora, where Socrates argued with his neighbours, is a quiet park of columns and olive trees. Nearly 700,000 people live in the municipality, and more than three million in the metropolitan area, so there is no shortage of fuel or food.

Escape is the key. The coast road south from the city runs along the Saronic Gulf, through the beach suburbs of Glyfada and Vouliagmeni, and on to Cape Sounion, where the ruined Temple of Poseidon stands on a cliff above the sea. The sunset there is famous, so do not be surprised by the crowds. North and west the mountains of Parnitha and Kithairon offer cooler air and winding roads, where pine woods and goat bells replace the horns of the city.

Summer in Athens is brutal, with temperatures that regularly pass forty degrees, so start early and rest at midday. The city is at its best in spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the light is soft. When night falls, roof terraces fill with people, and the floodlit Parthenon hangs in the sky above the lanes like a lantern.
t.sapporo@43.1,141.4:
Sapporo is a young city by Japanese standards. Until 1869 it was an empty plain at the foot of the mountains, and then the Meiji government, wanting to settle and develop Hokkaido, laid out a grid of streets in the American manner and called the project the Kaitakushi, the Development Commission. Today it is a metropolis of nearly two million, the fifth largest in Japan, and the only one with wide boulevards, a broad central park and a cheerfully northern attitude.

Odori Park runs through the middle, a long ribbon of lawns, fountains and flower beds that hosts the Snow Festival in February, when huge sculptures of ice and snow are built along it, and beer gardens in summer. The Sapporo brewery, founded in 1876, is a few steps away, and the city's red-brick former government building still stands in a park with tall trees. Food is the other pleasure: miso ramen was perfected here, and so were soup curry, grilled lamb called Genghis Khan and the kind of fresh seafood and dairy you expect from Hokkaido.

As a base for riders the city is unbeatable, because Hokkaido is the great motorcycle destination of Japan. The roads are wide and straight, with sweeping views, farmland and few cars, and out in the countryside you can ride for an hour without seeing a village. The season runs from about May to October, since snow and ice close many roads in winter. Watch for deer at dusk, and for the speed cameras and patrol cars that are common near towns.

Within Sapporo, traffic is orderly and the grid is easy to read. Fuel is plentiful, but outside the city stations can be far apart, so fill up before heading into the interior. The mountains to the south, around Jozankei and Lake Shikotsu, offer forested roads, hot springs and clear air, perfect for a day trip. Summer is mild and dry compared with the rest of Japan, with cool evenings that make the beer taste better.
t.kakinoshima site@41.9,140.9:
The Jomon people lived in Japan for more than ten thousand years, and the Kakinoshima site belongs to the story of how they did it. It lies in southern Hokkaido, on the Oshima peninsula, the knuckle of land that reaches toward Honshu across the Tsugaru Strait, with the nearest town of any size, Honcho, about twenty kilometres off. The country here is gentle, a mix of low hills, farmland and a coast that opens to the strait.

Jomon culture is named for the cord-marked pottery its makers decorated, and it lasted from about fifteen thousand years ago to roughly three hundred BC. These were hunter-gatherer-fishers who nevertheless built permanent villages, stored food, traded obsidian and jade and buried their dead in ritual ways. Several Hokkaido and northern Tohoku sites were inscribed as World Heritage in 2021 to show that settled life developed without farming. Kakinoshima is among the places associated with that story, and it is a quiet, open site with markers and displays rather than grand buildings.

Riding here is easy and rural. Roads on the peninsula are well surfaced, with long straight sections and mild bends, and traffic is light outside the ferry traffic from Honshu. In summer the air is cool and clear compared with Tokyo, and the sea on the horizon gives a sense of space. Fog can drift in from the strait, particularly in early summer, and winter brings deep snow that closes many side roads.

Fuel and food are limited near the site itself, so plan to refuel in larger towns such as Honcho or at the stations on the main road. Small restaurants in the area serve seafood, particularly scallops and squid, and local dairy products are good. The historical interest is quieter than a castle or temple, a reminder of how long people have lived by this sea. Take time to read the markers, and notice how the landscape feels almost unchanged.
t.parc national de la salonga nord@-1.5,21:
Salonga is the largest tropical rainforest reserve in Africa, covering about thirty-six thousand square kilometres of the Congo basin in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in two big blocks separated by a corridor of villages and farmland. UNESCO listed the park in 1984, and it has spent years on the list of World Heritage in Danger.

The star of the park is the bonobo, a close cousin of the chimpanzee found only south of the Congo River, and known for its matriarchal and peaceful society. Salonga also shelters forest elephants, the Congo peafowl, red colobus monkeys, and several kinds of crocodile. Walking in this forest means damp air, constant sound, huge buttressed trees and a deep green gloom. The ground is often wet, and the rivers are the real roads.

It would be dishonest to talk about a motorcycle route here. There are no through roads in the park and almost no roads near it, and travel is by river canoe, on foot, and by the occasional boat from Kinshasa. The region has seen conflict, and poaching has hit wildlife hard, so access depends on conservation groups and permits. Anyone planning a visit should arrange it with the park authority and an experienced operator, and check the security situation first.

If you do go, expect to be far from fuel, hospitals and phone coverage. The dry months, roughly June to August and December to February, are the easiest for travel, but the forest is wet at any time. Pack for heat, humidity and insects, carry water treatment, and be ready for long days of slow progress. What the place offers is something rare in the modern world, a forest so big that you can spend days without seeing another human being.
Where the northern block of Salonga is wet and tangled, the southern block feels like the farther side of the moon. It lies roughly a degree south of the equator in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in the great bowl of the Congo basin, and it is part of the same World Heritage reserve, which at thirty-six thousand square kilometres is the biggest protected tropical rainforest in Africa. A corridor of land between the two halves is home to people who farm, fish and hunt, and their villages are the only human mark on the map.

The park was created in 1970 and listed by UNESCO in 1984, and in 1999 it was added to the list of sites in danger, because war, poaching and the collapse of park management had left it exposed. Conservation groups and rangers have worked since to protect it, and it remains a place where the story is not yet settled. Bonobos live here, the apes that settle quarrels with affection rather than violence, as do forest elephants and the shy, striking Congo peafowl that was unknown to science until the 1930s.

The rivers rule this region. They run dark and slow between flooded banks, and the only practical routes into the forest are by pirogue, the dugout canoe, and on foot along narrow trails. Rainfall is heavy for most of the year, with a slightly drier spell mid-year, and the forest floor stays damp. The nearest roads are rough tracks between villages, often impassable in the rains.

If you are drawn to this place, treat it as an expedition and not a ride. Plan through the national park authority or a conservation partner, expect to carry every litre of fuel and water you will need, and check the security position well in advance. Medical help is a long way off. What you gain is the experience of a forest so big and quiet that it makes the rest of the planet feel crowded.
t.sarande@39.9,20.0:
Sarandë sits at the bottom of Albania's long coast, in a curving bay facing the Greek island of Corfu, which on a clear evening looks close enough to swim to. It is a town of about fifteen thousand, built in tiers up a steep hillside, with a promenade running the length of the waterfront and a view that makes the end of the SH8 feel like a reward. The road you have just finished, the coastal highway from Vlorë over the Llogara Pass, is among the most dramatic in the Balkans.

The name has a story. The Italians called the town Santi Quaranta, and the Greeks call it Agioi Saranta, both after forty Christian martyrs who were said to be commemorated in an early monastery here. Ruins of that church can still be found on the hill above the harbour, and the town has been shaped by Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman and Italian influence. The Greek minority in the surrounding district has kept its own traditions alive.

The riding on the way in is excellent. The Llogara Pass climbs to just over a thousand metres through pine and fir forest before the road drops in a long series of bends toward Dhermi and Himare, with the Ionian Sea below, limestone peaks above and not a lot of barrier in between. The surface has improved in recent years but is not uniform, and goats, dogs and slow trucks are routine on the bends. In summer the road is busy with holiday traffic, so aim for early morning or the shoulder seasons of May, June and September.

South of Sarandë lie two places worth a visit if you have the time. Butrint, a few kilometres down the coast, is a UNESCO site where Greek, Roman and Venetian ruins lie in a wooded lagoon landscape, and the Blue Eye, a deep spring of strikingly clear water, sits inland. Ksamil, nearer the border, has small beaches and clear water that are very popular in July and August.

Fuel stations are plentiful in the town and along the main road, though prices vary. Restaurants along the waterfront serve fresh fish and grilled lamb, and a long dinner with the lights of Corfu across the water is a sound way to end the day.
t.asahikawa@43.8,142.4:
It has around three hundred and fifty thousand people, a long, cold winter and a reputation for ramen, furniture and sake. The city sits at the confluence of several rivers, and its wide streets and big sky have a frontier feel that suits the island.

The Hokkaido Patchwork Road starts here, and it heads through some of the best riding in Japan. East of the city, the road leads to Biei and Furano, a landscape of rolling hills, flower fields and potato farms divided into a patchwork of colours, with lines of poplars and a few lone trees. To the south-east lies Daisetsuzan, the biggest national park in Japan, where Mount Asahidake, at 2,291 metres, is the highest peak in Hokkaido. The roads are wide and smooth, with long straights and gentle bends, and traffic is light. Summer is short and glorious, with long days, while snow can come in October, so the riding season is brief.

The city has surprises. Asahiyama Zoo, one of Japan's most popular, is famous for its penguin walk in winter and its polar bears viewed through a glass tunnel, and the shopping street, Heiwa-dori, was Japan's first permanent pedestrian mall. The soy-based Asahikawa ramen, with a thick layer of oil that keeps the broth hot, is the local dish, and the sake breweries offer tastings.

Fuel is easy in the city, with many stations, and it is sensible to fill up before leaving, since distances in Hokkaido are long and stations in the countryside often close early. Convenience stores and roadside stations, called michi-no-eki, offer food and rest areas, and local produce is excellent: corn, melons, potatoes and dairy.

Watch for deer and foxes on country roads at dusk. Drive on the left, and enjoy the open land.
t.port campbell@-38.6,143.0:
Port Campbell is a small coastal town of Victoria's southwest, set into a narrow gap in the limestone cliffs and facing the wild Southern Ocean. It is the base for the most famous part of the Great Ocean Road, and its little harbour and beach are protected by a headland, so the town feels sheltered while the coastline on both sides is raw. The nearest bigger places, Timboon and Cobden, are inland and a long way off in the paddocks, so the town has to serve everyone who comes along the coast with fuel, food and a bed.

The sea has been carving this coast for millions of years. The soft limestone stands in cliffs of sixty metres or so, and the waves cut caves, arches and stacks, of which the Twelve Apostles, about twelve kilometres east, are the best known. They are fewer than twelve now, as stacks fall every few decades. The collapse of London Bridge in 1990, a double-arched rock formation, left two tourists stranded on the outer part and rescued by helicopter. Nearby, Loch Ard Gorge is named after a clipper that wrecked here in 1878, when two young survivors, Tom Pearce and Eva Carmichael, were washed into the gorge and lived. The coast was feared by sailors and is called the Shipwreck Coast.

For a rider, the road is as good as the scenery and not as simple as it looks. The Great Ocean Road was built by returned soldiers after the First World War and dedicated as a memorial to those who died, and it winds along the cliff tops with long views and broad bends. Here the road is straighter than the section further east near Lorne, and wind is the main trouble, as the Southern Ocean blows hard and cold, sometimes sideways. Rain showers come fast and the weather can change within an hour, so carry a layer even in summer. Tourist coaches and camper vans are common near the Apostles, and speed limits are strictly enforced.

The best time to ride is early morning or late afternoon, when the light turns the cliffs gold and the crowds thin. Winter has a drama of its own, with big seas, but the air is cold. Port Campbell has a fuel station, a bakery and fish and chips on the foreshore, and it is a good place to refuel before riding on toward Warrnambool.
t.kardamyli@36.9,22.2:
The Mani is the middle finger of the Peloponnese, a rugged, rocky peninsula that points south toward Africa, and Kardamyli sits on its western coast, at the foot of the Taygetos range. The mountains rise steeply behind the village, with the highest peak at about two and a half thousand metres, and the sea sits right in front, so the whole place has the air of a stage set. Olive groves cover the slopes between the two, and the stone houses and towers of the old village climb the hill above the new one.

The village has a long literary history. Homer mentions a place of this name in the Iliad, and Patrick Leigh Fermor, the British writer and war hero, built a house nearby in the 1960s and lived there for decades, writing a famous book about the Mani. His house is on the coast just south of Kardamyli and is now partly open to visitors. Behind the village, the Viros gorge cuts into the mountains, a walking trail along a stream under plane trees, with small churches and caves along the way.

The ride to Kardamyli from Kalamata is a classic Greek coast road, with tight bends, short climbs and endless views of the Messenian Gulf. The surface is generally fair but can be rough in places, with rock fall and goats, and the road narrows through the small villages. It is best ridden early, in the soft light, before the heat and the holiday traffic. South of Kardamyli, the road climbs into the wild central Mani, with its stone tower houses, bleached rock and almost no trees, and the landscape becomes harder and more dramatic.

Kardamyli is a small place and fuel is limited, so fill the tank in Kalamata, which has about fifty thousand people and all the services you could want. The village itself has a handful of tavernas by the sea, where you can eat grilled fish, local olives and fresh bread, and a few cafés and shops along the main street. Summer is hot and busy, spring and early autumn are much better, and the sea stays warm enough for swimming well into October.
t.volos@39.4,22.9:
Volos sits at the head of the Pagasetic Gulf, a calm sheltered bay in central Greece, and the Greeks say it was from here, from the ancient city of Iolkos, that Jason and the Argonauts set sail in search of the Golden Fleece. A replica of the ship Argo rests near the waterfront, a handsome piece of nonsense that still draws the eye. The modern town is largely newer than you would expect, because earthquakes in 1955 damaged much of it, and so there are many broad, practical concrete blocks. In the neighbouring Nea Ionia, the name recalls the refugees who arrived from Asia Minor in the 1920s and brought with them a taste for strong spirits and good food.

That is the other reason to love Volos: tsipouro.
