In the tsipouradika, small taverns by the harbour, you order a bottle of the clear grape spirit and a plate of meze arrives free with every round, with octopus, mussels, grilled fish and fried cheese. You are not expected to rush, and nobody will mind if lunch lasts three hours. It is the correct way to say goodbye to a ride.

Behind the town rises Mount Pelion, the legendary home of the centaurs, and the roads that climb it make for outstanding motorcycling. The loop around the peninsula takes in thick forests of beech, chestnut and plane trees, hairpins that climb through the villages of Portaria and Makrinitsa, and slow, rewarding roads along the east coast to the beaches near Milina and Agios Ioannis. Surfaces are generally good, but the villages are tight, with stone-paved lanes and cars parked on the corners. In autumn chestnuts fall on the road, and in winter snow can sit on the higher sections. The Pelion narrow-gauge steam train from Ano Lechonia to Milies runs on summer weekends, crossing a stone viaduct.

With a population of more than eighty thousand, Volos has fuel stations on every main road, plus supermarkets and cafés in every street. Parking a bike near the harbour is easy, and many hotels have a courtyard or garage. Ferries to the Sporades islands leave from the port, so you may meet other travellers, and it is a good place to stock up before the mountain roads.
t.monastery of hosios loukas@38.4,22.8:
Hosios Loukas stands on a shelf of Mount Helicon, in central Greece, in a landscape of olive terraces and grey limestone, overlooking a wide green valley. The monastery was founded in the tenth century around the tomb of a hermit, Saint Luke of Steiris, who lived nearby and died in 953, and who was said to have predicted the Byzantine reconquest of Crete. It is one of the three great Middle Byzantine monasteries, with Daphni near Athens and Nea Moni on Chios, that UNESCO recognises together. Few people outside Greece have heard of it, which is a shame.

The glory is inside, in the church of the Theotokos and the larger katholikon, where the walls and domes shine with mosaics on gold backgrounds. Christ looks down from the dome, the saints stand in rows with long, solemn faces, and the marble floor and carved columns feel like a rich, quiet jewel box. In the crypt below, the saint's tomb is still venerated, and monks live at the site. The setting is peaceful, with cypress trees and mountains behind.

It has a dark chapter too. In June 1944, German troops carried out a massacre in the nearby village of Distomo, killing more than two hundred people, and a memorial there is a sobering stop for anyone passing. It is a reminder that this quiet countryside had a hard time in the war.

The riding is the pleasure of the approach. From the main road near Livadeia you climb through small villages on a winding road with olive groves, stone walls and terraced fields, and the surface is usually good, with the odd patch of loose gravel. The roads west toward Arachova and Delphi go over the shoulders of Parnassus and are among the best in Greece, with long climbs, deep valleys and big views. Summer heat is serious, so start early, and carry water.

Steiri and Kyriaki are small villages with a few tavernas but not much else. Livadeia, about twelve kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel stations, shops and cafés, and it is where you should fill up. Dress modestly when you visit the monastery, as shorts and bare shoulders are not allowed, and be prepared for it to close in the afternoon.
t.monasteries of daphni@38.4,22.7:
The real Daphni monastery is a Byzantine church of the eleventh century on the western edge of Athens, along the old Sacred Way to Eleusis, and it is a UNESCO site together with Hosios Loukas, which lies only a few kilometres from this point.

What surrounds you is a high, open plateau with terraces, thin soils and a surprisingly red colour in places, caused by bauxite, the ore of aluminium, which is mined in the mountains of this region. Helicon rises above to nearly 1,750 metres, and the ancient Greeks believed it was the home of the Muses. The roads run through thickets of oak and kermes oak, olive groves and pastures where goats graze. Eagles and buzzards soar on the thermals above the slopes, and in spring the verges are bright with wildflowers.

It is quiet riding, and quiet is the point. The roads between the villages are narrow, with tight bends and sometimes patches of loose stone, and in the afternoon the heat and the glare make attention hard to hold. Livestock wander across the road, and in the early morning you may meet a shepherd with a flock. Farm trucks move slowly, and there is little traffic in the evening.

Neither Steiri nor Kyriaki has more than a small shop and a taverna. The nearest proper town is Livadeia, about twelve kilometres away, where there are fuel stations, a supermarket and an old stone bridge over the Erkyna springs. Livadeia was once home to the oracle of Trophonius, where visitors were said to come out so shaken that they could not laugh again. It is an odd and fitting bit of local legend. If you are in the area, spend the afternoon at the nearby monastery of Hosios Loukas, where the mosaics are the real thing and the setting is just as good.
t.willow city loop@30.5,-98.7:
The Willow City Loop is thirteen miles of narrow, twisting ranch road in the Texas Hill Country, and for a few weeks each spring it is one of the most photographed roads in the state. In March and April the roadsides and meadows fill with bluebonnets, Indian paintbrush, and other wildflowers in blue, red and gold, and the low hills roll away in waves of colour. The loop runs through private ranchland, over cattle guards and through low-water crossings, with granite outcrops and live oaks along the way, and it passes the tiny hamlet of Willow City. Fredericksburg, the nearest real town, lies about twenty-five kilometres to the south-west.

Fredericksburg itself is worth the trip. It was founded in 1846 by German immigrants, and the Germanic character of the town remains in its stone houses, its main street of shops and biergartens, and the bakeries selling strudel and bratwurst. Peaches, grown on the surrounding farms, are the local pride in summer, and the vineyards of the Hill Country have made the region a growing wine destination. Close by, Enchanted Rock, a huge dome of pink granite, rises about four hundred feet above the surrounding country, and groans in the evening as it cools, a sound that gave it its name and its legends.

The loop itself is a delight but needs care. The road is narrow, with blind curves, loose gravel on the edges and a surface that is rough in places. Cattle and other livestock graze freely, and it is not unusual to meet a cow in the road. After heavy rain, the low-water crossings can flood quickly, and you must not try to ride through moving water. Traffic is dense on spring weekends, when carloads of photographers crawl along, so go on a weekday morning. Stay on the road, since the land on either side is private.

Fuel is available in Fredericksburg, but not on the loop, so fill the tank beforehand. The loop is a good place to finish a ride, with the afternoon light turning the hills gold, and a cool breeze after the heat of the day. Summer is hot, often above a hundred degrees, so bring water and sun protection, and watch out for rattlesnakes in the rocks.
t.riga@56.9,24.1:
Riga sits on the Daugava river a few kilometres from the Baltic, in the flat sandy lowlands of Latvia, and it has been a trading city since the early thirteenth century, when German merchants and crusaders founded it. As a member of the Hanseatic League it grew rich on timber, flax and grain, and the old town is still a maze of cobbled lanes, brick churches, merchants' houses and guild halls. The ornate House of the Blackheads, rebuilt after wartime destruction, stands in the main square, and the spire of Saint Peter's Church rises above it all.

The city has another face. At the start of the twentieth century Riga grew quickly, and architects covered whole streets with Art Nouveau, with masks, sculpted faces and curling vegetation, and today there are more of these buildings than in almost any other city in Europe. Wander the district north of the old town and you will find facade after facade that seem to compete in exuberance. Even the Central Market, in a row of old Zeppelin hangars, has a grandeur that few markets can match, and it is a good place to buy smoked fish, rye bread and berries.

For riders, the city is something to pass through with care, since the cobbles of the old town are slippery when wet and trams run on rails across many streets. The real riding lies outside. The beaches of Jūrmala, with wooden villas in the pine woods, are half an hour to the west, and the Gauja valley to the north-east, with the castle at Sigulda and sandstone cliffs, is a favourite with Latvian riders. The landscape is generally flat, with forest and fields, but the roads are quiet, and the long summer light, lasting past ten in June, makes evening rides a pleasure. Watch for elk and deer at dusk, and for gravel patches on some local roads.

Fuel is easily available around the city. Try Riga's black balsam, a herbal liqueur, and grey peas with bacon. The riding season is short, from May to September, and the air turns cold quickly in autumn.
t.arachova mountain town@38.5,22.6:
Arachova clings to the southern slope of Mount Parnassus at about 950 metres, a stone-built mountain town in central Greece whose houses climb the hillside in steps, one roof beneath the next. It is a place of narrow lanes and steep stairs, with a clock tower on the rock above the main road and the whole of the Pleistos valley falling away below, silver with olive trees. Delphi lies only eight kilometres to the west, and Arachova has long served as the mountain-town companion to that ancient sanctuary.

It also has its own history. Arachova played a part in the Greek War of Independence in 1821, when fighters from the town joined the uprising, and the town's festival of Agios Georgios in April is one of the great days of the Greek year, with dancing, traditional costume and roast lamb. The locals are known for weaving, and the shops along the main street sell woollen rugs and bags next to bottles of local wine. They also sell formaella, a hard cheese that is grilled or fried, as well as local sausages and honey. Winter sees the town fill with Athenians heading to the ski resort higher on the mountain, and snow can fall here, so riders should be careful between December and March.

The main road, the one from Livadeia to Delphi, passes right along the town, and it is busy with tourist coaches and trucks in season. Traffic can be slow in the narrow main street, but the roads beyond it are a pleasure. The climb up from the Boeotian plain toward Arachova is a succession of bends through limestone hills, and the descent toward Delphi and Itea has big views over the Gulf of Corinth. The surface is mostly good, though it can be polished and slippery in the wet, and there is occasional loose grit on corners.

Because Arachova is a popular weekend destination, it is well supplied, with fuel at the roadside, a good choice of tavernas and cafes, and many places to sit with a coffee and watch the street go by. Sit on a terrace and order something grilled, with a glass of the local red.

The air at this height is crisp even in summer, and it smells of oregano, pine and woodsmoke. Aim for spring, when the hillsides are green and the poppies are out, or for autumn. In midsummer, the days are hot and the evenings are mild.
t.delphi sanctuary@38.5,22.5:
Delphi clings to the south slope of Mount Parnassus, above a steep valley full of olive trees that runs down to the Gulf of Corinth, and it is hard to think of another place where the setting so exactly suits the story. To the ancient Greeks it was the centre of the world. Zeus is said to have released two eagles from opposite ends of the earth, and they met here; a carved stone called the omphalos, the navel, marked the spot. The sanctuary of Apollo was the home of the Pythia, a priestess who sat on a tripod over a crack in the rock and delivered riddling answers that kings, generals and city founders paid dearly to hear.

The site is a long climb up the Sacred Way, between the foundations of treasuries built by Greek cities to hold their gifts, past the base of the Temple of Apollo and up to a theatre and a stadium high on the hill. Beyond a bend in the road, in the sanctuary of Athena, the round tholos with its three standing columns has become the emblem of the place. The museum holds the Charioteer, a bronze statue of astonishing calm, found buried after an earthquake. Above, the cliffs called the Phaedriades catch the light, and the Castalian spring runs beside the road.

For riders, Delphi is reached by one of the great roads in Greece. From Athens the route runs through Thebes and Livadeia, then climbs into the mountains toward Arachova, a stone village known for its woven rugs and winter skiers, with long bends and cool air. From Arachova the road drops toward Delphi along the face of the mountain with views over the olive grove to the sea, a sequence of corners that is a joy at a steady pace. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel and for tour coaches that take the bends wide.

Delphi itself is small, so for fuel, Arachova or Amfissa, about twelve kilometres away, is the safe choice. Go early to the site to avoid the heat and the crowds, and ride in spring or autumn, when the hills are green or golden. Winter brings snow to the upper roads.
t.parnassus high road@38.6,22.6:
The road that leaves Arachova and climbs toward the ski station on Mount Parnassus is one of the best high roads in central Greece, and few visitors on the coach tours to Delphi ever take it. It starts in the town's last bends, where the stone houses give way to fir forest, and rises past the Kellaria and Fterolakka ski areas, with long views back down over the olive groves toward the Gulf of Corinth. Mount Parnassus itself reaches 2,457 metres, a massive block of limestone that was sacred to Apollo and the Muses in antiquity, and the road runs up most of its southern flank.

The ancient Greeks believed that the oracle at Delphi spoke the words of Apollo, delivered through the priestess known as the Pythia, and that the sanctuary stood at the centre of the world. The Corycian Cave, high on the plateau of Parnassus above Delphi, was a sacred place to Pan and the nymphs, and can be reached on foot from the plateau. These associations give the mountain a presence that goes beyond its height.

The forest here is mostly Greek fir, which grows dark and dense on the lower slopes, giving way to open, rocky ground above the tree line. In spring, there are crocuses and wild tulips on the high meadows, and in summer, grazing sheep and goats wander across the road. The bends are tight and steady, with gradients that keep you in second and third gear, and the surface can be rough near the top, where winter frost and snowploughs do their damage. It is a quiet road for most of the year, except at ski-season weekends, when traffic from Athens fills it.

Be aware that conditions change quickly with height. Even when it is warm in Arachova, the upper part of the road can be cold and windy, and snow may linger into late spring. In winter the road is often icy or covered, and chains may be required for vehicles, so check before you go. Fog also rolls in quickly, and the drops at the edge are unprotected in places.

There are no services on the mountain itself outside the ski season, so fill up at Arachova, which has fuel stations, tavernas and cafes. Amfikleia, to the north-east, and Delphi to the south-west, are the other nearby places. Carry water, and take a layer you can add at the top.
t.areopoli@36.7,22.4:
On 17 March 1821, in the main square of Areopoli, the Mani chieftain Petros Mavromichalis raised a flag of revolt against the Ottoman empire, and the Greek War of Independence began in earnest. The town was then called Tsimova, and it was later renamed Areopoli, after Ares, the god of war, in honour of the fighting spirit of the Maniots. That spirit is easy to credit when you walk around. The old town is a compact knot of stone tower houses, each with narrow windows and a fortress-like profile, built by rival clans who spent centuries feuding over land, honour and the right to the best olives.

The Mani is the central of the three southern prongs of the Peloponnese, a rugged, arid limestone peninsula under the mass of the Taygetos range. Its stony slopes are terraced with olive groves and dotted with chapels, many with Byzantine frescoes. The Maniots were famed for their independence, clan loyalties and their lament songs, and they remained resistant to outside rule for much of their history. Areopoli is the capital of Outer Mani, with a busy main square, a statue of Mavromichalis, a small museum of the revolution and several cafés and tavernas under plane trees.

A few kilometres to the south, the Diros caves are among the most remarkable in Greece, a long system of underground lakes and caverns hung with stalactites, which visitors tour by boat. They are well worth a stop, and they are cool on a hot day. The nearby coast has quiet coves and small fishing harbours, and the sea is deep blue.

The roads of the Mani are a delight for a motorcyclist, if you like your tarmac narrow and your views huge. From Areopoli, you can ride north towards Kardamyli, along the Taygetos coast, in a road of tight bends and sea views, or south to the tip of the peninsula through a landscape of stone and sky. The surface varies from smooth to patched, goats and sheep occupy the road in the early morning, and the afternoon heat in summer can be fierce. Spring, with wild flowers on the hills, and autumn are the best seasons. Winter brings rain and the occasional dusting of snow on Taygetos.

Areopoli is the largest town in the area, with fuel stations, supermarkets and banks, and it is the sensible place to fill up before heading south, where services become sparse. Local specialities include syglino, smoked pork, and the oil-rich cheeses of the region, and a plate of fried potatoes with eggs is a classic.
t.gerolimenas@36.5,22.4:
Gerolimenas sits in a deep, sheltered bay near the tip of the Mani, and it is the last proper harbour before the land runs out. The name is thought to come from the Greek for sacred harbour, a name that suggests an ancient history, though the village as it stands was developed mostly in the nineteenth century, when the Maniot families made money from trade and the sea. A few tall stone houses stand along the front, with a small quay, a handful of fishing boats and a taverna or two, and the water is startlingly clear.

The southern Mani is among the wildest corners of mainland Greece. The land is dry and stony, with scattered tower houses on every ridge, built in clusters that look like small fortresses, and abandoned villages whose roofs have fallen in. Vathia, a few kilometres to the east, is the most famous, a village of tall stone towers that stands almost empty on a bare hill, a haunting sight at sunset. Beyond Gerolimenas, the peninsula tapers toward Cape Tainaron, also called Matapan, the southernmost point of mainland Greece, where ancient Greeks believed there was an entrance to the underworld, and where there are ruins of a temple to Poseidon.

Riding here is slow, rough and gorgeous. The road from Areopoli runs south through low hills, past stone walls, prickly pear cactus and the occasional lonely chapel, and it is narrow, with tight bends and uneven surfaces, so a steady pace is wise. Goats on the road are common. In summer the heat is intense and the landscape bleached, so early morning and late afternoon are the better times, and spring offers wild flowers and green hills. In winter, storms can lash the coast, but the air is clear and the light superb.

There are few people around. In the evening, the village is quiet, with the sound of waves and the smell of grilled fish from the taverna, and the stars are bright in the clear air. The sea is excellent for swimming from the small stone pier, in water deep blue and cold at the edges. Quiet is the point.

Fuel is the main practical concern. There is none in Gerolimenas, and services in the southern Mani are sparse, so fill your tank at Areopoli, about twenty kilometres to the north, or at Gythio further on. A few small shops sell basics, and the tavernas serve fresh fish, octopus, and local lamb with lemon potatoes. Bring cash, as card machines are not universal.
t.cape tainaron@36.4,22.5:
The last proper road in the Mani runs out at a scatter of stone, a lighthouse and a lot of wind, and that is Cape Tainaron, the southernmost tip of mainland Greece. Ride south from Areopoli or Gytheio through the tower-house villages of the Deep Mani and the landscape gets steadily barer: limestone ridges, terraced walls with nothing growing on them, silver olive groves in the folds, and the Taygetos range standing behind you like a wall. The surface is mostly decent but narrow, and goats treat the tarmac as part of the pasture, so ride the blind bends as if one is waiting around each.

The old name matters here. Ancient Greeks believed a cave near Tainaron was an entrance to Hades, and Herakles was said to have dragged Cerberus out through it. There was a temple of Poseidon on the cape too, and in antiquity the place was a sanctuary and a landmark for sailors dreading the rounding of the peninsula. Today you walk the last stretch on a path rather than ride it, and you should, because the sea opens out to the horizon with nothing between you and Libya but water. Mani people were famous for their feuds, and the stone towers you pass all the way down were built partly for that, partly to keep the family's pride in the skyline.

Be sensible about supplies. Tavernas in the nearby villages tend to open on a seasonal rhythm, so a late lunch is safer than an early one, and anything you find will be simple: grilled fish, lemon-heavy salads, local sausage with orange peel.

Come in spring or October if you can. In April the slopes are green and dotted with poppies, and the light over the water is soft; in August the heat and the glare are punishing in leathers. Late afternoon is best of all, when the stone turns gold and the ride back north has the sun behind you. It is a dead end, so you will ride the same road twice, but the second time the view over your shoulder is the better one.
t.kalambaka@39.7,21.6:
Kalambaka sits at the foot of a cliff that does not look real. Behind the town the Thessalian plain simply ends, and a wall of grey-brown rock towers up in columns and domes, with the monasteries of Meteora perched on the summits. The nearest sizeable settlement is Kalambaka itself, with around eight thousand people, and the village of Kastraki hugs the rocks just 1.6 km away. For a rider, this is the natural gate to the Pindus mountains as well: the road to Metsovo and the Katara Pass climbs out of the plain from here.

The rocks are conglomerate and sandstone laid down by an ancient river delta, then split and carved by water and wind over millions of years into those towers. Hermits first lived in the caves and crevices, and from the fourteenth century monks built monasteries on the tops, hauling people and goods up in nets and baskets or on rope ladders. Six are still active today. The ride up to the monasteries is a short, twisty climb with hairpins and tour coaches, so go early or late, ideally near sunrise or an hour before sunset when the cliffs glow orange and the buses have gone.

As a base, Kalambaka is easy. It is a proper town, so you will find fuel, ATMs, supermarkets and plenty of tavernas around the main street and the square, and the grilled meat is reliably good. Greek cooking in this part of the country leans on lamb, feta and the local pies, and the thick pie crust filled with greens and cheese is worth ordering. Parking a bike beside the cafes is simple and nobody minds.

Plan for weather. Thessaly can be hot and still in summer, and the plain bakes by midday, while winter brings cold mornings and fog in the valley. The best months are May, June and September to October. Behind Kalambaka, the road toward the mountains is where the route really starts, so top up the tank here, because the Pindus villages are small and the next dependable pumps are not guaranteed until you drop down the far side.
t.metsovo@39.8,21.2:
Metsovo is a stone mountain town in the Pindus, about a thousand metres up, and it has a character of its own, thanks largely to its people. Many of the inhabitants are Vlachs, also called Aromanians, a community with its own Latin-derived language and a history as shepherds, traders and craftsmen who moved with their flocks across the Balkans. The town has long been prosperous, thanks to the patronage of wealthy benefactors, and the stone mansions with their wooden balconies and slate roofs speak of confidence. On weekends, the older residents still wear traditional dress, and you may hear Vlach spoken in the street.

The town sits on a steep hillside above a deep gorge, with the high Pindus ridges all around, covered in beech, fir and black pine. Metsovo is known for its smoked cheese, Metsovone, a firm, sharp cheese with a smoky flavour, and for its red wine, Katogi, made from local grapes and Cabernet Sauvignon grown on the slopes. The Tositsa and Averoff families, benefactors who made fortunes abroad, built museums, schools and a gallery in the town, and the folk museum, in a restored mansion, shows how a wealthy Vlach family lived. The Averoff Gallery holds a collection of nineteenth- and twentieth-century Greek painting.

The old road to Ioannina, the national road over the Katara Pass, climbs from Metsovo toward the high pass, and a motorway tunnel, built as part of the Egnatia Odos, now takes most of the heavy traffic under the mountain, which makes the old road quiet and pleasant for riders. The corners are broad, the surface is generally good, and the views over the forested slopes are lovely. Winters are cold and snowy, and the roads may need chains, while summers are cool and fresh, and spring and autumn are the best seasons for colour, particularly the red and gold of autumn beech woods.

Metsovo is a real town, with a population of a few thousand, and has what a rider needs. Fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and tavernas line the main road, and there are plenty of small hotels and guesthouses. Ioannina, about thirty-one kilometres to the west, is a much larger city with all services. The food here is hearty mountain fare, with grilled meats, pies filled with greens or cheese, and a hot dish of trahana soup in the cold weather. A glass of Katogi and a plate of smoked cheese in the evening is the proper reward.
t.katara pass@39.8,21.1:
The Katara Pass, at 1,705 metres, is the highest paved road pass in Greece, and it carries the old main road between Ioannina and Trikala over the spine of the Pindus. The name means curse, which is generally supposed to refer to the many travellers who crossed it in snow and wind and regretted the day they set out. For centuries it was the only route between Epirus and Thessaly, and trade caravans and armies crossed it along stone paths, long before the road was paved. Since the new motorway tunnels were opened, most of the traffic bypasses it, leaving the pass quiet.

The road climbs from Metsovo through dense forest of beech and fir, with long, easy bends and a surface that is mostly good, though it is patched in places after winter. Higher up, the trees thin out, and you emerge onto an open, windswept saddle of mountain grass and rock, with the high ridges of the Pindus rolling away in layers. At the top there is often cloud or mist, and the temperature can be ten degrees lower than in the town. A small chapel sits near the road, and in winter, the area is a skiing destination, with ski lifts on the slopes nearby.

For riders, Katara is one of the finest roads in northern Greece. The bends are smooth and rhythmic, the traffic is light, and the scenery is vast and empty. There is a sense of crossing something significant. Check the weather before you go, since fog, hail and thunderstorms can build quickly, even in summer. In winter, snow often closes the road, and snow chains are required. The best time is late spring, when the meadows are green and wild flowers bloom, or early autumn, when the forests turn gold.

The Pindus is bear and wolf country, and the largest wild areas in Greece lie here. You are unlikely to see either, but you may spot griffon vultures and eagles over the ridges, and sheep dogs, large and white, guard the flocks in summer, and it is wise to keep a respectful distance. Shepherds still bring their flocks to the high pastures, in a pattern of movement that goes back centuries.

Metsovo, about ten kilometres away, has stations and cafés, and Ioannina, further west, is the nearest large city. Bring warm clothes and a waterproof, because conditions change quickly at this altitude.
t.monodendri@39.9,20.7:
Monodendri is the village from which you see the Vikos Gorge best, and that is reason enough to come. It sits on the lip of the canyon in the Zagori region of Epirus, in north-western Greece, a district of about forty stone villages tucked into the folds of the Pindus mountains. The gorge, cut by the Voidomatis river, is about twelve kilometres long and nearly a thousand metres deep in places, and it is recorded as one of the deepest in the world in proportion to its width. From the Oxya viewpoint, a short walk from the village, you look straight down the grey limestone walls to the green ribbon of river below, with eagles and vultures floating at eye level.

The village itself is a lovely tangle of cobbled lanes, stone houses with slate roofs and wooden balconies, and a small square shaded by a plane tree. Just outside, the monastery of Agia Paraskevi, built in 1413, clings to the cliff edge, with a small chapel and a terrace over the abyss. Zagori's villages were wealthy in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, because many of their men emigrated to work as merchants and craftsmen and sent money home, which paid for the mansions, schools and the elegant stone bridges that arch over the streams. The whole district is a cultural landscape and a recognised heritage area.

The riding in Zagori is a joy, with narrow, winding roads that climb and drop through beech and oak woods, past stone bridges and mountain streams, and every bend reveals a new village or view. The surface is generally good but patchy, with some loose gravel, and hairpins on the steep sections. There is almost no traffic, apart from the occasional local pickup truck and a few walkers' cars. Fog can fill the valleys in autumn, and winters are cold, with snow on the high ground, so late spring and early autumn are best. The cobbled streets of the villages themselves can be slippery, especially when wet.

The country is rich in wildlife. Brown bears, wolves and chamois live in the high mountains, though you are unlikely to meet one, and the gorge is a haven for birds of prey. Walking trails of all difficulties run through the area, including the long descent into the gorge.

Ioannina, about forty kilometres away, is the nearest large city with services, so fill your tank there. Try the local pies, filled with wild greens and cheese, which are baked in a wood oven.
t.makrinitsa@39.4,23.0:
Makrinitsa is called the balcony of Pelion, and the name is exact. The village hangs on a steep slope more than six hundred metres above the Gulf of Volos, and from its terraces and the central square you look straight out over rooftops and plane trees to the blue water, with the city of Volos small and distant on the shore. The square, shaded by a huge plane tree and cooled by a marble fountain, is the centre of village life, and the church of the Virgin, with its fine frescoes and carved iconostasis, stands beside it. In the late afternoon, when the sun slants through the leaves, it is one of the most pleasant places in Greece.

The village is a maze of cobbled lanes and steps, lined with stone mansions with slate roofs, wooden upper floors and flower-filled balconies. Many of the houses date to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when Pelion's villages grew rich from silk, olive oil and trade, and today they are mostly guesthouses and tavernas. Cars are not permitted in the lanes, so you leave the bike at the edge and walk, which suits the place. The streets are steep, and a good pair of shoes is advisable.

Pelion has a place in Greek myth as the home of the centaurs, and in particular of the wise centaur Chiron, who taught Achilles, Jason and Asclepius. The mountain is green and wet, with chestnut, beech, plane and oak forests, and apple orchards on the slopes, and the climate is cooler and wetter than most of Greece. The air smells of wood smoke and damp leaves, and in autumn the chestnuts fall on the road.

The ride up from Volos is a series of tight hairpins through woods, with the road narrow and the surface in reasonable shape, though in places patched and slippery when wet. It is not a road for speed, but a good one for a leisurely climb with views opening behind you. Rain is common in the mountains, and fog sometimes covers the village, so carry waterproofs. In summer, weekends fill the lanes with visitors from Volos and Athens, and parking is limited, so come on a weekday if you can. Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild weather and fewer people.

The village has several small tavernas and cafés serving local dishes such as spetsofai, a stew of sausage and peppers, and spoon sweets, preserved fruit in syrup. Tsipouro, a clear grape spirit, is the local drink. Fuel is not available in the village, so fill up in Volos or at Agria, about seven kilometres away, on the coast.
t.chania pelion@39.4,23.0:
Up above Makrinitsa, where the villages thin out and the forest takes over, the road reaches a wide mountain saddle called Chania at about twelve hundred metres. It is the closest Pelion has to a high alpine place, with a small ski area on the slopes and a scattering of cafés and lodges that serve walkers in summer and skiers in winter. The surroundings are a deep, cool forest of beech, fir and chestnut, dotted with clearings where mist drifts through the trees, and the air is crisp even in July. After the heat of the plains, it feels like a different country.

The ski centre, Agriolefkes, is small and modest, but it gives the mountain a role in the winter economy, and the road is regularly cleared of snow. In summer, the slopes become meadows full of wild flowers, with bees and butterflies, and the area is a base for walks through the beech woods. The Pelion forests are among the greenest in Greece, and they are home to wild boar, foxes, jackals and a wide range of birds, including woodpeckers and jays. The soil is deep and the rainfall high, thanks to the moisture rising off the Aegean and the Pagasetic Gulf.

For motorcyclists, the road to Chania from Portaria is a fine climb, a series of broad hairpins and sweeping forest bends, with a good surface for the most part. Gradients are steady, and the road is wide enough for comfortable riding, though in places the edges are broken. In summer the traffic is light, and cool shade from the trees is a relief. From here you can continue on to the eastern coast and the villages of Zagora and Tsagarada, where the roads descend through chestnut forests toward the sea. In winter, snow and ice make the upper road hazardous, and chains may be required, so check the weather forecast.

The best time to come is late spring, when the forest is fresh and green, or autumn, when the beech and chestnut leaves turn gold. Fog and rain are common, even in summer, so bring waterproofs and a warm layer. Evening temperatures at this height can be surprisingly cool.

In season, a small cafe and taverna near the ski area serve hot drinks and grilled meat, and the Pelion habit of a long, slow lunch under the trees is well worth following.
t.tsagarada@39.4,23.2:
Tsagarada is not one village but four, strung down a steep wooded slope on the Aegean side of Pelion, each with its own square and church, and linked by lanes that wind through chestnut, plane and walnut trees. They climb from the sea toward the mountain crest, so that the highest hamlet has the smell of wet leaves and the lowest has a view over the water, and the whole thing feels more like a forest with houses in it than a village with trees. Streams run through the lanes and fountains splash everywhere. It is one of the wetter corners of Greece, and it shows.

The central square, in the hamlet of Agia Kyriaki, is dominated by an enormous plane tree, said to be about a thousand years old, with a hollow trunk wide enough for a small room and branches that shade the whole space. Under it you will find a kafeneio, a fountain and the church, and in the evening the whole village gathers there. The slate-roofed stone houses date mostly from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when the silk and olive trade enriched the district, and many have been turned into guesthouses.

The road here is the great pleasure. From Zagora or from the coastal junction, the road climbs and falls along the mountainside, in a long sequence of curves and hairpins through dense forest, with sudden gaps that open on a view of the Aegean far below. It is narrow, with a good but occasionally damp surface, and there are many blind corners, so keep your speed down and your eyes open. Cars come the other way in the middle of the road. After rain, leaves, mud and small rockfalls can litter the tarmac, and in winter, the higher roads can ice over. Spring and autumn are the loveliest times, and in summer the shade is a relief from the heat of the plains.

Below the village, steep paths and a winding road lead down to the beaches of Mylopotamos and Fakistra, where white pebbles and clear green water lie under cliffs of dark rock. The descent is spectacular, and the return climb is a test for any bike, but the swimming is superb.

Services are modest. The squares have tavernas, serving grilled meat, local cheese pies and fresh salads, and a few small shops sell basics. There is no reliable fuel in the village, so fill up at Agria, about fifteen kilometres to the west, or in Volos, and carry a layer for the evening chill.
t.milies@39.3,23.1:
Milies owes its fame to a train. In 1903, the narrow-gauge railway from Volos to Milies opened, built by the Italian engineer Evaristo de Chirico, the father of the painter Giorgio de Chirico, who spent part of his childhood in Volos. The track is only sixty centimetres wide, and the little steam train, nicknamed Moutzouris, crawls up the mountain through tunnels, over stone bridges and around the slopes of Pelion, with views of the gulf. The most famous structure on the line is the high stone viaduct at Kalamaki, with its curved arches. The train still runs on some days in summer for tourists, and on those days the village fills with visitors.

Long before the railway, the village was known for something else. In the early nineteenth century, Milies was a centre of Greek learning, home to a school and a library that helped keep the language and culture alive under Ottoman rule, and some of its scholars were figures in the Greek Enlightenment. The library, founded in the early 1800s, still survives, and the village church of the Taxiarchs has fine frescoes and carved woodwork. A fountain and a plane tree stand in the main square, and the stone houses with their wooden balconies lean over narrow lanes.

For motorcyclists, the road up from Volos winds through olive groves and orchards before entering the forest, and it is a pleasant, mostly well-surfaced climb, with plenty of bends and shade. The roads between Milies, Vizitsa and Agios Georgios Nilias are narrower, with patches of rough tarmac, but the traffic is light and the scenery is excellent, with sea views appearing through the trees. It is damp country, and after rain the surface can be slick, with leaves and mud on the bends. In winter, the upper roads may be icy, so spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Pelion is also a land of apples, chestnuts and herbs. The slopes are covered in orchards, and the local honey, sweets and tsipouro are sold in village shops. The area is known for its herbal remedies, a tradition that goes back to the centaur Chiron, the mythical healer who lived on the mountain.

The village has a few tavernas and cafés, serving local pies and stews, and some small shops. For fuel, the nearest sure source is Agria, about twelve kilometres away, or Volos, so fill up before the climb. Weekdays are quieter than weekends.
t.patchwork road@43.6,142.4:
The hills around Biei in central Hokkaido are so regularly patterned that visitors compare them to a quilt, and that is the origin of the name. Fields of wheat, potatoes, beans, sunflowers and flowers run over low rounded slopes in strips of green, gold, yellow, brown and purple, bounded by rows of larch and poplar and separated by narrow farm roads. The Tokachidake range, a line of volcanic peaks that smoke gently from time to time, rises on the horizon, and the whole scene shifts with the season, from the pale green of early summer to the gold of harvest and the white sheet of winter.

The Patchwork Road is a loose network of country lanes, rather than a single route, and the pleasure is in wandering. The roads are smooth, wide and well maintained, with gentle rises and falls that show off the fields to best effect, and the traffic is mostly tour cars and farm machinery. The speed limit is low and cameras and patrols are not unusual, but nobody here is in a hurry. Several lone trees on the hills have become minor celebrities because they appeared in advertisements, and people stop to photograph them. One, a poplar known as the tree of Ken and Mary, appeared in a car commercial in the 1970s and has drawn visitors ever since.

The farms are real and working, so it is important to stay on the road and keep out of the fields, since trampled crops and parked vehicles are a long-standing grievance among the farmers. Pull in only where there is space, and never block a farm track. Summer is the main season, from July to September, when the colours are strongest and the days are long. In late summer the harvest brings trucks and combines onto the roads. In winter, the road is covered in snow and ice, and riding is not advised.

Practical matters are easy. Asahikawa, about nineteen kilometres away, is Hokkaido's second city and has fuel, supermarkets and shops, and Biei itself has stations, cafes and bakeries. Local produce includes potatoes, sweetcorn, melons and dairy, and the soft ice cream flavoured with local milk is a ritual stop. Roadside stands often sell vegetables on an honour system.

Hokkaido has an excellent reputation among riders, with wide empty roads, cool summers and a friendly attitude to touring motorcyclists. Watch for deer and foxes at dusk and dawn, and keep a good gap on blind crests. The early morning light on the fields is the best.
t.biei@43.6,142.5:
Biei is a small farming town in the middle of Hokkaido that has made its living from being looked at. Its fame comes from the hills around it, the rolling patchwork of crops that stretches to the Tokachidake range, and from a few specific photogenic sights, including a pond so blue it looks fake. The Blue Pond was created by accident, after dams were built to protect the area from mudflows from the volcano, and the water is coloured by minerals suspended in it, mainly aluminium compounds that scatter the light. It shifts from milky turquoise to deep sapphire depending on the weather and the angle of view, and in winter it is lit up after dark.

The town itself is modest, with a central street, a small station built of local stone, and shops that sell vegetables, cheese and jam. Its greatest asset is a bakery culture and a love of fresh produce, and the potatoes, tomatoes and sweetcorn here are among the best in Japan. Cafes and restaurants serve farm-to-table meals, and the dairy is excellent. For a hearty meal, curry made with local vegetables or a plate of Hokkaido-style grilled lamb, known as Genghis Khan, is a good bet. There is also a hot spring area in the hills to the east, Shirogane Onsen, with a waterfall nearby that falls over a cliff in a graceful white veil.

For riders, Biei is a hub for exploring the hills. Smooth roads run north and south of the town, often with light traffic, and long views over the fields toward the mountains. The surface is excellent, the bends are gentle and the scenery is a constant. In summer there are lots of tour buses, rental cars and cyclists, so patience is needed, and the speed limits are low. The ride up to Shirogane Onsen and beyond to the Tokachidake slopes is a rewarding climb into forest and volcanic landscape, with steam rising from vents and a feeling of being close to something alive.

The town is easy for practical matters. Fuel stations are on the main road, convenience stores are open late, and there is a good choice of places to stay, from small inns to farm guesthouses. Asahikawa, about twenty-two kilometres away, has the airport, the city amenities and an excellent zoo. Roads in winter are icy and snow can fall from November to April.

The best months are July and August for flowers and green hills, and September for golden wheat and clear air. A morning ride through the hills, with mist lying in the hollows, is the high point of the whole region.
t.furano@43.3,142.4:
Furano lies in the middle of Hokkaido, in a basin ringed by the Tokachi mountains and the Yubari range, and it is known for lavender. The fields of Farm Tomita and the surrounding farms turn purple in July, and visitors come from across Japan to see them. The climate here is continental, with hot summers and cold, snowy winters, and the long hours of summer light let farmers grow lavender, melons, potatoes and onions. The town is small, and the settlement of Shimo-furano is right beside it, while Ashibetsu, a former coal town, lies thirty kilometres or so away.

The landscape is different from the rest of Japan. Fields stretch in tidy patches of colour, which gives the road its patchwork name, hedged by lines of poplars and set against the dark volcanic profile of Mount Tokachi in the distance. The roads are straight and gently rolling, with the occasional curve around a hill, and the surface is generally excellent. Hokkaido is a favourite with touring riders because of the space and the low traffic, and in summer there are many bikers on the island. Watch for deer, foxes and the occasional bear, though sightings near the main roads are rare.

Hokkaido was settled by Japanese farmers mainly in the late nineteenth century, and before that the island was the land of the Ainu people, whose language gave many places their names. Furano itself comes from the Ainu word for stinky, probably for a smelly river. The food is excellent: dairy products, sweet corn, melons and Furano wine, plus the soup curry that Sapporo made famous, and ramen with butter and corn.

For practical matters, Furano has fuel stations, convenience stores and many cafes. In July, lavender season brings crowds, and accommodation books up, so reserve ahead. Alternatively, go in June for fresh green fields, or in September for harvest and clear air. In winter the town becomes a ski resort, with powder snow that is famous among skiers. Early evening light on the fields is soft and golden, and it is a lovely time for a final slow ride.
t.engure@57.2,23.2:
Engure is a quiet place on the Gulf of Riga, where the land is flat, the pine forests run right to the dunes and the water is shallow and cold. The village sits on a coast of pale sand and low dunes in western Latvia, with a long beach where you can walk for kilometres without meeting anyone, and behind it lies Lake Engure, a big, shallow, reed-fringed lake that is one of the most important bird habitats in the country. It is a protected nature park, with thousands of waterfowl, from ducks and grebes to cranes and swans, and in spring and autumn the migration brings clouds of birds.

This is the Kurzeme coast, and its history is wrapped up with fishing and the sea. Villages here were built by fishermen, whose boats were drawn up on the beach and whose nets were hung on poles to dry, and traces of the tradition survive in the little museums, smokehouses and boats on the shore. The smoked fish of this coast, flounder, herring and sprats, is excellent, and roadside stalls sell it still warm from the smoker. The Baltic Sea also produces amber, which washes up after storms, and local people hunt for it along the tideline.

The riding is easy and flat, with long straight roads running through pine forest, past farms and small villages, and the surface is generally decent, though some of the side roads are gravel. The scenery is gentle, a sea of green with the occasional church spire, and traffic is light except on summer weekends when Riga people come to the beaches. Be careful of elk and deer at dusk and dawn, since collisions are a real risk in Latvia, and watch for sandy patches on the road. The light is long in summer, and in June it barely gets dark at all.

The nearest larger town is Tukums, about twenty-two kilometres away, which has fuel stations, supermarkets and a pleasant old centre, and it is wise to fill there, since the villages on the coast have limited services. Engure itself has a shop, a cafe or two and guesthouses, though opening hours can be short outside the summer. Bring mosquito repellent in the warmer months, because the forest and the lake keep the insects well supplied.

The best time to come is in June or early September, when the weather is mild and the beaches are quiet. A swim in the Baltic is bracing, and the sunsets over the sea are long and gold.
t.roja@57.5,22.8:
Roja is a fishing town at the mouth of a small river in north-western Latvia, on the coast of the Gulf of Riga, and it carries the sea in its character. The harbour is a working one, with fishing boats, a small marina and a smell of salt and smoke, and the town has a long maritime history. A fishing museum tells the story of how people along this coast lived and worked, from the sailing boats of the nineteenth century to the large collective fleets of the Soviet era, when Roja was a significant fishing port. The beach nearby is wide, clean and often empty, and a pine forest runs along the dunes.

The area is on the edge of the Slitere region and the Livonian Coast, where a small community of Livonians, a Finno-Ugric people closely related to the Estonians, once lived in fishing villages. Their language is almost gone, but the culture is still honoured, and a few villages near Cape Kolka, the northern tip of Kurzeme, keep the traditions alive with festivals and flags. The Cape itself, where the Baltic Sea meets the Gulf of Riga in a swirl of waves, is a short ride to the north and a popular spot for watching the clash of currents and for finding amber on the shore.

The ride along the coast is a pleasure of an unhurried kind. The road runs through forest and beside dunes, with the sea glimpsed through the trees and the surface generally good. It is flat and quiet, with long straights and easy bends, and few vehicles outside the summer season. Elk and deer cross at dusk, so be watchful, and expect patches of sand blown across the tarmac. In summer, the roads are busy with local holidaymakers, but they are never crowded. Autumn is a lovely time, with the forest turning gold and the sea moody and grey.

Roja has a handful of shops, cafes and a small petrol station, though the choice is limited, and the larger town of Talsi, about thirty-two kilometres inland, has more stations and supermarkets. It is sensible to fill the tank in Talsi or Tukums before heading up the coast. Local food focuses on fish, with smoked flounder and salmon, fish soup and rye bread, and you can buy it from kiosks near the harbour.

The sunset here, over the open water, can last a very long time in summer, and the sky turns every colour from orange to deep blue.
t.cape kolka@57.8,22.6:
Cape Kolka is the place where Latvia comes to a point, and where two seas meet. The Baltic Sea lies to the west and the Gulf of Riga to the east, and at the tip, a long sandy spit extends into the water, so you can watch waves from two directions collide. It is a flat, windswept, quiet place, with pine forest behind and a beach of pale sand strewn with driftwood. The nearest town of any size is Roja, about thirty kilometres away, and the nearer settlements are small fishing villages, so fuel and supplies need planning.

The area is part of Slītere National Park, which protects a remarkable stretch of coast, including old dunes, wet forests and the Blue Hills, an ancient shoreline now several kilometres inland. Migrating birds funnel along the cape in spring and autumn, and it is one of the best places in northern Europe to watch them. Kolka itself was historically home to the Livonians, a small Finnic people whose language is almost gone, but whose culture is honoured here. A memorial and a Livonian community house recall their fishing tradition.

The ride along the Kurzeme coast is gentle and peaceful rather than dramatic. The road runs through pine forest and coastal villages, with occasional gravel stretches, and the surface varies from good asphalt to rough patches. Traffic is light, and the distances are long, so the pleasure is the quiet and the smell of resin and salt. Elk and deer cross the road at dawn and dusk, so slow down in the forest. Wind off the sea can be strong, and the water is cold even in summer.

At Kolka, there is a small lighthouse and a viewing point, plus a cafe in season, but options are limited. Fill the tank in Roja or Ventspils before heading out, and carry water. Smoked fish, particularly flounder and herring, is a coastal staple, along with dark rye bread and local beer. Midsummer, around the twenty-third and twenty-fourth of June, is a big celebration in Latvia, with bonfires and flower wreaths, and the northern light lingers late into the night. It is a lovely place to finish a ride and watch the sun go into the sea.
t.riga@57.0,24.1:
Riga is the largest city in the Baltic states, and it wears its history on its facades. The old town, with its cobbled lanes, Hanseatic merchant houses and church spires, was founded in 1201 by the German bishop Albert, and for centuries the city was a leading trading port. The district of Art Nouveau buildings, built in the early twentieth century, is one of the richest in Europe, with more than seven hundred buildings decorated with masks, sphinxes and swirling ornament. Both areas are on the UNESCO list. About 740,000 people live in the city, so there is no shortage of fuel, hotels or food.

As a place to begin a ride, Riga is straightforward. The roads out to the coast are wide and well kept, and once you pass the suburbs the land flattens into pine forest and farmland. The Vidzeme coast road runs northeast along the Gulf of Riga, with sandy beaches, dunes and small fishing villages. Traffic in the city is typical for a capital, and the trams and cobbles in the old town are slippery when wet, so take care. Park the bike in a secure place.

The Central Market, housed in five huge former Zeppelin hangars, is worth a visit for breakfast: smoked fish, rye bread, pickles, berries and dairy products in great quantity. Latvian food is simple and hearty, with grey peas and bacon, potato pancakes, sour cream and dark bread, and the local balsam, a herbal liqueur, is an acquired taste. The Daugava river runs through the city, and the view from the tower of St Peter's church takes in the whole of the old town and the river.

The best season for riding is late May to early September, when the days are long and the weather mild. In June, it hardly gets dark. Winter is cold and icy, with snow and sub-zero temperatures. The Baltic is not a warm sea, but beaches at Jurmala, just west of the city, are popular in summer. Before leaving, take a short walk through the old town at morning, when the streets are quiet, and then head north into the open.
t.saulkrasti@57.3,24.4:
Saulkrasti means sun coast, which is a bold name for a place on the Baltic, and the town has spent more than a century living up to it. It lies about forty kilometres north of Riga, on a strip of white sand backed by dunes and tall pine woods, and it began as a string of fishing hamlets before the railway brought holidaymakers from the capital in the late nineteenth century. Today it is the main seaside resort of the Vidzeme coast, a town of wooden villas, a long beach promenade and a pier, with a gentle, slightly old-fashioned air.

The beach is the main attraction, a broad stretch of fine sand that slopes slowly into the water, with a dune ridge behind covered in pine and heather. A boardwalk runs through the dunes and the forest, and in summer the beach fills with sunbathers, while the winter sea is wild and grey and lined with ice. After autumn storms, amber washes up on the shore, and some people walk the tideline for hours looking for it. Sunset over the sea is a favourite event, as the sun goes down to the west over the Gulf of Riga, and people gather on the dunes to watch.

For riders, the coast road north from Riga is easy, flat and pleasant, with pine forest on either side and occasional glimpses of the sea. The Via Baltica, the main road to Estonia, runs nearby and carries heavy traffic, so the smaller coastal roads are more fun. The surface is generally good, with some patches of wear, and the bends are gentle. Elk and deer are a hazard at dusk and dawn, and in summer the road is busy at weekends with Riga residents heading for the beach. The best months are June to September, though May and early October are quiet and often sunny.

Services are good. The town has fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and cafes, many of them geared towards summer visitors, and a range of guesthouses and hotels. Local food includes smoked fish, rye bread and fresh berries in season, and a plate of grilled salmon with potatoes and dill is a good way to finish the day. Sigulda, about twenty-nine kilometres inland, is a larger town and the gateway to the Gauja valley.

If you want to see the town at its best, walk the boardwalk at the end of the day, when the sun is low, the pines smell of resin and the beach is quiet.
t.salacgriva@57.8,24.4:
Salacgrīva sits where the Salaca river meets the Gulf of Riga, close to the Estonian border, and it has lived on fish for as long as anyone can remember. The river is known for its lampreys, eel-like fish that run upriver in autumn and are caught in traditional weirs, and the local people hold a lamprey festival and serve them grilled or smoked, an acquired taste that locals love. The harbour is full of boats, and the smell of smoke from the fish houses hangs over the town. Salmon, herring and sprats are also on the menu, and a plate of smoked fish with rye bread is the town's best advertisement.

The Salaca is one of the best known rivers of Vidzeme, and in its upper valley are sandstone cliffs and old mill sites. At the mouth, the river meets the sea in a flat landscape of reeds and sand, and a long, clean beach runs along the coast, with dunes and pine woods behind it. The area was once part of Livonia, and the old Livonian fishing culture left its mark on the place names and traditions. Some of the old fishing practices, including the use of stone-and-wood weirs, are still demonstrated, and the town has a small museum that tells the story.

The riding along the coast is gentle and peaceful, with flat roads through forest and farmland, and long straight sections with the sea glimpsed through the trees. The Via Baltica, the main highway, passes through the town, and carries traffic to and from Estonia, so it can be busy with lorries, but side roads are quiet. The surface is generally good, and the bends are easy. Be wary of elk at dawn and dusk, and of sand blown across the road near the dunes. Summer is the season for riding, with light evenings and warm weather, and autumn brings golden forests and misty mornings.

Salacgrīva has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, and there are guesthouses and a campsite. The nearest larger town is Limbaži, about thirty-four kilometres away, which has more services, and Ainaži, about twelve kilometres to the north, is a small town on the border known for its historic maritime school. Cash and cards are both widely accepted, and prices are reasonable.

The best time to come is late summer, when the sea is at its warmest and the fish are fresh. A walk along the beach in the evening is a good way to end the day.
t.ainazi@57.9,24.4:
Ainaži is the last town in Latvia, and the road that ends here sits right on the border with Estonia, with the Estonian town of Ikla just across. It is a quiet place of about thirteen hundred people, set on the shore of the Gulf of Riga, with a harbour, a few streets of low wooden houses and a long, sandy beach backed by pines. The next town of any size is Salacgrīva, about twelve kilometres south, which has the fuel, shops and cafes, so top up there. Ainaži is the end of the Vidzeme Seacoast Road, and it feels like it: calm, a little windswept, and happily forgotten.

The town has a particular history. In the nineteenth century, it was a centre of Latvian seafaring, and a maritime school opened here in 1864, the first in Latvia, training generations of sailors. A museum in the old school building tells the story of the seamen and shipbuilders who made the town prosperous. Nearby, the Salaca river and the coastal woods are part of the North Vidzeme Biosphere Reserve, a protected landscape of dunes, bogs and old pine forest that is rich in birds.

The riding along this coast is a gentle one. The road runs close to the sea, sometimes behind dunes, through forest, and past old fishing settlements with smokehouses and drying nets. The surface is generally good, but traffic is light and the pace is slow. Boulders and driftwood litter the beaches, a reminder of how many storms the shore takes. Moose and deer are present in the forest, and at dusk it is wise to ride cautiously.

For rest, the beach is the place. Sand and shallow water make for easy paddling, and the sunsets over the gulf are long and lovely in summer. Smoked fish is the coastal delicacy, often sold from roadside stalls, along with dark bread and local berries. Midsummer is a big celebration, and the bonfires and singing continue through the short night. The border is open under Schengen, so you can ride on into Estonia, but it makes a pleasant place to stop and look at the water.
t.llano@30.8,-98.7:
Llano sits on a bend of the Llano River in the central Texas Hill Country, where granite and limestone meet, and for a small town it has a surprising amount of stone about it. The courthouse square is built of the local pink granite, the old bridges are stone and iron, and the river itself runs clear and green over great pale boulders. The country around is the Llano Uplift, a dome of ancient Precambrian rock, some of the oldest exposed in Texas, pushed up through the younger limestone, and at nearby Enchanted Rock a huge bald granite dome rises out of the oak and juniper like the back of a buried whale.

The town was founded in the 1850s, and at the end of the century a mining and railway boom brought prospectors hunting for iron and graphite, though the great fortune never quite materialised. A big railway bridge over the river still stands as a ruin, along with an older road bridge, and both are worth a look. The courthouse square is the heart of the place, with its rows of low stone buildings, antique shops and cafes, and Llano has long been known across Texas for its barbecue, which is a serious matter here, cooked over oak and mesquite and served on butcher paper. If you arrive at lunchtime on a weekend, expect a queue and wait with good humour.

For a rider, Llano is the hinge of the Hill Country loop. The roads that leave it, Highway 29 east and west, Highway 16 south toward Fredericksburg, and the farm roads that wander off into the hills, are some of the best in Texas, with long rolling curves, dips, low-water crossings and views over cedar-covered ridges. In spring, the roadsides are carpeted in bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush, and in summer the heat is fierce and the afternoon thunderstorms violent. Autumn and early spring are the best seasons. Watch for deer, which are plentiful, and for gravel on the corners.

Llano has several stations, a supermarket, a few motels and plenty of places to eat, so it is a natural stop to fill up, rest and plan the next stretch. Kingsland and Buchanan Dam, near the Highland Lakes, are another handful of kilometres away if you need more. Park near the courthouse square, stroll round, and leave room for the barbecue. In summer, carry plenty of water and avoid riding in the middle of the afternoon.
t.isedotai stone circles@40.2,140.3:
In a quiet corner of Akita prefecture, near the town of Takanosu in the north of Japan's main island, a set of stone circles lies on a low terrace above the Yoneshiro river. The Isedotai stone circles were built around four thousand years ago by the people of the Jomon culture, hunter-gatherers who lived in the Japanese archipelago for more than ten thousand years and made some of the oldest pottery in the world. The site is part of the Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, listed by UNESCO in 2021, a series of seventeen sites across Hokkaido and the north of Honshu that illustrate the long, settled life of these people.

The circles are made of river stones, carefully arranged in rings and patterns, and they were probably used for rituals and burials. The site was found in the 1990s during the construction of an airport access road, and the road was rerouted to protect it. A small museum beside the circles displays pottery, clay figures and other finds from the excavations, and helps you picture the people who gathered here.

The riding in this part of Akita is gentle and scenic, with roads following the river valleys through rice fields, forests and small villages, with mountains rising on all sides. Traffic is light, and the roads are well surfaced and well signposted, though often narrow. To the north west lies the Shirakami-Sanchi, a vast beech forest straddling the border with Aomori, listed by UNESCO for its untouched woodland. To the east, the mountains of the Ou range offer winding roads and hot springs.

Takanosu, a town of around twenty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the larger city of Odate is about twenty kilometres away. Odate is the home of the Akita dog, the breed of the famous loyal dog Hachikō, who was born near here. The local food includes kiritanpo, rice pounded and grilled on skewers, then cooked in a hot pot with chicken and vegetables. Winters in Akita are long and snowy, making riding impossible for several months, but summer and autumn are beautiful, with green rice fields giving way to golden harvests and blazing autumn colours.
t.korekawa site@40.5,141.5:
The Korekawa site lies on the southern edge of Hachinohe, a port city on the Pacific coast of Aomori prefecture in northern Honshu, and it is one of seventeen locations in the UNESCO listing of the Jōmon prehistoric sites of northern Japan. The Jōmon were hunter-gatherers who lived in these islands for over ten thousand years, making some of the oldest pottery in the world and developing a remarkably settled, sophisticated way of life without farming. At Korekawa, waterlogged layers preserved things that usually vanish: wooden bowls, combs, bows and baskets, many of them coated in red lacquer, showing a level of craft that surprises everyone who sees them.

The Korekawa Jōmon Museum, next to the site, displays these finds, and it also houses one of Japan's national treasures: the Gasshō Dogū, a clay figure from about 3,500 years ago, sitting with knees drawn up and hands pressed together as if in prayer. It came from the nearby Kazahari site. Standing in front of it, you feel an odd kinship across the millennia.

Hachinohe itself is a working fishing port, one of the biggest in Japan, and its morning markets are legendary. Tatehana wharf hosts a huge Sunday market at dawn, where locals and visitors eat grilled fish, noodles and sweets among hundreds of stalls. The local dish is senbei-jiru, a soup in which special wheat crackers are broken into a broth with vegetables and meat or fish; it sounds odd and tastes excellent. Squid and mackerel are local pride.

For riders, Hachinohe is a gateway to some fine coastal roads. Head south along the Sanriku coast, with its rias, cliffs and fishing villages slowly rebuilt after the 2011 tsunami, or north towards the Shimokita peninsula and Lake Towada inland, a caldera lake with the beautiful Oirase gorge running out of it. The roads are well surfaced and traffic is light outside the city, but autumn brings heavy rain and winters are cold with snow, especially inland. Fuel and services are easy in a city of nearly a quarter of a million people. Be aware that Japanese petrol stations often close in the evening in rural areas, so fill up in town.
t.futatsumori site@40.7,141.2:
Futatsumori is a gentle hilltop near the town of Shichinohe in Aomori prefecture, overlooking Lake Ogawara, and to an untrained eye it is simply a grassy field among woods and farmland. But this is one of the largest shell mounds in the Tōhoku region, piled up by Jōmon people over thousands of years as they gathered shellfish from the lake and the sea, and it belongs to the same World Heritage group of Jōmon sites as the better-known Sannai-Maruyama. The shell heaps, rich in calcium, neutralised the acid soil and preserved bones, tools and ornaments that would otherwise have dissolved.

What makes Futatsumori particularly interesting is how the shell content changes over time. In earlier layers, the shells are mostly seawater species; later layers are freshwater clams, which tells archaeologists that Lake Ogawara was once an inlet of the sea and gradually became a lake as the coastline shifted. Bone needles, harpoons and even the buried remains of dogs show people living in close relationship with their environment and their animals. It is an archaeology of daily life rather than of kings.

Lake Ogawara itself is a large, shallow lake fed by rivers from the Hakkōda mountains and draining to the Pacific, famous for shijimi clams, smelt and eels. The landscape around is open, rolling and pastoral, with dairy farms, vegetable fields, and wide skies. In autumn, swans and other migrating birds gather on the water. The Hakkōda range to the west, with its volcanoes, hot springs and dense beech forests, is one of the great riding destinations of northern Japan.

The roads here are quiet and well surfaced, with some gentle curves through the farmland and around the lake shore, and in summer they are a joy. In winter, however, Aomori is one of the snowiest places in the world, and roads in the Hakkōda mountains are closed for months; spring brings the famous snow corridors on the Hakkōda-Towada Gold Line, where the snow walls can be several metres high when the road reopens. Misawa, fifteen kilometres off and home to a large air base, is where to refuel and eat properly. Shichinohe is smaller but has basics. Try the local garlic and Aomori apples.
t.archaeological site of tiryns@37.6,22.8:
Homer called it Tiryns of the great walls, and when you stand next to them you see that he was not exaggerating. The citadel rises from a low limestone ridge in the Argolid plain, and its walls are built of blocks so enormous that later Greeks decided only the Cyclopes, one-eyed giants, could have lifted them. The name stuck: Cyclopean masonry. Tiryns was one of the great centres of the Mycenaean world in the late Bronze Age, linked in legend to Heracles, who was said to have served its king, and its galleries are the best part. These long corridors are roofed with corbelled stone vaults, their walls polished smooth over the centuries by sheep sheltering from the weather.

The site is quiet compared to Mycenae, a short ride north, which means you can wander almost alone in the morning, with only lizards and the drone of insects for company. From the top you look out over a flat sea of orange and lemon groves to the bay and the fortress-crowned town of Nafplio. In spring, when the citrus blossoms, the whole plain smells sweet; in high summer the heat comes off the stones like an oven, so get here early or late.

Riding in the Argolid is a mix. The plain itself is a grid of straight, flat roads lined with groves and irrigation channels, nothing special except for the scent, and you will share them with farm pickups and the odd tractor. But head east towards Epidaurus and the roads begin to climb and twist through olive terraces and pine, with views back over the gulf, and the run to Ancient Epidaurus and its theatre, famous for its acoustics, makes a wonderful afternoon. South-west the coast road towards Leonidio is narrower and more dramatic still.

Nafplio, just three or four kilometres away, is the obvious base. It was the first capital of modern Greece after independence, and its old town of Venetian houses, bougainvillea and marble lanes is one of the prettiest in the country. Fuel, food and accommodation are everywhere, and the Palamidi fortress above town is worth the climb, though there are a lot of steps. Argos, to the north, is the other big town for supplies. Bring water to Tiryns; there is little shade and only basic facilities at the site.
t.tagoyano site@40.9,140.3:
In the far north of Honshu, on the Tsugaru plain of Aomori Prefecture, the Tagoyano site is a shell midden left by people of the Jomon period, the long era of hunter-gatherers who lived in Japan for over ten thousand years and made some of the oldest pottery in the world. The mound consists mainly of shells of shijimi, a small freshwater clam that thrived in the brackish water of the old lagoon. Along with the shells, archaeologists found pottery, tools and bones, and the site has become part of the Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021. There is little to see above ground now, just a grassy area and information boards, but the picture it paints is rich: people living by water, fishing, gathering, making beautiful vessels.

Nearby, at Kamegaoka, the famous Jomon figurine with goggle-shaped eyes, the shakoki dogu, was found, and the station at Kizukuri in Tsugaru town has a giant replica of it on its façade, a slightly surreal sight. To the north lies Lake Jusan, still producing shijimi clams today, and the Shirakami mountains with their ancient beech forest are to the south-west. Mount Iwaki, the single volcanic cone of the Tsugaru region, dominates the skyline on clear days.

The riding is relaxed. The Tsugaru plain is flat and agricultural, with rice fields and apple orchards. In autumn, the red apples hanging over the road are a sight in themselves, Aomori being the apple capital of Japan. Roads are straight and quiet, and the run along the coast of the Sea of Japan towards Ajigasawa and the Shirakami mountains, or north to the Tsugaru Peninsula and Cape Tappi, is wonderful, with cliffs, fishing villages and wind turbines. The main issue is the weather: the winters here are among the snowiest in the world, and riding season really runs from May to October.

Goshogawara, about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and it is home to the Tachineputa festival in August, with enormous illuminated floats. Shimokizukuri is closer for basics. Try a bowl of shijimi miso soup and a slice of apple pie, and listen for the Tsugaru shamisen, the fast, percussive folk music of the region, often played live in local restaurants.
At over a thousand metres in the mountains of Arcadia, on a rocky shoulder above the gorges of the Neda, stands one of the best preserved temples of ancient Greece, and since the 1980s it has stood under a vast white tent. The Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae was built in the fifth century BC by the people of nearby Phigalia, who dedicated it to Apollo the helper, it is said, for saving them from plague. Ancient writers attributed its design to Iktinos, one of the architects of the Parthenon. It was the first Greek monument in Greece to be listed as a World Heritage Site, in 1986.

The tent is there to protect the temple from weather while restoration continues, and it gives a strange, cathedral like atmosphere inside, with the grey limestone columns rising under the canopy. The temple is unusual in many ways: it faces north, it mixes Doric, Ionic and the earliest known Corinthian column, and its marble frieze, now in the British Museum in London, showed battles of Greeks against Amazons and centaurs.

The setting is the real reward. The mountains here are wild and bare, with oak and holly scrub, and the views stretch to the Ionian Sea on clear days. The air is clean and cool even in summer, and the silence is deep.

The roads to Bassae are some of the finest in the Peloponnese for riding: narrow, twisting and mostly empty, climbing from Andritsaina, a village of stone houses with a famous library, or from the coast at Tholo through Perivolia and Phigalia. Surfaces vary, with patches, gravel and the odd rockfall, and goats wander across. In winter, snow can close the road. Spring and autumn are perfect, and summer afternoons are hot.

Fuel is scarce in the mountains. Andritsaina has very limited services; Megalopoli, twenty two kilometres away, or the coast towns are safer bets. Kopanaki, to the south, is a small town. Bring water and food, and check the temple's opening hours, which can be short in winter.
t.sannai maruyama site@40.8,140.7:
On the outskirts of Aomori, at the northern tip of Honshu, archaeologists working on a site for a baseball stadium in the early 1990s found the remains of a large village of the Jomon period, a hunter gatherer culture that lived in Japan for over ten thousand years. Sannai Maruyama was occupied for around a thousand years, from about 5,900 to 4,200 years ago, and its finds changed ideas about the Jomon: long houses, pit dwellings, storehouses, burial grounds, and a huge structure of six massive chestnut posts, now reconstructed as a tall wooden tower. In 2021 it became part of the World Heritage listing of Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan.

The site is now a park with reconstructed buildings and a museum displaying pottery, clay figurines, lacquerware and jade ornaments. The Jomon made some of the oldest pottery in the world, decorated with cord markings, which gave the culture its name. Entry to the site and parts of the museum is free.

Aomori is a port city on Mutsu Bay, famous for apples, scallops and the Nebuta festival in early August, when giant illuminated floats of warriors and demons are paraded through the streets. The Nebuta Museum, by the station, displays floats all year round.

The riding around Aomori is outstanding.
