South of the city, the Hakkoda mountains rise to over fifteen hundred metres, and the road over them, Route 103 and Route 394, is a superb ride through beech forest and past hot springs such as Sukayu Onsen, with its huge cypress bath. Further south, Lake Towada and the Oirase gorge are famous for autumn colours. Winter snow is extremely heavy, and the mountain roads are closed or difficult from late autumn to spring.

Aomori handles fuel, cash and food. Order the scallops, eat an apple or two, and the miso curry milk ramen, an Aomori curiosity that is better than it sounds. Summer is mild and pleasant, autumn is glorious, and winter is long and snowy.
t.zagori cultural landscape@39.9,20.8:
In the mountains north of Ioannina, forty-odd stone villages cling to the slopes of the Pindus, linked by cobbled mule paths and arched bridges that seem to grow out of the rock. This is Zagori, a region of grey slate roofs, plane trees, rushing streams and one of the deepest gorges in the world, Vikos. In 2023 it was added to the World Heritage list as a cultural landscape, recognising how people and mountains shaped each other here over centuries.

The history is surprising. Under the Ottomans, Zagori enjoyed a privileged self-government, and many of its men went abroad as merchants and traders, to Constantinople, Romania and Russia. They sent money home, and that wealth built the solid mansions, churches and schools you see today, as well as the famous stone bridges, many paid for by local benefactors. Kipi, with its triple-arched bridge, and the area around Kalogeriko and Plakida are the classic places to see them.

For riding, Zagori is a delight and a challenge. The roads climbing from the Ioannina–Konitsa highway into the villages are narrow, steep and full of hairpins, often with drops on one side and no barriers. The climb to Papingo, with its tight switchbacks below the limestone towers of Astraka, is unforgettable. Surfaces are mostly good but can carry gravel, goats and the occasional fallen rock. In spring the hills are full of wildflowers; in autumn the forests glow. Winter brings snow to the higher villages.

Vikos Gorge, cut by the Voidomatis river, is best seen from the viewpoint near Monodendri, where the walls drop almost vertically for hundreds of metres. The Voidomatis is famously clear and cold, and the whole area lies within the Vikos–Aoös National Park, with bears, wolves and chamois in the high forests. The smell of wild oregano and pine fills the air on a warm day.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. Ioannina, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is the reliable choice, with Konitsa and the main road as backups; the villages themselves have no stations. Food, though, is everywhere: tavernas in every village serve pites, the region's famous savoury pies of greens, cheese or meat, along with grilled lamb and local wine. Stay a night if you can; the villages after dark are magical.
t.archaeological sites of mycenae and tiry:
The plain of Argos is a wide, flat basin of orange groves and olive trees tucked into the Peloponnese, and on its edge, a few kilometres apart, stand the two strongholds that gave the Greek Bronze Age its name. Mycenae sits on a rocky spur between two ravines, with Argos eleven kilometres to the south-west and the sea beyond, and Tiryns lies lower down near the shore, on a low rocky mound that once stood by the water.

Mycenae was the seat of kings in the late Bronze Age, in the centuries before about 1200 BC, and Homer made it the home of Agamemnon, who led the Greeks against Troy. The citadel is entered through the Lion Gate, a massive gateway with two carved lionesses above the lintel, one of the oldest monumental sculptures in Europe. Inside, the grave circles contained royal burials and gold, which Heinrich Schliemann dug up in 1876, and he famously telegraphed that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon. The golden mask he found was probably several centuries older than any Trojan War, but the romance has survived. Outside the walls, the Treasury of Atreus is a vast beehive tomb, with a lintel stone weighing over a hundred tonnes, and its cool interior is a surprise on a hot day. Tiryns, by contrast, is famous for its walls, built of boulders so huge that later Greeks said only Cyclopes could have lifted them.

The approach is enjoyable. From Athens the road runs along the Saronic Gulf and over the Corinth canal, then climbs through the pass of Dervenakia, with the motorway taking most of the traffic and tolls to pay. Smaller roads leading to Mycenae pass through orchards, with narrow bends and good views, and in spring the fields are bright with poppies. In summer the heat is fierce, particularly on the exposed hill, so go as early as you can, bring water and sunscreen, and check the opening hours, which are shorter in winter.

Argos, with twenty-two thousand people, is the town for fuel, supermarkets and a reliable lunch, and Nafplio, the handsome seaport half an hour away, is the best choice for an evening. Greek coffee, cold and iced frappé alike, is available in every village, and the local lamb and souvlaki are good. Autumn and spring are the best seasons for the light and the temperature.
t.phaistos@35.1,24.8:
The Messara is Crete's largest plain, a broad, fertile trough between the Psiloritis range to the north and the low Asterousia hills to the south, and at its western end a long ridge rises above the valley of the Geropotamos river. On that ridge stood Phaistos, one of the great palaces of the Minoan civilisation, the culture that flourished in Crete in the second millennium BC. The first palace was built around 1900 BC and destroyed by an earthquake, and the second, rebuilt on top, was a larger and more graceful construction, with a broad staircase to the west court, storerooms, royal apartments and a central courtyard. The view alone makes the climb worth it, with Mount Ida snowy in spring on one side and the blue haze of the Libyan Sea on the other.

Phaistos is the home of one of archaeology's great puzzles, a small clay disc found in the palace in 1908, stamped on both sides with a spiral of tiny pictures of heads, shields, birds and fish. The Phaistos Disc, dated to around 1700 BC, remains undeciphered, and nobody has even proved that it is a script. It is now kept in the archaeological museum in Heraklion, but the site has a copy in the shop.

Unlike Knossos, Phaistos was never reconstructed with concrete, and the ruins stand in their natural state, honey-coloured stone on a green hill. Close by are the Minoan villa of Agia Triada and the Roman city of Gortyn, which holds a famous law code carved in stone in the fifth century BC. Matala, a small beach resort on the coast, is known for the caves cut into its sandstone cliff, which were used as tombs and later by hippies.

The roads across the Messara are broad and straightforward, with olive groves and greenhouses on either side, and the corners come only when you climb into the hills. The surface can be rough, and goats and delivery vans share the road. Tympáki and Moíres have fuel, supermarkets and tavernas, and Zarós, in the hills, is known for its spring water. Go in spring, when the flowers are out and the heat is mild, because midsummer afternoons are brutal and the site has little shade.
t.odai yamamoto site@41.1,140.6:
Some of the oldest pottery in the world was found on a hillside near the northern end of Honshu, and nobody was looking for it. At Odai Yamamoto I, on the Tsugaru Peninsula in Aomori prefecture, archaeologists dug up fragments of fired clay that date back more than sixteen thousand years, among the earliest known ceramics in Japan, made by hunter-gatherers at the end of the last Ice Age. The site is part of the Jomon prehistoric sites of northern Japan, a World Heritage listing from 2021 that celebrates a long era of settled life without agriculture, with Sannai Maruyama as its best-known example.

You get here by travelling to the far north. The Tsugaru Peninsula points up at Hokkaido across a narrow strait, and the road follows the eastern shore past small harbours, fishing boats drying nets and grey, windy beaches. The land is open, the forests are cypress and beech, and the sky seems bigger than farther south. In summer it is cool and breezy, with sea fog in the mornings, and in winter the peninsula is battered by snow and gales that can close the roads.

Tsugaru has its own dialect, cuisine and music. The Tsugaru shamisen, played with a percussive, almost violent attack, came out of these windy shores, and the apple orchards inland around Hirosaki and Goshogawara produce a large share of Japan's apples. The writer Dazai Osamu was born in Kanagi, in the same district, and his travel book about the peninsula is still read. The ride from here connects to the Omori Katsuyama stone circle near Hirosaki, another Jomon site, by roads that run through orchard country, flat and quiet, with the snow-capped cone of Iwaki-san as a backdrop for much of the way.

Practicalities matter in the north. Goshogawara is the nearest town of any size, some thirty kilometres from here, and stations are thin on the east coast, so fill the tank in Aomori or Goshogawara before you start. The best time to ride is from late May to October, with the clear air of early autumn the finest, when the apples are ripening. Sites are modest in the open air, and the museum nearby is the place for the story, so allow time for it. Bring a windproof layer, because the Tsugaru breeze finds every gap.
t.apollo bay@-38.8,143.7:
Apollo Bay is where the Great Ocean Road stops being a headline and starts being a town. It sits in a curve of bay on the south coast of Victoria, with the forested Otway Ranges standing directly behind and Bass Strait rolling in from the front. A population of about fifteen hundred swells in summer when holidaymakers arrive, and you notice the change in how busy the main street and the foreshore are.

The famous road itself was built by returned soldiers after the First World War, starting in 1919 and finishing in 1932, as a memorial to the dead, and that history is easy to forget when you are focused on the next bend. Between Lorne and here the road clings to the cliffs and the views drop away to surf beaches. Inland from Apollo Bay, the ride changes character: you climb into the Otways, where tall mountain ash, tree ferns and damp green air replace the open sea, and the road narrows and twists through the shade.

This is a good place for the practical things. There is fuel in town, which matters because services thin out toward Cape Otway and beyond, and there are plenty of cafes, bakeries and fish and chip shops along the main street, with a bay view if you sit outside. The harbour is a working fishing port, and the smell of salt and diesel is part of it.

Nearby is plenty to see. Cape Otway Lighthouse, built in the 1840s, is one of the oldest on the Australian mainland. Koalas live in the gum trees by the road around Kennett River, and you can often spot them without a walk. Weather matters: the Southern Ocean produces rain, wind and sudden cold even in summer, so carry a waterproof layer. Early morning is the best time to ride, before the coach traffic gets going, and weekdays are calmer than weekends.
t.kydonia@35.5,24.0:
Kydonia is the old name of Chania, and the city carries its past visibly. The Minoans had a settlement here on the Kastelli hill, above what became the Venetian harbour, and ancient writers mention Kydonia as one of the leading cities of Crete. The Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Venetians and Ottomans each left something on the same rocky ground, and today you find all of them stacked in the old town: Venetian palazzi, Ottoman mosques, a lighthouse at the end of the mole, and a harbour front lined with tavernas.

Chania sits on the north-west coast of Crete, with the White Mountains, the Lefka Ori, rising to over two thousand metres just south, their summits holding snow into spring. For a rider it is a lovely base, the gateway to some of the best roads on the island: the climb up to the Omalos plateau and the Samaria Gorge, the winding route south to Sougia and Paleochora, and the coastal road west toward Kissamos and Falasarna. Roads in Crete are a mixture of good and bad, with potholes, loose gravel, goats on the tarmac and drivers who treat the white line as a suggestion. Take care on mountain bends, especially after rain, when the surface becomes slick, and watch for the summer heat that can make midday riding unpleasant.

Chania itself, a city of more than fifty thousand, has everything: fuel on the outskirts, large supermarkets, cafés, and a municipal market in a cross-shaped building with fish, cheese, olive oil and herbs. In the old town the lanes are too narrow for comfortable riding, so leave the bike at the edge and walk. Parking is tight in high summer.

Crete's food is a reason to visit alone. Try dakos, a rusk topped with tomato and mizithra cheese, graviera cheese, wild greens called horta, and snails cooked with rosemary. The local raki, a clear spirit, often arrives free at the end of a meal, and it is rude to refuse, though a bike rider might just take a sip.

Go in May or October if you can. Summer is crowded and hot, but spring brings wildflowers across the mountains and the sea is swimmable by late May. Evening light on the Venetian harbour is the best time of day.
t.irie site@42.5,140.8:
Hokkaido's southern coast sits on the edge of Funka Bay, a large, nearly circular inlet of the Pacific that is well sheltered, and about ten kilometres from the town of Date there is a shell mound that records how people lived here some four thousand years ago. Irie is one of the sites that make up the Jōmon Prehistoric Sites of Northern Japan, which UNESCO listed in 2021, a group of settlements and ritual places left by hunter-gatherer-fishers who lived without agriculture but built permanent villages, and who made the remarkable coiled-cord pottery that gives the era its name. The mound consists of discarded shells, fish bones and other debris, along with graves, and it is a rich archive of daily life.

What makes the Jōmon people so interesting is that they were sedentary without being farmers. The mild coast and the bounty of the sea, with shellfish, salmon and sea mammals, allowed them to stay in one place, trade jade and obsidian over long distances and bury their dead with care.

The country around is varied. Date is known as the warmest town in Hokkaido, with a mild climate and little snow, and Mount Usu, an active volcano that erupted in 1977 and again in 2000, rises nearby. Lake Toya, a circular caldera lake, is a short ride inland, and the roads around it circle the water with views of small islands and the mountain behind. Niseko, a famous ski area, is farther away, and the road to it winds through farmland and forest.

The riding in Hokkaido is some of the best in Japan: long roads, light traffic, big skies and a generosity of space rare in the rest of the country. The summers are mild and the best time is June to September, since winter closes many roads. Watch for deer at dusk, particularly on rural roads, and for sudden fog on the coast. Date, with thirty-five thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, while Niseko has fewer services.

The seafood, particularly scallops, sea urchin and fresh crab, is very good, and local dairy products are famous. A hot spring bath at Lake Toya is the perfect end to a day's ride.
t.historic centre of riga@57.0,24.1:
Riga is the biggest city in the Baltic states, and its old centre reads like a history of northern trade. The city was founded in 1201 by a German bishop, soon became a leading member of the Hanseatic League, and grew rich on timber, flax, furs and grain moving between Russia and western Europe. The medieval core, packed with merchants' houses, guild halls and church spires, still has the layout of those days, with narrow cobbled lanes and squares, and the House of the Blackheads, a brotherhood of unmarried merchants, with its ornate gabled facade, stands in the Town Hall Square.

Just beyond the old town, the city has another claim to fame. Riga has one of the largest collections of Art Nouveau buildings in Europe, built in the early twentieth century when the city was booming, and streets such as Alberta iela are lined with fantastical facades, covered in masks, sphinxes, peacocks and swirling vegetation, many designed by Mikhail Eisenstein, father of the film director Sergei. The combination led to the UNESCO listing of the historic centre in 1997.

For motorcyclists, Riga is a pleasant place to arrive but a hard place to ride in the old centre, where cobbles, tram lines and pedestrian zones dominate. It is better to park on the edge, perhaps near the Daugava embankment, and explore on foot. The Central Market, housed in five huge former Zeppelin hangars, is a great place to try smoked fish, rye bread, pickles, cheeses and honey. For a dark and herbal drink, Riga Black Balsam, a local liqueur, is a rite of passage. Local dishes include grey peas with bacon, and cold beetroot soup in summer.

The ride out to Jūrmala, on the Gulf of Riga, takes about half an hour, and the road passes through pinewoods onto a long white sand beach, lined with wooden villas from the nineteenth century, a spa resort that was beloved of the Russian and Soviet elite. The coast is flat, so there are no mountains, but the long straight roads through pine forest are relaxing, and the sea air smells of resin.

Riga has everything for travellers: fuel on the outskirts, supermarkets, hotels and plenty of cafés. Summer evenings are very long, with light until nearly midnight in June, while winter is cold, dark and snowy.
t.dripping springs@30.2,-98.1:
Dripping Springs sits on the eastern edge of the Texas Hill Country, west of Austin, where the flat blackland prairie gives way to limestone hills, live oaks and cedar. The name comes from the springs that seep from a ledge nearby, and the town proudly calls itself the gateway to the Hill Country. It is also, by its own declaration, the Wedding Capital of Texas, thanks to the number of ranches and barns in the surrounding hills that host ceremonies, so you will often see a bride or two on a weekend.

The countryside here is built on the Edwards Plateau, a thick layer of limestone that has been carved by water into hills, valleys, caves and springs. The water that percolates through the rock emerges in clear creeks and swimming holes, and a few kilometres to the north, Hamilton Pool, a collapsed grotto with a waterfall and a pale green pool, is a famous spot. The rock also makes for good soil for vines, and the highway west toward Fredericksburg is lined with wineries and distilleries, as well as a famous barbecue restaurant at Driftwood, a few miles south.

Riding here is a pleasure. The roads through the hills, such as Ranch Road 12 and the back routes toward Wimberley, are well surfaced and winding, with gentle gradients and long views across the ridges. Cedar and oak crowd the verges, and low-water crossings can flood quickly after heavy rain, so avoid them in wet weather. Spring is the best season, when bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush cover the roadsides, and autumn is mild and clear. Summer is hot, with temperatures in the thirties for weeks on end, and the best time to ride is early morning.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Dripping Springs, which has stations on the main highway, along with cafes, bakeries and Tex-Mex restaurants. Bee Cave and Austin lie to the east, with everything you could want. Expect traffic on weekends, especially on Highway 290, where visitors head to the wine country. Watch for deer and armadillos at dusk, and for cattle on the open ranges. A cold drink and a plate of brisket in the shade of an oak tree are the right way to end a ride here.
t.fredericksburg@30.3,-98.9:
Fredericksburg is a German town that happens to be in Texas. It was founded in 1846 by settlers who came from the German states under a land company led by John Meusebach, who named the town after Prince Frederick of Prussia, and the legacy of those early families still shapes everything from the architecture to the menu. The long Main Street is lined with limestone and timber buildings, many of them with steep roofs and shutters, and German bakeries, beer halls and sausage shops are still going strong.

The town is full of small details that tell the story. The Sunday houses, tiny cottages built by farm families so they could stay in town for church and shopping at the weekend, are a local invention, and a few have been preserved. The Vereins Kirche, an octagonal community church, stands as a replica in the middle of town, and it was used by settlers as a church, school and fort. Admiral Chester Nimitz, who commanded the Pacific Fleet in the Second World War, was born here, and the National Museum of the Pacific War in the town is one of the best in the country.

The riding around Fredericksburg is some of the best in Texas. The Hill Country roads, such as Highway 16 north toward Enchanted Rock and Ranch Road 965, have good surfaces and a satisfying rhythm of rises and bends, with views over ranches and vineyards. Enchanted Rock, a vast dome of pink granite about twenty-five kilometres north, glows in the late sun, and Native Americans considered it sacred because of the sounds it makes as it cools at night. Spring wildflowers draw crowds, so go on a weekday. The nearby Willow City Loop is a famous drive for bluebonnets.

Fuel and food are no problem, with a population of eleven thousand and plenty of stations. Peaches from the surrounding orchards ripen in summer and are sold at roadside stands, and the local wine, mostly Texan reds and whites, is worth sampling, though not before riding. The town fills up on weekends, particularly in spring and during the Christmas season, so book accommodation ahead. Bring a lightweight jacket for the evenings, which can be cool even in summer, and sit on a terrace with a pretzel and a cold beer.
t.thebes@38.3,23.3:
Thebes, or Thiva in Greek, is one of the great names of mythology and one of the least visited of the great places of the ancient world. The modern town, of about twenty-two thousand people, sits on a low ridge in the plain of Boeotia, north of Athens, surrounded by cotton and wheat fields. The mountains rise on all sides, Helicon to the west, Parnassus beyond, and the Cithaeron range to the south. Almost nothing of the ancient city is visible, but its stories are told in every schoolbook.

The legends are among the darkest in Greek lore. Founded, it was said, by Cadmus, the Phoenician prince who sowed the teeth of a dragon and watched an army of warriors spring up, Thebes was the home of Oedipus, who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, killed his father and married his mother. His daughter Antigone defied the king to bury her brother, and the war of the Seven Against Thebes followed. Dionysus was said to have been born here. Greek tragedians returned to these stories again and again, and the city's name became a byword for doom.

In history, the city was equally dramatic. In the fourth century BC, under the general Epaminondas, Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra and briefly became the leading power in Greece. Its elite unit, the Sacred Band, made up of paired lovers, fought to the death against Philip of Macedon at Chaeronea in 338 BC, where a stone lion still marks their grave. A few years later, Alexander the Great razed Thebes after a revolt, sparing only the house of the poet Pindar. A small archaeological museum in the town displays finds from the region, including painted coffins and Mycenaean tablets.

For a rider, Thiva is a crossroads on the way to Delphi, with the road from Athens running across the plain and then climbing toward Livadeia and the slopes of Parnassus. The surface is good and the traffic moderate. Fuel is easy here, with stations along the main road at the edge of town, and a number of simple tavernas serve grilled meat, salads and local wine. Summers are very hot, so start early, and spring is the best season, when the fields are green and the poppies are out. Fill up before heading to the mountains.
t.torquay surf coast@-38.3,144.3:
Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road really begins, even though the famous arch and the signage are a little further down the coast. This is surf town in the proper sense: Bells Beach is a few minutes away, the Easter surf contest there is one of the oldest in the world, and brands like Rip Curl and Quiksilver grew out of garages and sheds in this exact patch of Victoria. With around thirteen thousand residents it is a proper town, not a village, so fuel, coffee, bakeries and a good supply of wetsuit shops are all right here.

For a rider, the coast road from Torquay to Anglesea is the start of something good rather than the good bit itself. The surface is generally excellent, the corners flow with the dunes and heathland, and the sea shows up and disappears behind coastal scrub in a way that keeps your head turning. Further on, past Aireys Inlet and its lighthouse, the road begins to cling to the cliffs and the traffic begins to compete with the view. Victorian speed limits are enforced firmly and the cameras on busy holiday weekends are not shy, so treat the signed limits as real.

The road itself carries a bit of history. Returned soldiers from the First World War built much of it by hand between 1919 and 1932 as a memorial to those killed, and the arch at Eastern View still carries that spirit. Knowing that makes the unhurried pace slightly easier to accept, especially behind a caravan.

Weather here is the Southern Ocean's business. A warm morning can turn into a cold southwesterly by lunch, and a gusty crosswind on the exposed sections is normal, so wear layers you can adjust. Early starts beat the crowds, and the light on the cliffs around sunrise is lovely. Geelong is about twenty minutes up the road if you need a bigger town, but for most riders Torquay is the place to top the tank, eat something decent and take a look at the surf before pointing the bike south-west.
t.zelenogradsk@55.0,20.5:
Zelenogradsk was called Cranz when East Prussia was German, and it was one of the Baltic coast's best-known seaside resorts, a place where the people of Konigsberg came by train for the sea air and the long sand beach. Today it is a small Russian town of about fifteen thousand people on the Kaliningrad exclave, wedged between Lithuania and Poland, with a promenade, a pier and a scattering of old villas whose carved wooden balconies survive from the earlier era. Cats are the town's mascot, and statues of them appear in squares, on walls and on lamp posts.

It is also the gateway to the Curonian Spit, a narrow sandy peninsula nearly a hundred kilometres long that separates the Curonian Lagoon from the Baltic Sea. Created by waves and wind over thousands of years, the spit has dunes up to sixty metres high, forests of pine and birch that were replanted to stop the sand from burying villages, and a shore of pale sand with amber washed up after storms. UNESCO recognised it in 2000 as a shared Russian and Lithuanian site. The road south from Zelenogradsk runs along it between the sea and the lagoon.

Amber is a major theme in the region. The world's largest deposit lies along the coast to the west, at Yantarny, and for centuries it was gathered, traded and worked into jewellery, and the amber road of antiquity led from here to the Mediterranean. Small shops in Zelenogradsk sell it, and locals will tell you how to tell real from fake by a drop of salt water or a gentle heat. It is worth buying a small piece as a souvenir.

Zelenogradsk has about fifteen thousand people, and so has fuel stations and shops, and it is the last reliable place to fill up before the spit. The roads here are flat and straight, running through pine woods, and the surface is generally good, with speed cameras and police checks that are common. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends. The Baltic is cold, the beach wide and windy, and the weather changes quickly, with rain and fog rolling in from the sea. Bring a windproof layer. Travel to this region requires attention to current visa and entry rules, so check them well before you go.
t.rybachy curonian@55.2,20.9:
Rybachy was Rossitten when this part of the Curonian Spit belonged to Germany, and the village is known in scientific circles for one thing: birds. In 1901, an ornithologist named Johannes Thienemann founded the world's first bird observatory here, and for more than a century researchers have caught, ringed and released millions of migrants as they funnelled down the spit on their way between Scandinavia and Africa. The spit is a natural bottleneck, with the sea on one side and the lagoon on the other, and in spring and autumn the sky fills with finches, thrushes and birds of prey.

The landscape is one of the most unusual in Europe. The spit is a ribbon of sand, no more than a few kilometres wide and in places just four hundred metres, built up by wind and sea, and the dunes, among the highest moving dunes in the continent, rise as grey-gold hills above the pines. The sand has buried villages in the past, and the forest planted to hold it in place is now a feature of the landscape. On a still evening the air smells of resin and salt, and the sea sounds like breath.

Nida, the main village on the Lithuanian side, lies about twenty kilometres to the north, and is known for the summer house the novelist Thomas Mann built in the early 1930s, now a small museum looking over the lagoon, and for the Parnidis dune, a high viewpoint with a sundial. A border crossing lies between the two settlements, and rules for crossing change, so check conditions and carry the right documents before you attempt it. Do not assume that a route is open.

For riders, the road along the spit is flat, straight and narrow, with forest on both sides and glimpses of water, and there is something calming about it. Speed limits are low, and there are checks for entry to the national park. Services are few. Rybachy has a shop or two and a handful of guesthouses, but fuel is scarce, and the nearest large town is Zelenogradsk, some thirty kilometres south, so fill up there. Mosquitoes can be fierce in summer, and in winter the wind is bitter. Early morning in May or September, when the birds are moving, is the best time to be here.
t.kaali@58.4,22.7:
Around three and a half thousand years ago, something from space hit the island of Saaremaa, and the people living nearby saw it. Kaali is the site of a meteorite impact, and the main crater, about a hundred and ten metres across and some sixteen metres deep, is a circular pond of dark water surrounded by a grassy bank. Eight smaller craters lie scattered around it in the surrounding fields and forest. It is one of the best-preserved small impact sites in the world, and a rare find in Europe.

The effect on the local people must have been dramatic, and many scholars believe the event left its mark on regional mythology. Some of the older Nordic and Baltic stories about a sun that falls from the sky may have their roots here, though that is speculation. Archaeologists have found traces of settlements and an ancient sacrificial site around the main crater, suggesting the place was sacred for centuries. Today a small visitor centre and a circular path make it easy to walk around the main hole.

Saaremaa is itself a gentle place. The island is flat and low, with limestone bedrock, juniper heaths and thin fields, and a coast full of reed beds, small harbours and windmills. The roads are generally quiet and well surfaced, with long straight stretches and a handful of bends where they curve around bays or villages. The ride across the island has a calm, unhurried rhythm, with open skies and plenty of birds, and the wind is a regular factor, particularly on exposed stretches.

From the mainland, the route to Saaremaa runs through Virtsu and Muhu on a short ferry ride, then across a causeway to the larger island. Kuressaare, about seventeen kilometres from Kaali, is the main town, with fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and a fine medieval episcopal castle surrounded by a moat. It is a spa town as well, with a long tradition of mud baths and health resorts. The local cooking features fresh fish, rye bread, smoked meat and a firm cheese from the island, and in summer you can eat outside until late.

The windmills at Angla, toward the north, stand in a row beside the road, and are worth a stop on any ride across Saaremaa. Come in June, when the days are very long, to enjoy the full effect.
t.panga cliff@58.6,22.3:
Panga is the highest cliff on Saaremaa, and at just over twenty metres it is a good example of how scale is relative. In a country as flat as Estonia, twenty metres of Silurian limestone rising out of the Baltic counts as a mountain range. The cliff runs along the northern coast of the island for about two and a half kilometres, a pale band of layered rock with a green fringe of grass on top and a rough beach of stones and seaweed at the foot. The sea looks very big from up here, and on a clear day you can see all the way to the horizon.

The rock is part of the Baltic Klint, a line of limestone escarpments that runs along the southern edge of the Gulf of Finland, and the layers at Panga are packed with fossils of corals and shellfish from the seas that covered the region more than four hundred million years ago. Wind and waves slowly undercut the base, and every few years a section collapses, which is why the paths along the top keep a safe distance from the edge. Look but do not lean. Juniper grows on the heath above, and in late spring the meadows are full of orchids.

The ride to Panga is flat, quiet and pleasant, along roads that cross open fields and juniper heaths, passing old farms and the odd windmill. The surface is generally good, with some gravel stretches near the coast, and traffic is light, so this is a place to ride at an easy pace and enjoy the open air. The north coast road runs on to the ferry harbour at Triigi, from which boats cross to the neighbouring island of Hiiumaa, so you can extend the ride if you have time. Wind can be fierce on the open coast, and the temperature drops quickly after sunset, even in summer.

A small car park and a few signs mark the spot.

The cliff is best at sunset, when the limestone glows gold and pink and the sea turns the colour of pewter.
t.kihelkonna@58.4,22.0:
Kihelkonna lies on the west side of Saaremaa, where the island begins to dissolve into a scatter of peninsulas, reefs and low islands. It is a small village with a stone church, a school and a few shops, and its main importance is as a gateway to Vilsandi National Park, a protected area of coast, islets and shallow sea that is among the best places in the Baltic for birds. In spring and autumn, huge flocks of geese, ducks and waders gather here on their way between Siberia and the north Atlantic, and in summer the islands are covered with nesting terns and gulls.

The land is low and flat, with a lot of juniper, reed and open meadow, and the coast is rimmed with boulders, pebble beaches and shallow bays. The sea freezes in some winters, and the ice pushes up into ridges that last long into the spring. A narrow, sandy neck of land called Harilaid reaches out to the north, with a lighthouse at the end, and it is a favoured spot for walkers and bird watchers. The whole area has a stark, open beauty that is very different from the lush Estonian mainland.

For riders, the roads around Kihelkonna are quiet and easy, with long straight stretches, a few gentle bends and a surface that is mostly sealed, with gravel on some of the smaller coastal routes. The wind is the main character, blowing steadily from the Baltic and making the bike feel lively on open stretches. Traffic is light, and you are as likely to meet a tractor as a car. It is a good ride to take slowly, with stops to look at the sea, the windmills and the farms with their thatched roofs.

The nearest town of any size is Kuressaare, about thirty-one kilometres away, with petrol stations, supermarkets and restaurants, so start with a full tank. In the village, you may find a café or a small shop, but hours are limited. Local specialities include smoked fish, rye bread and the island's own beer, and farm stays often serve a hearty breakfast.

The light here has a luminous, washed quality, particularly in the evenings, when the sea turns silver.
t.kalamata@37.0,22.1:
Kalamata is the doorway to the Mani, and the olive capital of Greece, as the dark purple Kalamata olive is known the world over. Groves of olive trees fill the plain of Messenia, and the city sits at the head of the gulf with the great wall of the Taygetos range rising behind it, its summit at Profitis Ilias well over two thousand metres, often capped with snow into spring. The city is a lively mix of seafront, markets and a pedestrian old town, and was rebuilt after a damaging earthquake in 1986.

It also has a place in the national story. On 23 March 1821, Kalamata was the first major town to be liberated in the Greek War of Independence, and local people celebrate the anniversary. The ruined castle on the hill above the old town, with its Frankish and Venetian walls, looks over the plain.

The route south enters the Mani, the central of the three peninsulas of the Peloponnese, a stern, rocky land of stone tower houses, bare hills and tiny villages. The road follows the coast, then climbs through hairpins into the interior. The surface is mostly good, and the traffic is light outside the summer weekends. The Taygetos road to Sparta, the Langada pass, is one of the great mountain roads of Greece, cutting through pine and plane forest, with a descent of many hairpins. Be careful with gravel and with goats on the road, and in winter, check for ice and snow.

Kalamata has over fifty thousand people and all the fuel, food and supplies you could want. Farther south, villages are small, so fill up before you leave. The olive oil is outstanding, and the local figs, honey and pasta are worth carrying away. Order a plate of lamb and potatoes in a taverna, with a village salad and a glass of cold white wine, and enjoy the sea breeze. Ride early in summer, because the sun by midday is strong, and give yourself time at the southern tip, the ancient Cape Tainaron, where the road ends and the sea begins.
t.acropolis@38.0,23.7:
The rock itself is a surprise. The Acropolis rises about a hundred and fifty metres above Athens, a limestone outcrop with steep sides and a flat top, and for most of ancient history it was the city's fortress and shrine. The buildings you see today, the Parthenon, the Propylaia gateway, the little temple of Athena Nike and the Erechtheion with its stone maidens, were mostly built in the second half of the fifth century BC under Pericles, with the sculptor Phidias overseeing the work. The Parthenon was finished in 432 BC.

Its later history is rough. The Parthenon became a church and then a mosque, and in 1687, when the Venetians besieged the Ottoman garrison, a shell hit the gunpowder stored inside and blew the roof off. In the early nineteenth century, much of the sculpture was removed by Lord Elgin, and the argument over the Parthenon marbles in London continues. Restoration work has been under way for decades, so scaffolding is a normal part of the view.

For a rider, Athens is a challenge. The roads around the rock are crowded with cars, scooters and taxis, with little patience for hesitation, and the summer heat is intense. The best time to visit the site is when it opens in the morning, before the crowds and the sun, or in the late afternoon, and the marble surface is slippery when worn. Outside the city, the Attiki Odos toll motorway circles the Athenian plain, and the roads south-west to Epidaurus cross the Corinth canal and enter the dry hills of the Peloponnese.

Fuel is easy across the city. For lunch, ask for a gyro or souvlaki in the Plaka, the old district below the Acropolis, where the lanes are narrow and the tavernas are many, and finish with a Greek coffee or a cold frappé. Take water, a hat and sensible shoes if you are climbing, and leave your helmet in a secure place. The best moment is sunset, when the stone turns honey-coloured and the city lights come on below.
t.archaeological site of mycenae@37.7,22.8:
The Lion Gate is the thing everyone remembers. Two stone lionesses, facing each other across a central column, stand over the entrance to the citadel, carved some three and a half thousand years ago in the Bronze Age, and the walls beside the gate are built of boulders so huge that later Greeks thought only the Cyclopes could have lifted them. Inside is a royal burial ground, the Grave Circles, where in 1876 the German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann found gold masks and weapons, and declared that he had looked upon the face of Agamemnon. The mask is older than Agamemnon would have been, but the name stuck.

Mycenae was the centre of a civilisation that dominated the Greek world between about 1600 and 1200 BC, and its stories fed the epics of Homer, the myths of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra and the tragedies of Aeschylus. Nearby, the Treasury of Atreus, a beehive tomb with a magnificent corbelled dome, is one of the best-preserved Mycenaean monuments, entered through a long stone passage. The site was listed by UNESCO in 1999.

The surroundings are stark and beautiful. The citadel sits on a ridge between two hills, above a dry valley of olive groves and orange orchards in the Argolid, and the view stretches down to the plain and the sea. The roads from Nafplio or Argos are narrow and gently winding, with traffic that is light outside the main tourist season. In summer the sun is merciless, and the site has little shade, so go early, carry water, and wear a hat.

Services are limited close to the site. The village of Mykines is small, so fill the tank in Argos or Nafplio, where there are petrol stations and many places to eat. Nafplio, the first capital of modern Greece, is a handsome seaside town with a Venetian fortress above it and is a good place to stay. The ride continues toward Athens and the monastery of Daphni, with its eleventh-century mosaics, so the day covers the Bronze Age, Byzantium and the long road between them.
t.ofune site@42.0,140.9:
Ofune is a Jomon settlement on the southern tip of Hokkaido, in the hills above Hakodate, and it is a lot bigger than the signboards make it look. The Jomon were hunter-gatherers who lived in the northern forests of Japan for something like ten thousand years, long before rice farming, and they built a settled life around chestnuts, fish, deer and the odd well-travelled trade good. Ofune was inhabited for centuries and is now part of the Jomon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan, which UNESCO recognised in 2021. Reconstructed pit houses hold the grass in place, and the scale of the pits tells you someone intended to stay.

Hokkaido itself changes how you ride. The roads are wider and emptier than on the main island, and the cadence is long straights, gentle bends and rolling forest. Near Hakodate they tighten, particularly on the road climbing around the old volcano of Komagatake. Rubber matters here because the tarmac cools fast, even in July, and fog from the Tsugaru Strait can drift in without warning. Deer are the real hazard on rural roads at dusk, and in autumn you will see warning signs showing a leaping stag every few kilometres. Pay attention to them.

Hakodate itself is the base. It sits on a narrow isthmus with a harbour on one side and the open sea on the other, and it was one of the first Japanese ports opened to foreign ships in the 1850s. Red brick warehouses survive along the waterfront, and the night view from the top of Mount Hakodate is one of the famous ones in the country. Ferries from Aomori arrive here, so it is where many motorcyclists step onto Hokkaido for the first time. Fuel is plentiful in the city and along the main roads, though small stations in the hills can close early.

Eat squid here if you eat anything. The morning market near the station sells it so fresh that it is still moving, and the salt ramen of Hakodate is the local answer to richer bowls elsewhere. Honcho, the nearest bigger town to Ofune, is quieter, with a few shops and a convenience store, and it has what you need. In summer the light lasts late, and it is a gentle thing to be at the site near evening, when the grass has gone gold and the only sound is wind.
t.takasago burial site@42.5,140.8:
The Takasago burial site lies in the Date area on the shore of Funka Bay, in southwestern Hokkaido, and it belongs to the Jomon period, when people in these northern lands buried their dead with care and ceremony. Excavations turned up graves with ornaments of shell and other goods, which suggests a settled community with trading links. The site is part of the northern Jomon group that earned UNESCO listing in 2021. There is not much to see above ground, and a rider who expects dramatic ruins will be disappointed, but the information boards and the surroundings give a good sense of why people lived here: the bay was rich in fish and shellfish, and the hills behind held game and forest foods.

Funka Bay, also known as Uchiura, is a nearly closed inlet of the Pacific with a quiet shore and a long sweep of coastline road. Route 37 follows it with long bends and the occasional dip into small fishing villages. Behind the shoreline rise two volcanoes that shape the region, Usu and Showa-Shinzan, along with Lake Toya, a round caldera lake that is one of the best rides in this part of Hokkaido. The loop around the lake is easy and the views of the island in the middle are fine from several angles. Usu last erupted in the early 2000s and the signs are still visible on the slopes.

Date is a town of around thirty-five thousand, with all the fuel, convenience stores and restaurants you could need, and it is only twelve kilometres from the site. The name comes from a lord of the Date clan, whose retainers moved here in the nineteenth century to open land during the Meiji era. Muroran, further along the coast, is a steel town with a famous bridge and some dramatic seaside cliffs. Niseko, to the north, is a different world of ski resorts and pale volcanic slopes.

Weather in Hokkaido can switch quickly. Summer is gentle, with highs rarely stifling and long daylight. Autumn arrives early, and the first frost can come in October. Bears do live in the hills here, so give any forest track a little care.
Kiusu sits within the city limits of Chitose, but you would never guess it from the gentle forest and the soft ground underfoot. This is one of the strangest ancient monuments in Japan: circular graves enclosed by a raised embankment of earth, made by Jomon people about three thousand years ago. They dug a great ring pit, piled the soil into a bank around it, and placed their dead inside. The largest circles are many metres across, and the earthworks are still easy to read as mounds, grassy and a bit like a stage set. It forms part of the northern Jomon listing, which UNESCO inscribed in 2021. The reason for such labour is still discussed, but the effort tells you the dead mattered to the group.

Chitose is known to most travellers for the New Chitose Airport, so it is a common start or end point for rides in Hokkaido. That makes this one of the easiest ancient sites to reach from a landing. Fuel, food and rental shops are a few kilometres away, and the city has everything. From here a ride south goes to Lake Shikotsu, a deep, clear caldera lake ringed by volcanoes including Tarumae and Eniwa, whose cone is a good silhouette in the afternoon. The road around the lake is quiet and well surfaced, and the water stays cold and very blue even in August.

Roads in this part of central Hokkaido are broad and smooth, with long, easy bends and good visibility. Speed limits are low and enforcement is real, with unmarked cars, so keep it measured. The surface can be slick in morning dew and after rain, and gravel sneaks onto corners near farms. Deer and fox cross at dusk. In winter the roads are closed to everyday motorcycling because of snow and ice, and the riding season runs from May to October.

The surrounding landscape is wet woodland, volcanic soil and marsh. Kitahiroshima, fifteen kilometres away, is a lively town where the farmland begins. The air smells of pine and cold water, and early morning here is calm.
t.ventspils@57.4,21.6:
Ventspils is a port town on the western coast of Latvia, at the mouth of the Venta River, and it has two faces. One is the working harbour, which handles oil, coal and timber and has done since the Hanseatic League, and the other is a handsome, tidy waterfront town with a long white beach and a big public park. The beach has held the Blue Flag for many years, and the water is shallow and cold, with fine pale sand. The town's older centre is small, with wooden houses and cobbled streets around the Livonian Order castle, built in the thirteenth century and one of the best preserved in the country.

Cows are the city's odd emblem. In 2002 a public art project placed painted cow statues across the town, and a number remain, standing on corners and in squares, a bit silly and quite charming. Children climb on them, and tourists photograph them. Ventspils has also invested in playgrounds, a seaside promenade and a modern library, and it has a polished, well-kept look that surprises people who arrive expecting a rough industrial port. Ferries run from here to Sweden, crossing the Baltic to Nynashamn near Stockholm.

The riding on this coast is mostly straight and flat, with long avenues of pine and spruce, wide fields and little traffic. Curves come in gentle form, and the real pleasure is the quiet. The coastal strip of Kurzeme is lightly settled, and the Slitere and Kolka area, to the east, is a protected landscape of forest and dunes where you might see elk or wild boar. Piltene, a small town about twenty kilometres from Ventspils, has the charm of a place that was once a bishopric and is now a quiet river village. Wind off the Baltic can be strong, and the water is cold even in August.

The route south to Riga takes around three hours by the main roads, through Kandava and Tukums. Fuel is easy in Ventspils and along the main road, though small villages are far apart. Smoked fish is a local speciality, and black bread and rye are served everywhere. Summer is bright and long, with light until almost eleven.
t.austin@30.3,-97.7:
Austin sits where the flat Texas blackland prairie meets the limestone Hill Country, and that line, the Balcones Escarpment, is the reason the city is a good place to start a ride. West of downtown the land rises suddenly into oak and juniper hills cut by creeks, with the Colorado River, dammed into the long Lake Austin and Lake Travis, curling between them. The city grew here in the nineteenth century as the capital of the Republic of Texas, and the pink granite Capitol, which is taller than the one in Washington, still dominates the skyline.

Getting out takes some patience. The first stretch through Rollingwood, West Lake Hills and the western suburbs is stop-and-go on weekday afternoons, with a lot of traffic lights and a lot of cars. Once you cross into the hills, the road becomes much better, with real curves, elevation changes and wide views over the lakes. The famous Hill Country roads such as the Ranch Roads, numbered in the hundreds, rise and fall over limestone ridges and dip through low-water crossings. Watch out for gravel on the apex, deer at dawn and dusk, and a good deal of cyclists on weekends. Spring is spectacular because the bluebonnets and other wildflowers come out in April, while summer is brutally hot, often above thirty-five degrees, so go early.

Austin has plenty of character to enjoy before leaving or after returning. Live music is everywhere, and the city proudly calls itself the live music capital of the world, with venues along Sixth Street and South Congress. Food means barbecue, in the Central Texas style: brisket smoked slowly over oak and served on butcher paper, usually with white bread and pickles, and queues for the best places can be long. Breakfast tacos are a daily ritual. The Congress Avenue bridge also holds a very large colony of Mexican free-tailed bats, which stream out at dusk in the warm months, a fine free show.

As for practical matters, Austin is a large city with fuel and repair shops on every corner, so there is no need to worry. Do remember to fill up before heading deep into the Hill Country, where small towns like Willow City have little. Carry plenty of water in summer, and plan around rush hour.
t.kuressaare@58.3,22.5:
Kuressaare is the only real town on Saaremaa, Estonia's largest island, and it wears that distinction lightly. About fifteen thousand people live here, and the place is built around an old bishop's castle, a square, grey limestone fortress with a moat, which dates from the fourteenth century and is one of the best-preserved medieval castles in the Baltic region. The castle is surrounded by a park with earth ramparts, and the pale town streets, lined with wooden and limestone houses, lead down to a small harbour on the shallow Baltic coast. The air here is clean and salty, with a hint of juniper and seaweed.

The town became a spa resort in the nineteenth century, when people came to take the mud cures, and a number of the old buildings from that period survive, including the elegant Kurhaus on the seafront. Saaremaa itself has an unusual character, as the island's people have kept a distinct dialect and traditions, and it was only opened to visitors after the Soviet era ended, having been a restricted border zone for decades. Locals will tell you with pride about the island's cheese, rye bread, smoked fish and beer.

The riding here is a pleasure of a quiet sort. The island is flat to gently undulating, with long straight roads lined by juniper, pines and meadows, and little traffic outside the town and the main road to the ferry. Along the way you pass old windmills, thatched farms and the large crater lake at Kaali, formed when a meteorite struck several thousand years ago, a rare, well-preserved impact site. The surface is generally good, with some gravel on minor roads, and distances are short. The wind can be strong, and the northern sea light is lovely, especially in the long evenings of June.

Kuressaare has all the services you need, with fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, so fill your tank here before heading to the quieter parts of the island, where stations are fewer. The ferry from the mainland runs to Muhu, which is joined to Saaremaa by a causeway, and it can be busy in summer, so check the timetable and arrive early. Spring and early autumn are calm seasons, with fewer people and clear light. On a still evening you can sit by the castle moat and hear nothing but the swifts overhead.
t.haapsalu@58.9,23.5:
Haapsalu is a small seaside town on the west coast of Estonia with a surprising amount of history and an odd fame for lace and mud. The town grew around an episcopal castle built in the thirteenth century by the bishops of Ösel-Wiek, a big fortress with a cathedral inside its walls, now a romantic ruin on the edge of the bay. Legend tells of the White Lady, a woman said to have been walled up alive for loving a choirboy, whose ghost appears at the cathedral window on August full moons; the town celebrates the story with a festival and a lot of theatrical flair.

In the nineteenth century the town became a fashionable spa, because of the curative mud from the shallow bays, and the Russian aristocracy took the train here from St Petersburg. The composer Tchaikovsky holidayed here in the 1860s, and there is a bench dedicated to him on the seafront promenade. The old railway station, built for the imperial family, has one of the longest covered platforms in Europe, now home to a small museum of railway history. Local women still knit the Haapsalu shawl, a lace so fine it can be pulled through a wedding ring.

The riding around Haapsalu is flat, quiet and leisurely, with long straight stretches between birch woods, wetlands and low coastal meadows. The nearby Matsalu National Park is a major stop for migrating birds in spring and autumn, with geese, cranes and swans on the wet meadows. Roads are generally good, though many minor lanes are gravel, and the wind off the sea can be fresh. Traffic is light, and even in summer the roads are not busy, but watch for elk and deer at dawn and dusk, which can be a real hazard in the Baltic countryside.

Haapsalu, with nearly twelve thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, so you can stock up before heading on. The town has a seaside charm, with wooden villas painted in soft colours, a long promenade and the smell of the sea and smoked fish. The best months are May to September, but the autumn light is wonderful too. Sit by the water at the end of the day and watch the sun go down over the bay, which takes a very long time in June.
t.curonian spit@55.3,21.0:
Nothing prepares you for the sand. The Curonian Spit is a sliver of land nearly a hundred kilometres long, split between Lithuania and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, lying between the Baltic Sea and the Curonian Lagoon and never more than a few kilometres wide. Great dunes, among the highest moving sand hills in Europe, run along its length, with pine forest holding the rest in place. UNESCO recognised it as a cultural landscape in 2000, because people have fought to keep this strip alive for centuries.

The sand has a history of its own. Villages were buried by drifting dunes in earlier times, and in the nineteenth century foresters planted pine and grass to fix the surface. Nida, the main village on the Lithuanian side, is a small place of wooden houses and smoked-fish stalls, where the writer Thomas Mann built a summer house in the early 1930s, now a museum. The Parnidis dune above the village has a sundial and a view across to the Russian border, and in Juodkrante, further north, the Hill of Witches is a wooded trail of carved wooden figures.

Riding here is a matter of patience. Cars enter the national park by paying a fee at a checkpoint, speed limits are low, and the single road is narrow and winding through forest, with cyclists and walkers. You reach the spit by a short ferry from Klaipeda to Smiltyne. Wind off the Baltic can be strong, and the sand blows across the road in places. Summer weekends are crowded, while May and September are quiet, and winter is bleak and fine.

Services are limited, so fill up in Klaipeda before crossing and carry some water. Nida has restaurants and cafes serving smoked flounder, eel and fresh fish, and amber shops along the lanes. Elk sometimes wander the woods, and the beaches on the Baltic side are wide and pale, with cold, clear water. Try to be at the dunes for sunset, when the light turns the sand pink.
t.warrnambool@-38.4,142.5:
Warrnambool is the western gateway to the Great Ocean Road, or the end of it, depending on which way you ride, and it is a solid, comfortable regional city of about thirty thousand, where the dairy farms of south-west Victoria meet a cold, wild coast. The town spreads along the shoreline, with long beaches, a breakwater and good sea views, and the centre has all the practical comforts of a place that does not depend entirely on tourism.

The coast here is known as the Shipwreck Coast, and with good reason. Dozens of vessels went down on these cliffs and reefs in the nineteenth century, and the Flagstaff Hill Maritime Village in Warrnambool tells their story. The most famous wreck is the Loch Ard, which sank in 1878; only two young people survived, a ship's apprentice named Tom Pearce and a passenger, Eva Carmichael, and the gorge where they came ashore is a short ride from the road further east. Also important is the whale story. Southern right whales come to Logans Beach, just east of the town centre, between about May and October to give birth, and a viewing platform lets you watch them from the cliff. It is one of the best land-based whale-watching spots in the country.

The riding around Warrnambool is more relaxed than the twisting section near Lorne. Roads run through flat farmland with long straights and wide views, and the wind off the Southern Ocean can be fierce, so a firm grip on the bars is wise. Tower Hill, a collapsed volcano a few kilometres west, has a lake inside the crater and walking tracks where you may spot emus, koalas and kangaroos. The old town of Koroit has handsome Irish-influenced buildings and a long history of potato farming.

Fuel is easy here, along with food of all kinds, from fish and chips on the foreshore to cheese from the dairy farms nearby. The weather is changeable, and cold fronts can bring heavy rain, so bring a waterproof layer.

If you have time, the road east toward the Twelve Apostles is one of the great coastal rides in the world, and the light in the late afternoon is superb.
t.otways rainforest@-38.0,144.7:
Werribee South and Point Cook lie on the western shore of Port Phillip Bay, at the point where Melbourne's urban sprawl runs out onto the flat, windy plain toward Geelong. It is an unglamorous end to a ride that began in the damp green of the Otway Ranges, but it has its own odd charm. The land here is flat as paper, divided into market gardens that produce much of the lettuce and cauliflower Melburnians eat, and the sky is huge.

Behind you, the Otways are wild country. The forest of mountain ash and myrtle beech grows in some of the wettest parts of Victoria, with tree ferns, moss and lichen along the road, and the light falls in green shafts through the canopy. Cape Otway has a lighthouse dating from 1848, among the oldest on the Australian mainland, and the koalas that sit in the manna gums by the road are rarely in a hurry. The Twelve Apostles, a row of limestone stacks off the coast further west, are the great sight on the Great Ocean Road, though only a handful of the stacks now stand.

Closer to the finish, there is an interesting history lesson. Point Cook is the birthplace of Australian military aviation, as the country's first flying school opened there in 1914, and the RAAF was later formed here. A small museum and old hangars remain beside the shore. At Werribee, there is a handsome pastoral mansion in a park and a large wetland, the Western Treatment Plant, that is paradoxically among the best bird-watching sites in Victoria, with thousands of ducks and waders.

Riding on the plain is straightforward. The roads are straight, the speed limits tight, and the wind can be strong. Cameras are common, and truck traffic is heavy near the Princes Freeway. Evenings are best, when the light is gentle and the market gardens glow.

Fuel is easy here, with plenty of stations and cafes, and the city is only a short run from here along the freeway.
t.apollo bay overnight@-38.8,143.7:
Apollo Bay is where the Great Ocean Road takes a breath. The town sits in a curve of the Otway coast, with a long beach on one side and the wooded Otway Ranges stacked up behind, and it has about fifteen hundred permanent residents, many more in holiday season. It began as a timber and fishing settlement, and the working harbour is still there, with a fishermen's co-operative selling fresh seafood. After a day on the coast road, with its endless bends, it is a relief to stop somewhere that feels like a normal town.

The road itself has a history. The Great Ocean Road was built between 1919 and 1932 by returned soldiers from the First World War, and it was conceived as a memorial to those who died. Much of it was dug by hand and carved from steep cliffs, and the stretch east of Apollo Bay clings to the edge of the Southern Ocean with the limestone formations of the Twelve Apostles still some way to the west. Inland, the Otway rainforest is a surprise, with tall mountain ash, myrtle beech and tree ferns, fed by rainfall that is higher than almost anywhere in Victoria.

For riders, a night here makes sense because the surrounding roads reward time. East toward Lorne, about thirty-six kilometres, the road twists along the cliffs with sea views and sharp bends, and in summer it is slow with tourist traffic and cyclists. West, the road to Cape Otway climbs into the forest and ends at Australia's oldest surviving lighthouse on the mainland, which dates from the 1840s, with koalas often visible in the gum trees along the way. Inland, the climb to Lavers Hill is one of the finest short rides in the state, with tight hairpins in deep shade. The surface can be damp and slippery, and fog is common.

Practically, Apollo Bay has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries and a cluster of pubs and cafes along the beachfront. Accommodation fills quickly in summer and school holidays, so book ahead. Fuel is scarce outside town, so top up before heading west or inland. In the morning, with the sea quiet and the road empty, it is the best time to be out.
t.morskoye@55.2,20.9:
This part of the spit belongs to the Kaliningrad region, the village of Morskoye on the map, and the border at its northern end is not a crossing point for tourists, so a rider on the Lithuanian side cannot simply carry on along the road. Nida is where the Lithuanian part ends.

The spit itself is a thing of wonder. It is about a hundred kilometres long and in places less than four hundred metres wide, a ribbon of dunes and pine forest between sea and lagoon, shared by Lithuania and Russia, and listed by UNESCO in 2000 as a cultural landscape. For centuries the villages here fought the wandering sand. Some were buried and moved, and the forest that covers the spit today was planted in the nineteenth century to hold the dunes. The highest, near Nida, rises about fifty metres, one of the tallest shifting dunes in Europe, and from its top you can see lagoon on one side, sea on the other and, to the south, the Russian dunes marching away.

Nida is a pleasant fishing village, where Thomas Mann built a summer house in the early 1930s, where smoked fish is sold from stalls and amber from souvenir shops, and where the beaches are wide and white. The road along the Lithuanian part of the spit is lovely: a quiet, curving single carriageway through pine and birch, with glimpses of water, and an entry fee collected at the gate. Speed is limited and enforced, as it should be in a national park.

Nida has about sixteen hundred people, with limited services, so fill in Klaipeda, the ferry city to the north, before you cross by ferry from Smiltyne. Summer brings crowds and mosquitoes, and September has the best light. Winter is cold and windy, and the empty beach is bleak and beautiful.
t.liepaja@56.5,21.0:
Liepaja calls itself the city where the wind is born, and a morning on the seafront makes the claim credible. It sits on the Baltic coast of western Latvia, between the sea and a long, narrow lake, and the wind blows in from the west across a very wide beach of fine pale sand. About eighty-five thousand people live here, in a city of wooden houses, art nouveau facades, parks and a lively music scene. Liepaja is known as the cradle of Latvian rock, and each summer the beach hosts concerts.

The city has a layered, slightly austere history. In the late nineteenth century, Tsar Alexander III built the Karosta naval base on its northern side, a self-contained town of barracks, churches and an enormous naval cathedral, and the Soviets later used it as a base for submarines. Parts of Karosta were closed and forbidden to civilians for decades, and the former military prison is now a museum, where you can take tours or even spend a night. The rows of grim barracks and crumbling forts are strangely compelling, and the beaches beyond are wild and empty.

The ride from Liepaja goes inland to Kuldiga, the old town of the Duchy of Courland, about sixty kilometres to the north-east. The road runs through open farmland and forest, flat and easy, with long straights and the occasional village. Kuldiga has a brick bridge from the nineteenth century, a handsome old centre of wooden houses, and the Venta Rapid, a waterfall about two hundred and fifty metres wide, said to be the widest in Europe, though only a couple of metres high. In spring, fish leap upstream there.

Liepaja has plenty of fuel, with stations on the main roads, and good places to eat: smoked fish, rye bread and a dark local beer are all worth trying. Latvia drives on the right, the speed limit on open roads is generally ninety, and the police are watchful. Summer is the best season, though the sea is cold. Autumn brings gold in the birches and fewer people.
t.great ocean road point 4@-38.9,143.5:
The last stretch of road to Cape Otway runs for kilometres through tall forest, and the trees are full of koalas. Manna gums line the lane to the lighthouse, and the animals can be spotted sleeping in the forks of the branches, grey furry lumps with their heads tucked in. Stop on the verge and look up, and you will soon see one, though the ride is slow because other drivers do the same. Apollo Bay is some eighteen kilometres back along the road, the only real town for a long way.

Cape Otway Lightstation, built in 1848, is the oldest surviving lighthouse on mainland Australia. It stands on a cliff above the point where Bass Strait meets the Southern Ocean, one of the most dangerous passages in the world, and the coast to the west is known as the Shipwreck Coast, after the hundreds of ships lost on its reefs. The lighthouse guided immigrant ships on their final approach to Melbourne, and the lightkeepers' cottages and a telegraph station and wartime radar station are now open to the public, with an entry fee.

The road to the cape is a quiet detour from the Great Ocean Road, a narrow, winding lane with plenty of curves and a surface in fair condition. In the forest it is cool and damp, with the smell of eucalyptus and wet earth, and on the headland the wind is strong and salty. Wildflowers bloom on the heath in spring, and whales sometimes pass offshore in winter, heading for warmer water. Echidnas and wallabies are occasionally seen.

A cafe at the lightstation serves coffee and cake. The detour adds about an hour to the day, and it is best done in the morning, before the light fades. The road is open all year, though rain and fog are common in winter, and the best season is late spring to autumn. Keep your speed low in the forest, since koalas and kangaroos cross the road without warning.
t.great ocean road point 5@-38.7,143.1:
The Twelve Apostles were never twelve, and there are not even that many now. The limestone stacks rising from the Southern Ocean off the Port Campbell coast were once called the Sow and Piglets, then renamed to attract tourists, and there were never more than nine. One collapsed in 2005 in front of watching visitors, leaving seven. They stand a short way offshore, golden and pink in the evening light, with waves breaking at their feet. Port Campbell is a short ride to the west.

The stacks are the remains of cliffs, carved by wind and waves over millions of years. The soft limestone erodes at the base, forming caves and arches that eventually collapse, leaving the stacks isolated in the sea, and the process continues, so that the coastline here is always changing. A boardwalk leads from the car park to the viewing platforms, and in the quieter hours of early morning or evening the place is magical, with the sun low and the sea turning gold. Helicopter flights operate from a nearby base, and the noise can intrude.

The Great Ocean Road here is a gentler affair than the Otways section, running over flat farmland with long straights and open bends, and the wind is a constant. The surface is good, and the speed limits are strictly enforced. The coast is wild, with cliffs falling away on the south side, and a ride along it in the morning mist is atmospheric.

The site is busy for most of the day, with coaches arriving in numbers, so mornings and late afternoons are best. A visitor centre has a cafe and toilets, and motorcycle parking is easy. The weather is changeable, with a cold wind off the Southern Ocean even in summer, so bring a layer. The road is open all year, and the best season for clear skies is late summer and autumn.
t.great ocean road point 6@-38.6,143.0:
Port Campbell is a small fishing village in a cove, where a creek cuts a notch in the limestone cliffs, and it is the natural base for the Shipwreck Coast. The jetty and the little beach are protected from the Southern Ocean, and the main street has a few cafes, a pub and a general store. A few hundred people live here, and Timboon is the nearest sizeable village inland.

The coast around the town is full of dramatic scenery. A few kilometres east is Loch Ard Gorge, named after an iron clipper that wrecked on the reef in 1878 on its voyage from England. Only two people survived: a young ship's apprentice, Tom Pearce, who was washed into the gorge, and a young woman, Eva Carmichael, whom he rescued and carried to safety. Their story is told on the signs along the walk. London Bridge, a rock arch that once connected to the cliff, fell into the sea in 1990, stranding two tourists on the outer section who had to be rescued by helicopter.

The road along this part of the coast is straight and open, running through windswept farmland with a few gentle curves, and the sea is a mix of blue, green and white. The cliffs are cut by gorges and blowholes, and a walk along the clifftops to view the arches and stacks is easy from the car parks. The wind is strong and constant, and a visor and a good jacket are essential.

Port Campbell has a petrol station and a small supermarket, and it is the best place for fuel and a meal between Apollo Bay and Warrnambool. Fish and chips from the shop near the jetty are a local tradition. Accommodation is limited and in demand, so book ahead in summer. The road is open all year, but winter brings storms with huge waves and sometimes closures, and the best months for a ride are February to April.
t.hokkaido patchwork road point 2@43.6,142:
Around Biei the land does something you rarely see in Japan: it opens up. Instead of tight valleys and forested slopes, there are long, soft hills covered in fields, each a different colour depending on the crop, wheat, potatoes, buckwheat, beans, sugar beet, so that from any rise the landscape looks like a quilt laid over a sleeping body. That is the Patchwork Road, a loose network of farm lanes north and west of Biei town, with Asahikawa a little over twenty kilometres away and the Tokachi volcanoes standing to the south-east.

The scenery became famous partly through photography. A photographer who settled in Biei in the 1970s and 1980s shot these hills in every season, and his pictures turned a farming district into a pilgrimage. Single trees on the ridgelines became celebrities in their own right, appearing in advertisements, and some have names such as the Ken and Mary tree or the Seven Stars tree, along with a pair called the parent-and-child trees. Local farmers have been patient with the crowds, but please do not walk into the fields: these are working farms, and trampling crops, or carrying soil on your boots from one field to another, causes real damage.

The riding is relaxed rather than technical. The lanes rise and fall gently, often narrow, sometimes without a centre line, and the corners are wide and easy. Watch out for tractors, tour buses stopping suddenly, and cars pulled half onto the verge for a photo. The best season is midsummer, when the fields are at their most colourful and the weather is dry and mild, but late spring has green fields and snow still on the volcanoes, and early autumn brings golden wheat stubble.

Biei town has fuel, food and a station, and Asahikawa, Hokkaido's second city, has everything else, including a famous zoo and a soy-based style of ramen. Hokkaido summers are short and the evenings cool, so carry a layer, and remember that wildlife, including deer and occasionally foxes, use the farm roads at dusk. It is the gentlest checkpoint on the ride, a place to slow down and look.
t.hokkaido patchwork road point 3@43.6,142:
A little west of Biei, the hills lean towards the Asahikawa basin and the views stretch further. From the tops of the farm roads here you can look back across the patchwork to the Tokachi range, a line of volcanic peaks, the most active of them Tokachi-dake, which often trails a thin plume of steam. In June and July the slopes still carry streaks of snow, and in the evening light the whole range turns pink while the fields below go dark.

This side of the Patchwork Road is a little quieter than the most photographed lanes. The roads are ordinary farm roads, paved but narrow, connecting scattered farmsteads with big barns and the red or blue roofs that are typical of Hokkaido, a reminder that the island was settled late, mostly from the late nineteenth century onward, by farmers who adopted American and European methods. Before that, Hokkaido was the land of the Ainu, the indigenous people whose place names survive everywhere, including in Biei itself.

What grows here depends on the year and the rotation, so the patchwork changes from season to season. Potatoes flower white and purple in July, wheat ripens to gold in August, and buckwheat fields turn white in late summer. In winter all of it disappears under deep snow, and the hills become smooth white curves with single dark trees, a landscape photographers love but riders cannot use, since snow lies here from late autumn into spring.

For a rider, it is a place of quiet roads and light rather than speed. Keep the pace down, watch for farm vehicles pulling out of gateways, and expect gravel on some side roads. There are few shops between the farms, so carry water and snacks, and use Biei or Asahikawa for fuel; Asahikawa is the nearest city and has every service. Late afternoon is the best time for photographs, when the shadows lengthen across the hills, and a good final stop is one of the farm cafes or roadside stations in the area, where Hokkaido dairy products, including very good soft-serve ice cream, are a local point of pride.
t.shimo furano@43.3,142.4:
Furano sits in a long, flat valley in the middle of Hokkaido, with the Tokachi range rising to the east and the Yūbari mountains to the west, and the town calls itself the island's navel. It even holds a summer festival in honour of the claim, with residents painting faces on their bellies and dancing through the streets. That sense of humour suits the place: Furano is a friendly, relaxed farming town that has become one of Hokkaido's best-loved destinations without losing its everyday character.

The valley is famous for lavender. Farmers began growing it in the mid-twentieth century for perfume oil, and when the market collapsed, the fields survived because photographers and visitors started coming to see them. In July the slopes around Furano and neighbouring Nakafurano turn purple, and the air smells of it for kilometres. Other crops fill the rest of the valley: melons, which are a local pride, onions, carrots, wheat, and grapes for a local winery.
