A long-running Japanese television drama about a family living in the wilds near Furano made the town famous in the 1980s and 1990s, and some of the sets remain as attractions.

In winter the valley turns into a ski resort, with dry, powdery snow and a slope that has hosted World Cup races. Summer and early autumn are the riding seasons. The roads around Furano are wide and quiet, with gentle curves along the valley and through the farmland, and climbs into the hills towards Biei or over to the Tokachi side offer more interesting corners. Wildlife, including deer, crosses the roads at dawn and dusk, and the weather can change quickly, with mist and rain coming over the mountains.

Furano has fuel, convenience stores, cafes and supermarkets, all within a few streets of each other, so refuelling bike and rider takes no planning at all. Local dishes include curry topped with an omelette, a speciality that local restaurants promote as their own, along with dairy products and cheese from the area. If you have time, a short walk through the lavender fields or a visit to one of the farm shops makes a gentle break, and in the evening the light over the Tokachi range is something special.
t.near hampton@-37.9,144.9:
Port Phillip Bay is so large that from its northern shore you cannot see the other side, and the stop is right on that shore, along the beaches between Elwood and Brighton, a few kilometres south of Melbourne's centre. As a base for setting out and coming home it works well: the city is close, but the bay gives a sense of space, and on a summer evening, with the light going gold over the water and people swimming and walking their dogs along the sand, it is hard to feel stressed.

Brighton is famous for its bathing boxes, a row of small wooden huts on the beach, each painted in bright colours and stripes, many of them decades old and changing hands for astonishing sums. They are one of the most photographed sights in Melbourne, especially at sunset. A little to the north, St Kilda has a long pier where, at dusk, a colony of little penguins comes ashore among the rocks of the breakwater.

Beach Road, which runs along the shore, is a favourite with cyclists, especially on weekend mornings, when large groups ride along it in tight formations. Be patient and give them space. The road is otherwise easy, with traffic lights, roundabouts and views of the bay. From here, the rides lead north-east to the Yarra Valley and the Black Spur, a winding road through towering mountain ash forest, and west to the Grampians, a range of sandstone mountains rising abruptly from the plains of western Victoria.

There are fuel stations, cafés and restaurants all along the bayside suburbs, so getting coffee and breakfast before setting off is easy. Melbourne's weather is famously changeable, sometimes described as four seasons in one day, and a hot northerly wind can be followed by a sudden cool change from the south-west, with a dramatic drop in temperature and gusty winds. Always carry an extra layer. At the end of the day, if the weather is warm, a swim in the bay is a fine way to cool off.
t.near williamstown@-37.9,144.9:
Williamstown was Melbourne's first port. Before the Yarra was dredged to allow ships to reach the city, vessels anchored off Point Gellibrand, at the mouth of the river, and the town that grew up there still has the feel of an old maritime settlement, with bluestone warehouses, pubs, churches and a timeball tower that once signalled the time to ships in the bay. Rides finish here on Hobsons Bay, off this historic waterfront, and it is a fine place to do so.

The Strand, along the waterfront, has views across the bay to the skyline of Melbourne, especially beautiful at sunset, when the towers glow and the lights come on. A former navy minesweeper, HMAS Castlemaine, is moored as a museum ship, and ferries run across the bay to the city. The beach, on the southern side of the peninsula, is popular in summer, with a long promenade and cafés.

To the north, the West Gate Bridge crosses the Yarra on a high span. During its construction in 1970, one of its sections collapsed, killing thirty-five workers, one of the worst industrial accidents in Australian history, and a memorial park stands beneath the bridge. Today the bridge carries heavy traffic between the western suburbs and the city.

The Yarra Valley ride that finishes here takes you north-east of Melbourne to the wine country of the Yarra Valley and over the Black Spur, a winding road through tall mountain ash forest, among the tallest flowering plants in the world. Coming back across the city, the Monash Freeway and the West Gate jam up readily, so plan your return for a quieter time. Williamstown has fuel, cafés, pubs and fish and chip shops, and eating fish and chips on the foreshore, looking at the city, is a classic Melbourne way to end the day.
t.near romsey on the way back@-37.4,144.7:
The Macedon Ranges rise abruptly from the plains north-west of Melbourne, a cluster of old volcanic hills covered in forests, gardens and farmland, and this stop is on their north-eastern side, near the small town of Romsey. Just to the west stands Hanging Rock, a jagged volcanic formation made famous by Joan Lindsay's novel Picnic at Hanging Rock and Peter Weir's 1975 film, about a group of schoolgirls who vanish during a picnic on Valentine's Day in 1900. The story is fiction, but the rock has an eerie atmosphere, and the walk to the top is worth it.

Mount Macedon, the highest point of the ranges, is crowned by a large memorial cross, and the slopes below are dotted with grand old gardens, laid out by wealthy Melbourne families in the late nineteenth century as summer retreats from the heat of the city. In autumn, the European trees in these gardens turn red and gold, a sight that draws visitors from all over Victoria. The region is also known for its cool-climate wines, especially sparkling wines and Pinot Noir.

Honesty about the swimming: this is not a land of beaches, and swimming spots are limited. There are reservoirs, but many are water supply catchments where swimming is not allowed. Some towns have public pools, and in summer the creeks have the odd pool, though they can be shallow and muddy. If you need a swim on a hot day, ask locally or consider a detour to a town pool.

On the way back to Melbourne from the Grampians, the roads through the Macedon Ranges are a pleasant alternative to the Calder Freeway, winding through forests and farmland, with good views. They can be narrow, with tight bends and wildlife, especially kangaroos at dawn and dusk. Romsey, Lancefield and Woodend have fuel, cafés and bakeries. The ranges are cooler and wetter than the plains, so bring a layer, even in summer.
t.near sunshine west@-37.8,144.8:
The suburb of Sunshine took its name from a harvester. In the early twentieth century, H. V. McKay built a huge factory here to manufacture the Sunshine Harvester, a machine that revolutionised wheat farming in Australia, and the suburb grew up around the works. In 1907, a court case involving McKay's company, known as the Harvester Judgment, established the principle of a basic wage, enough to support a worker and his family in reasonable comfort, a landmark in Australian labour history.

It is not a beautiful place, but it is a practical finish point for rides that have spent the day on the Great Ocean Road and in the Otways.

The Great Ocean Road, built by returned soldiers after the First World War and dedicated as a memorial to their fallen comrades, follows the coast west of Melbourne for more than two hundred kilometres, with cliffs, beaches, surf towns and rainforest. The Twelve Apostles, limestone stacks standing in the sea off Port Campbell, are its most famous sight, though there are fewer than twelve of them, and they keep collapsing. Inland, the Otway Ranges are covered in tall forests of eucalyptus, tree ferns and myrtle beech, with waterfalls and winding roads.

Coming back into Melbourne after a long day on the coast, the Princes Freeway is fast and busy, and traffic can be heavy on Sunday evenings. Sunshine West has fuel, supermarkets and takeaways on every arterial road, with food from Vietnam, Africa, the Middle East and southern Europe. Melbourne's weather can change quickly, so be prepared for anything from a heatwave to a cold southerly change.
t.saint leonards@-38.2,144.7:
Matthew Flinders, mapping Port Phillip in 1802, came ashore near Indented Head, a few kilometres up the coast from here, and climbed the hills to look over the bay. St Leonards is a quiet seaside town at the eastern tip of the Bellarine Peninsula, with a long pier, a sheltered beach and views across the water to the Mornington Peninsula and the distant towers of Melbourne.

The pier is the classic photo spot. At sunrise, the light comes across the bay and catches the old timber posts, and on clear days you can see the You Yangs to the north-west and Arthurs Seat across the water. The beach is calm and shallow, ideal for a paddle or a swim on a hot day.

The Bellarine is a pleasant landscape of rolling farmland, vineyards and coastal villages. Portarlington, up the coast, is famous for its mussels, grown on ropes in the bay, and has a festival in their honour. Queenscliff, at the tip of the peninsula, is a historic town with a fort, old hotels and a ferry across the Rip to Sorrento.

The riding on the Bellarine is gentle, with roads winding through farmland and along the coast. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and the roads into Geelong are busy. The wind off the bay can be strong.

There is a store and a café or two in town, enough for a quick coffee; for a full tank and more choice, Drysdale and Clifton Springs are a short ride inland. If the timing suits, keep the mussels for Portarlington, where they come out of the bay a few hundred metres from the plate.
t.sorrento@-38.3,144.7:
This is where Victoria began, briefly. In 1803 a British expedition under David Collins landed near Sorrento to found a settlement, but the site lacked water and the soil was poor, and after a few months they gave up and sailed to Tasmania. A small reserve marks the spot, with the graves of some of the settlers.

Sorrento sits near the tip of the Mornington Peninsula, between the calm waters of Port Phillip Bay on one side and the wild surf of Bass Strait on the other. The front beach, on the bay, is sheltered and shallow, ideal for swimming, while the back beach faces the ocean, with rock pools and big waves. The town itself is a holiday resort, with limestone buildings, cafés and galleries.

At the tip of the peninsula, Point Nepean National Park protects old forts and a quarantine station. In August 1914, a gun at Fort Nepean fired across the bow of a German ship trying to escape, the first Allied shot of the First World War. Nearby, at Cheviot Beach, Prime Minister Harold Holt disappeared while swimming in 1967, and his body was never found.

The ferry to Queenscliff crosses the Rip, the narrow, turbulent entrance to the bay, and on rough days it can be a lively ride. On the peninsula, the roads are winding and scenic, especially the climb to Arthurs Seat, with views over the bay.

Fuel is simpler in Rye or Blairgowrie than in Sorrento's busy main street. Once that is done, take fish and chips down to the front beach and eat them on the sand while the ferry noses out towards the Rip; seagulls will supervise.
t.near clifton springs@-38.1,144.5:
Clifton Springs looks north across Corio Bay, and on a clear afternoon the view is the reason to stop: the water in front, the industrial skyline of Geelong to the west, the granite bumps of the You Yangs rising out of the plain beyond, and on the best days the Melbourne towers far to the north-east. The town is part of the Bellarine Peninsula, a fist of farmland, vineyards and small seaside towns that closes off the western side of Port Phillip.

The name comes from the mineral springs at the foot of the cliffs, which drew day-trippers by steamer in the late nineteenth century when taking the waters was fashionable. The old jetty and the bluffs along the shore still give a hint of that era, and the shoreline walk is a decent leg-loosener.

As riding goes, the Bellarine is gentle. Roads roll between Drysdale, Portarlington and Queenscliff, with a few nice crests and open views but nothing technical. What you will notice is the wind, which comes hard off the bay and Bass Strait and can push a bike around on the exposed stretches. Summer weekends bring holiday traffic, caravans and families heading for the beaches; a weekday or a winter morning is a different, quieter world. Queenscliff, at the tip, has the ferry across the heads to Sorrento, a handy way to turn a ride into a loop around the bay.

Drysdale, a few minutes away, is the local service centre with fuel, a supermarket and bakeries, and Geelong covers anything larger. Local wineries on the peninsula open cellar doors, though of course that is for passengers or for later. Grab a coffee, look at the bay, and decide whether the next leg is the ferry or the long run west towards the Otways.
t.near wyndham vale@-38.0,144.6:
Wyndham Vale is one of the new suburbs on Melbourne's western fringe, where housing estates spread across the basalt plains towards Geelong. The landscape is flat, open and often windswept, with stone walls built by early settlers from the volcanic rock and low volcanic hills such as Mount Cottrell rising from the grassland. It is not the most scenic place on its own, but it is where the city releases you towards the coast and the Otways.

The plains have a quiet, stark beauty. Native grasslands once covered them, and remnants survive in reserves, with wildflowers in spring. Kangaroos can sometimes be seen at dawn on the edges of the estates. To the south lies Werribee, with its grand Werribee Park mansion, built in the 1870s by wealthy pastoralists, and the Open Range Zoo. To the west, the granite outcrops of the You Yangs rise from the plain, with tracks and lookouts popular with walkers and mountain bikers.

The riding here is mostly about getting somewhere. The Princes Freeway runs fast and straight towards Geelong, while minor roads cross the plains in long straights with few bends. Wind is the constant companion, gusting across the open land, and summer can bring scorching heat and fire risk. Traffic around the new estates can be heavy at peak hours.

Fuel, supermarkets and fast food are plentiful in Wyndham Vale and Werribee. For something better, head to Werribee or carry on towards Geelong. Beyond, the ride continues to the Great Ocean Road and the rainforests of the Otways, where the riding becomes far more rewarding. Take a break, drink plenty of water on hot days, and prepare for the curves ahead.
t.near bacchus marsh@-37.8,144.4:
Coming into Bacchus Marsh from the east, you ride through an arch of tall elms: the Avenue of Honour, planted after the First World War with a tree for each local man who enlisted. It is a moving entrance to a town that sits in a deep, fertile bowl where the Werribee and Lerderderg rivers meet, ringed by dry hills. The flats along the rivers have been orchards and market gardens since the nineteenth century, and roadside stalls still sell apples, pears and vegetables straight from the farms.

The landscape around the town is more dramatic than most of Melbourne's surroundings. To the west, the Werribee Gorge has been cut deep through ancient sedimentary rock, and to the north the Lerderderg Gorge winds into a rugged state park of eucalyptus forest. Kangaroos, wallabies and wedge-tailed eagles are common, and the gorges glow orange in the evening light.

For riders, the most interesting road is the climb west over the Pentland Hills towards Ballarat, where the Western Freeway rises steeply out of the bowl, offering wide views back over the town and the plains. The older roads through Myrniong and the hills to the north are slower and more fun, with tighter corners and quieter traffic. Summer brings heat and bushfire risk, and on days of total fire ban the hills can feel tense. Wind is a constant companion on the open ridges.

Bacchus Marsh has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, so it is an easy and pleasant place to stop. A coffee on the main street, a bag of local apples and a short walk under the elms make a satisfying break before heading west into the Grampians, a long ride away across the volcanic plains of western Victoria.
t.near woodend@-37.4,144.5:
Woodend is the gateway to the Macedon Ranges, a country town of old stone and weatherboard buildings, cool-climate gardens and excellent cafés, about an hour north-west of Melbourne. Its clock tower, a memorial to King Edward VII, stands at the main intersection, and the town has the slightly genteel air of a place where city people have long come to escape the summer heat.

The great attraction nearby is Hanging Rock, a volcanic formation of tumbled pinnacles rising out of the plain just north-east of town. It was made famous by the novel and film Picnic at Hanging Rock, and it remains a strange, atmospheric place with walking tracks up through the rocks. To the south, Mount Macedon rises higher, covered in forest and grand gardens, with the Memorial Cross on its summit.

The riding around here is excellent. The roads through the Macedon Ranges climb and wind through tall forest and open farmland, with tight bends on the mountain itself and faster sweepers on the country roads towards Kyneton, Lancefield and Daylesford. Surfaces vary from smooth to rough, and in winter the mountain can be frosty, foggy or even dusted with snow. Wildlife is common at dusk.

For food, Woodend is a strong choice, with bakeries, cafés and pubs along the main street serving everything from a quick pie to a long lunch. Fuel is available in town. The Calder Freeway runs past, making it easy to get here quickly from the city, but take the old roads out of town if you have time.
t.near trentham@-37.3,144.3:
Trentham is a small town on the Great Dividing Range, set high and cool among tall forest and potato paddocks between Daylesford and Woodend. Its main street has a handful of heritage buildings, a historic bakery and pub, and a quiet, unhurried charm that makes it a favourite stop for riders and weekenders alike.

The town grew in the gold rush era and later as a timber and farming centre. Just outside it, the Trentham Falls tumble over a basalt ledge into the Coliban River gorge, one of the longest single-drop falls in Victoria. A short walk from the car park brings you to the viewing platform, and after rain the falls are impressive. The surrounding Wombat State Forest stretches for miles, a mix of messmate, peppermint and manna gum, home to koalas, kangaroos and many birds.

The roads around Trentham are a pleasure. The run to Daylesford winds through forest with a mix of tight and open bends, and the routes towards Blackwood and Greendale dip into steep valleys. Surfaces can be rough and patched, with gravel at the edges, and the forest roads often stay damp in winter. At this altitude it can be much colder than Melbourne, and fog is common on autumn mornings.

As a start and finish, Trentham is perfect: quiet, scenic and with enough services for a coffee and a bite. Fuel options are limited in town, so it is worth topping up in Daylesford, Kyneton or Woodend. Take a photo by the falls or in the main street, and you have a memento of a quintessential Victorian highland village.
t.near gordon@-37.6,144.1:
Gordon is a small township on the old road between Melbourne and Ballarat, perched on the slopes of the Great Dividing Range. Like many places in this part of Victoria, it grew during the gold rush, when diggers and coaches streamed west towards the goldfields. Today it is a quiet village with a pub, a few shops and wide views over farmland and forest.

The landscape is open and rolling, with the Western Freeway running nearby and old volcanic hills dotting the horizon. To the north, the Lerderderg State Park protects a rugged gorge carved by the Lerderderg River, a surprisingly wild landscape so close to the city. To the west lies Ballarat, with its grand gold-rush architecture and Sovereign Hill.

For riding, the freeway gets you here quickly, but the real joy is in the back roads. The routes north through Blackwood and the Lerderderg area wind through forest and steep valleys, with tight corners and some rough sections. Heading towards Daylesford, you will find flowing roads through farmland and bush. Surfaces vary, and wildlife is common, so stay alert.

As a photo stop, Gordon offers big skies and an authentic slice of rural Victoria. Fuel is available in Ballarat and Bacchus Marsh, and there may be limited options in smaller towns, so plan accordingly. The local pub is a good place to rest and refuel the body before continuing your ride into the High Country or back towards Melbourne.
t.near point cook@-38.0,144.7:
Point Cook sits on the western shore of Port Phillip Bay, a fast-growing suburb on flat basalt plains between Werribee and Altona. The land here is open and windswept, with long views across the water to the city skyline. It is not a destination for twisty roads, but it has some surprising history.

RAAF Base Williams at Point Cook is regarded as the birthplace of the Royal Australian Air Force, and military flying began here in 1914. The RAAF Museum displays aircraft from the earliest days to the jet age and is worth a visit for anyone with an interest in aviation. Nearby, Point Cook Coastal Park and the Cheetham Wetlands protect saltmarsh, lagoons and a remarkable range of birdlife, including migratory shorebirds.

As a start and fuel stop, Point Cook is practical. There are plenty of service stations, cafés and shopping centres, and the Princes Freeway provides quick access west towards Geelong and the Great Ocean Road. Morning traffic can be heavy, especially heading towards the city, but the outbound direction is usually clear.

Wind is the main riding consideration here. The plains are exposed, and strong gusts off the bay can push a bike around, especially on the freeway. Once you head west towards the Otways, the landscape becomes more varied, with forests, hills and the coast offering some of Victoria's finest riding. Point Cook is the calm beginning of a big day.
t.near mickleham@-37.5,144.9:
North of Melbourne, the Hume Freeway runs up a long corridor of basalt plain, and Mickleham sits just off it, where old farming land is rapidly turning into new housing estates. Look past the roofs, though, and the older landscape is still there: stony paddocks, dry-stone walls built by early settlers, scattered red gums and the low volcanic cones that punctuate the plains.

Those stone walls are a quiet treasure. Many were laid in the nineteenth century from the basalt boulders cleared off the fields, and they still run for long distances across the paddocks north of the city. Mount Ridley, a gentle rise nearby, and the grasslands around it give a sense of what this volcanic country looked like before the suburbs arrived. Woodlands Historic Park, a short ride south near the airport, protects old red gums and grassy woodland where eastern grey kangaroos graze.

The riding through here is about connection. Mickleham Road and the routes north towards Kilmore and Wallan are mostly straight, with long sightlines and gentle undulations, and they lead towards hillier country around the Macedon Ranges and the Great Dividing Range. Traffic is growing fast, and trucks are common, so be patient at intersections. Wind across the plain can be strong and gusty.

There is little in Mickleham itself beyond the new estates, but fuel and food are easy to find in Craigieburn and along the Hume. Treat this stretch as a breather between the city and the hills, and enjoy the sense of space while it lasts.
t.greece mani peninsula route point 3@36.7:
Around Areopoli the Mani stops being a pleasant coastal road and starts to look like what it is: a rugged spur of limestone pushing south into the Mediterranean, with the high ridge of Taygetus behind and a dry, stony landscape in front. The soil is thin, the stone walls run in every direction, and the villages are clusters of grey towers that look more like a fortress than a home. Gytheio, the nearest sizeable town on the Laconian side, lies about nineteen kilometres away.

The Maniots have a reputation, and it has mostly been earned. For centuries they were a society of clans, each with its own tower house, who resisted Ottoman rule and fought each other with enthusiasm. Areopoli itself is named for Ares, the god of war, which tells you something. It was here, on 17 March in the old calendar, in 1821, that Petrobey Mavromichalis raised the banner of revolt, and the town square has the statue to prove it. The old quarter has narrow stone lanes, towers with tiny windows and a number of Byzantine churches decorated with frescoes, usually kept locked but sometimes opened by a caretaker if you ask politely.

Very close by are the Diros caves, a long system of underground passages with lakes and stalactites that you tour by boat. They are well worth the detour, especially on a hot afternoon when the cool damp of the cave feels like a gift. The surrounding coast is rocky and wild, with a few tiny harbours below the road, and the sea is a deep, startling blue.

The roads here are the kind a rider enjoys: relatively quiet, undulating, with a medley of sweeping bends and short climbs, and a surface that is usually decent though sometimes patched. In summer the sun is fierce and the wind can blow hard across the exposed ridges, so carry water and wear a proper layer. Gytheio is the safe bet for fuel and shops, and Areopoli lies on your route with cafés and a plain, honest feeling that suits a day in the saddle.
t.greece mani peninsula route point 4@36.5:
Further south the Mani gets harder and more beautiful in about equal measure. The southern part of the peninsula, often called the Deep Mani, is a thin finger of limestone with almost no trees, scrub in place of woodland, and a bare, silvery look in the afternoon light. The sea is always close, a bright band on either side, and the wind seldom drops. Gytheio, the only larger town in range, is more than thirty kilometres behind.

What makes the landscape unforgettable is the architecture. Tall stone towers, built by the Maniot clans from the seventeenth century onward, stand in groups on the hilltops, some ruined, some restored, with tiny windows and flat tops from which family feuds were once conducted. A few villages are nearly abandoned, and others have been brought back to life with a small guesthouse and a taverna. In between you pass little Byzantine chapels, whitewashed and low, often sitting in a field of rock with no other building in sight. The Maniots were never fully subdued by the Ottomans, and the sense of obstinate independence lingers.

For riding, it is a rewarding stretch if you like space and silence. The road runs along ridges and across saddles, with long clear views to both coasts, bends that tighten and open without fuss, and very little traffic outside the main holiday weeks. The surface can be rough in places, with the occasional pothole or patch of gravel where the verge collapses, so keep the pace sensible. Goats are common and unpredictable. In summer the heat is intense by midday, with little shade, so start early, carry water and finish by mid-afternoon.

Spring is the best time here, when the thin soil produces a rush of wildflowers and the air smells of sage and wild thyme. Autumn is nearly as good, with warm sea and clear light. For fuel and shopping, Gytheio is the safe place to plan around, with Areopoli on the way, and the villages along the route have the odd taverna worth a stop. Sit down, order something simple, and look at the towers.
t.greece mani peninsula route point 5@36.4:
The end of the line is a place with the name Taenaron, or Matapan in the older sea charts, the southernmost tip of mainland Greece. Few places in Europe feel so much like the edge of something. The land narrows to a spine of rock, scrub and wind, the sea opens to the south, and on a clear day the horizon seems to curve. There are no towns in range, only a handful of tiny settlements, so treat it as a place to reach prepared and unhurried.

In ancient times this was a sacred place. A temple to Poseidon stood near the cape, and there was a cave here that the Greeks believed was an entrance to the underworld, the place where Heracles was said to have dragged the hound Cerberus up into the light. Whether or not you believe that, the cave and the ruins exist and the mood is oddly fitting: bare rock, a restless sea and the feeling of being at a boundary. A lighthouse stands at the far end of the cape, reached on foot, and the walk across the rocky headland takes a bit of time, so wear proper footwear rather than riding boots with slick soles.

The ride toward the cape follows a road that gets quieter and narrower the further south it goes. The surface can be broken, with sand and gravel on the bends, and the wind can be strong enough to nudge a bike sideways on the exposed ridges. That is not a reason to avoid it, only to keep the speed down and to enjoy the sense of remoteness. Little coves along the way have clear, deep water, and the small harbour of Porto Kagio, with its tavernas on the shore, is a fine place to have lunch and look at the bay.

Plan your timing carefully. In summer the heat is severe by noon and there is almost no shade, so go early. Spring brings wildflowers and green slopes, and the light in October is gentle and golden. Fill the tank and your water bottles before you leave the larger towns of the Mani, and allow time for the walk, the view and the quiet before you turn back north.
t.gytheio@36.8,22.6:
Gytheio is where this ride ends, and it is a good place to arrive: a small harbour town on the Laconian Gulf, with colourful neoclassical houses along the waterfront, fishing boats tied up in a row, and tavernas where the octopus hangs drying in the sun. About four thousand people live here, so there is fuel, a market and a choice of places to sleep, and Sparta, the nearest larger town, lies about thirty-seven kilometres inland.

In ancient times this was Gythion, the port of Sparta, and it kept the Spartan fleet. The shore holds the remains of a Roman theatre, and just offshore, linked to the mainland by a causeway, lies the islet of Marathonisi. Homer's Iliad has Paris and Helen stopping on an island called Kranae after leaving Sparta, and local tradition identifies Marathonisi with it. On the islet stands a stone tower, built in the 18th century in the sturdy style of the Mani, a reminder that this region was proud, clannish and used to defending itself.

The Mani Peninsula is the rugged southern finger of the Peloponnese, a country of grey limestone, tall stone tower houses and little settlements strung along the coastal roads. The riding here is characterful rather than fast: tight bends, narrow villages, surfaces that can be rough, and views over bare hills and an open sea. Goats, small trucks and cyclists share the road, so allow time. Come in spring, when wildflowers soften the rock, or autumn, when the heat has eased and the sea is still warm.

In the evening, find a table on the waterfront, order grilled fish or something from the nearby sea, and watch the lights come on across the bay. Ferries run from here to the island of Kythira, and the harbour has a working feel that never quite turns into a resort. After a long day over rocky roads, there are worse places to park the bike, sit down, and let the salt air and the sound of the boats do the rest.
t.monodendri@39.9,20.8:
Monodendri is a stone village on the rim of the Vikos Gorge, in the Zagori region of Epirus in north-western Greece, and the first thing you notice is how everything is built from the same grey-gold stone: houses, cobbled lanes, walls and slate roofs. Zagori is a cluster of around forty-odd villages, and in Ottoman times they enjoyed unusual privileges and autonomy, so merchants grew rich and built grand houses, churches and the arched stone bridges that cross the rivers. Paved mule paths, called kalderimia, still link many of them.

At the edge of the village a path leads to the Monastery of Agia Paraskevi, a small whitewashed chapel set right on the cliff, with a drop below that makes you step carefully. Further along, the viewpoint known as Oxya looks across the Vikos Gorge, which is often described as one of the deepest in the world relative to its width. The Voidomatis river runs along the bottom, and on a clear day the opposite walls glow in the afternoon light, with eagles and griffon vultures riding the air.

The road here is the kind that rewards a careful rider. It climbs from the plain near Ioannina through oak and plane forest, twisting up in narrow, sometimes rough bends, with little shoulder and occasional rockfall or loose gravel. Traffic is light, and often the only thing you meet is a local van or a flock of sheep. Early summer and autumn are lovely, while winter brings cold, snow at altitude and the risk of ice, so check the forecast before you commit to the heights.

Fuel is not something to gamble on in these villages. The nearest big town is Ioannina, roughly twenty-four kilometres away, with the bigger lake city offering everything you could need, so fill up there before heading into the mountains. In the village, small guesthouses and tavernas serve pies, mountain greens, local cheese and sturdy red wine, all in a setting where the main sound after dark is a distant river. Allow time to wander on foot, since this is a place to look closely.
t.abashiri@44.0,144.3:
Abashiri is a port town on the Okhotsk Sea coast of north-eastern Hokkaido, and its fame rests on two things: ice and a prison. From about late January to March, drift ice from the Amur river region far to the north arrives on the current and fills the sea, and boats take visitors out through the floes in a ship with a reinforced bow. The sea goes quiet, white and creaking, a landscape that feels like the edge of the world.

The prison belongs to the late nineteenth century. When Hokkaido was being opened up by the Meiji government, convicts were used as labour to build roads and railways, and Abashiri became one of the harshest places they were sent. The old wooden buildings now serve as a museum, and a modern prison still operates nearby. It adds a sombre note to a town otherwise known for seafood, with crab, scallops and salmon roe on every menu, and for the lakes on the doorstep, Lake Abashiri and the wide, shallow Lake Notoro.

About forty-two thousand people live here, so fuel, shops and a good choice of places to eat and sleep are close, which is why it works so well as the beginning of a ride east to the Shiretoko Peninsula. The roads leading out of town run across broad plains with potato and beet fields, long straights and gentle bends, and the pace is relaxed. Distances here are large, and the sea breeze can be strong, so gusts and cool temperatures should be expected even in summer.

The best season is summer, when wildflowers run along the coast, especially in the coastal meadows of the Okhotsk, and the light is long. September offers clear air and fewer riders, while winter belongs to those prepared for ice and snow. Before heading east, take a few minutes at the harbour, check the weather for the peninsula, and eat something substantial, because the next stretch of the route runs into wilder country.
t.near bacchus marsh@-37.8,144.3:
Coming into Bacchus Marsh from the east, you ride through an arch of tall elms: the Avenue of Honour, planted after the First World War with a tree for each local man who enlisted. It is a moving entrance to a town that sits in a deep, fertile bowl where the Werribee and Lerderderg rivers meet, ringed by dry hills. The flats along the rivers have been orchards and market gardens since the nineteenth century, and roadside stalls still sell apples, pears and vegetables straight from the farms.

The landscape around the town is more dramatic than most of Melbourne's surroundings. To the west, the Werribee Gorge has been cut deep through ancient sedimentary rock, and to the north the Lerderderg Gorge winds into a rugged state park of eucalyptus forest. Kangaroos, wallabies and wedge-tailed eagles are common, and the gorges glow orange in the evening light.

For riders, the most interesting road is the climb west over the Pentland Hills towards Ballarat, where the Western Freeway rises steeply out of the bowl, offering wide views back over the town and the plains. The older roads through Myrniong and the hills to the north are slower and more fun, with tighter corners and quieter traffic. Summer brings heat and bushfire risk, and on days of total fire ban the hills can feel tense. Wind is a constant companion on the open ridges.

Bacchus Marsh has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, so it is an easy and pleasant place to stop. A coffee on the main street, a bag of local apples and a short walk under the elms make a satisfying break before heading west into the Grampians, a long ride away across the volcanic plains of western Victoria.
t.furano@43.4,142.4:
Furano lies in the middle of Hokkaido, in a basin ringed by the Tokachi mountains and the Yubari range, and it is known for lavender. The fields of Farm Tomita and the surrounding farms turn purple in July, and visitors come from across Japan to see them. The climate here is continental, with hot summers and cold, snowy winters, and the long hours of summer light let farmers grow lavender, melons, potatoes and onions. The town is small, and the settlement of Shimo-furano is right beside it, while Ashibetsu, a former coal town, lies thirty kilometres or so away.

The landscape is different from the rest of Japan. Fields stretch in tidy patches of colour, which gives the road its patchwork name, hedged by lines of poplars and set against the dark volcanic profile of Mount Tokachi in the distance. The roads are straight and gently rolling, with the occasional curve around a hill, and the surface is generally excellent. Hokkaido is a favourite with touring riders because of the space and the low traffic, and in summer there are many bikers on the island. Watch for deer, foxes and the occasional bear, though sightings near the main roads are rare.

Hokkaido was settled by Japanese farmers mainly in the late nineteenth century, and before that the island was the land of the Ainu people, whose language gave many places their names. Furano itself comes from the Ainu word for stinky, probably for a smelly river. The food is excellent: dairy products, sweet corn, melons and Furano wine, plus the soup curry that Sapporo made famous, and ramen with butter and corn.

For practical matters, Furano has fuel stations, convenience stores and many cafes. In July, lavender season brings crowds, and accommodation books up, so reserve ahead. Alternatively, go in June for fresh green fields, or in September for harvest and clear air. In winter the town becomes a ski resort, with powder snow that is famous among skiers. Early evening light on the fields is soft and golden, and it is a lovely time for a final slow ride.
t.near kilmore on the way back@-37.2,144.9:
Kilmore has a fair claim to be the oldest inland town in Victoria, and the stone buildings along its main street back it up. It sits in a gap in the Great Dividing Range, a natural passage that the early overlanders used on the road between Melbourne and the Murray, and the Hume Highway still slips through here today. This stop lies a little south of the town, in sheep and cattle country between Kilmore, Broadford and Lancefield, where the land rolls in broad folds of yellow-brown grass and dark clumps of gum trees.

The area has known hard times. In February 2009 the bushfires of Black Saturday started near Kilmore East and swept through the hills to the north and east, and the scars on the landscape and in the community are still part of the local story. The regrowth is lush now, but locals remember, and you will see memorials and signs of the recovery as you ride. In summer, the fire risk remains real, and on days of extreme fire danger, riding in the forest is a poor idea.

Lancefield, to the west, has a different claim to fame. A swamp near the town produced one of the richest deposits of ice age animal bones in Victoria, including those of giant kangaroos and wombat-like creatures, and the find gave scientists a window into the megafauna that once roamed here. Today the town is a quiet place with a handsome bluestone hotel and a few cafes, a pleasant stop on a Sunday ride.

For fuel and supplies, Kilmore, with nearly eight thousand people, has petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a good selection of pubs. Broadford is smaller but has the basics, and Lancefield has a general store. The riding here is mostly easy, with long bends and gentle hills, and a good surface on the main roads. Early morning, when mist lies in the hollows and the paddocks glisten with dew, is the best time to be on the road. Expect kangaroos in the evening and be generous with your braking distance.
t.near saint leonards@-38.2,144.8:
Matthew Flinders, mapping Port Phillip in 1802, came ashore near Indented Head, a few kilometres up the coast from here, and climbed the hills to look over the bay. St Leonards is a quiet seaside town at the eastern tip of the Bellarine Peninsula, with a long pier, a sheltered beach and views across the water to the Mornington Peninsula and the distant towers of Melbourne.

The pier is the classic photo spot. At sunrise, the light comes across the bay and catches the old timber posts, and on clear days you can see the You Yangs to the north-west and Arthurs Seat across the water. The beach is calm and shallow, ideal for a paddle or a swim on a hot day.

The Bellarine is a pleasant landscape of rolling farmland, vineyards and coastal villages. Portarlington, up the coast, is famous for its mussels, grown on ropes in the bay, and has a festival in their honour. Queenscliff, at the tip of the peninsula, is a historic town with a fort, old hotels and a ferry across the Rip to Sorrento.

The riding on the Bellarine is gentle, with roads winding through farmland and along the coast. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and the roads into Geelong are busy. The wind off the bay can be strong.

There is a store and a café or two in town, enough for a quick coffee; for a full tank and more choice, Drysdale and Clifton Springs are a short ride inland. If the timing suits, keep the mussels for Portarlington, where they come out of the bay a few hundred metres from the plate.
t.near metsovo@39.8,21.1:
Metsovo is a stone mountain town in the Pindus, about a thousand metres up, and it has a character of its own, thanks largely to its people. Many of the inhabitants are Vlachs, also called Aromanians, a community with its own Latin-derived language and a history as shepherds, traders and craftsmen who moved with their flocks across the Balkans. The town has long been prosperous, thanks to the patronage of wealthy benefactors, and the stone mansions with their wooden balconies and slate roofs speak of confidence. On weekends, the older residents still wear traditional dress, and you may hear Vlach spoken in the street.

The town sits on a steep hillside above a deep gorge, with the high Pindus ridges all around, covered in beech, fir and black pine. Metsovo is known for its smoked cheese, Metsovone, a firm, sharp cheese with a smoky flavour, and for its red wine, Katogi, made from local grapes and Cabernet Sauvignon grown on the slopes. The Tositsa and Averoff families, benefactors who made fortunes abroad, built museums, schools and a gallery in the town, and the folk museum, in a restored mansion, shows how a wealthy Vlach family lived. The Averoff Gallery holds a collection of nineteenth- and twentieth-century Greek painting.

The old road to Ioannina, the national road over the Katara Pass, climbs from Metsovo toward the high pass, and a motorway tunnel, built as part of the Egnatia Odos, now takes most of the heavy traffic under the mountain, which makes the old road quiet and pleasant for riders. The corners are broad, the surface is generally good, and the views over the forested slopes are lovely. Winters are cold and snowy, and the roads may need chains, while summers are cool and fresh, and spring and autumn are the best seasons for colour, particularly the red and gold of autumn beech woods.

Metsovo is a real town, with a population of a few thousand, and has what a rider needs. Fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and tavernas line the main road, and there are plenty of small hotels and guesthouses. Ioannina, about thirty-one kilometres to the west, is a much larger city with all services. The food here is hearty mountain fare, with grilled meats, pies filled with greens or cheese, and a hot dish of trahana soup in the cold weather. A glass of Katogi and a plate of smoked cheese in the evening is the proper reward.
